<!-- thm-1: body_md -->
\label{thm Radon-Nikodym derivative for the transported measures}
    Let $s > \frac{3}{2}$ and  $\sigma< s-\frac{1}{2}$ close enough to $s-\frac{1}{2}$. Let $t \in \mathbb{R}$. Then, for every $N \in \mathbb{N}$, the transported measure $\Phi_N(t)_\# \mu_s$ has a density $G_{s,N}(t,.)$ with respect to $\mu_s$ given by:
    \begin{equation*}
        \begin{split}
        G_{s,N}(t,u) &= \textnormal{exp}\big( -\frac{1}{2}( 
\left\lVert \Pi_N \Phi_N(-t)u \right\rVert 
_{H^s}^2-  
\left\lVert \Pi_N u \right\rVert 
_{H^s}^2) \big) \\
        &= \textnormal{exp} \left(R_{s,N}(\Phi_N(-t)u) - R_{s,N}(u)-\int_0^{-t} Q_{s,N}(\Phi_N(\tau)u)d\tau \right) 
        \end{split}
    \end{equation*}
    Moreover, the transported measure $\Phi(t)_\# \mu_s$ has a density $G_{s}(t,.)$ with respect to $\mu_s$ given by:
    \begin{equation*}
        G_s(t,u) = \textnormal{exp} \left(R_{s}(\Phi(-t)u) - R_{s}(u)-\int_0^{-t} Q_{s}(\Phi(\tau)u)d\tau \right)
    \end{equation*}
    which is continuous on $H^{\sigma}(\mathbb{T})$. In addition, the densities $G_{s,N}(t,.)$ converge to $G_s(t,.)$ uniformly on compact sets of $H^{\sigma}(\mathbb{T})$.
<!-- end thm-1 -->
<!-- cor-1: body_md -->
\label{cor mu_s quasi-invariant}
    Let $s > \frac{3}{2}$. Then, the Gaussian measure $\mu_s$ is quasi-invariant along the flow of \eqref{NLS}.
<!-- end cor-1 -->
<!-- thm-2: body_md -->
\label{thm density in L^p wrt mu_s,R}
    Let $s>\frac{3}{2}$ and $R>0$. Let $t\in \mathbb{R}$. Then, for every $N\in \mathbb{N}$:
\begin{align*}
     \Phi_N(t)_\#\mu_{s,R} &= G_{s,N}(t,u) d\mu_{s,R} & &\text{and,} & \Phi(t)_\#\mu_{s,R} &= G_{s}(t,u) d\mu_{s,R}
\end{align*}
Moreover, the densities $G_{s,N}(t,.)$, $G_s(t,.)$ belongs to $\mathbb{L}^p(d\mu_{s,R})$; and $G_{s,N}$ converge to $G_s(t,.)$ in $\mathbb{L}^p(d\mu_{s,R})$.
<!-- end thm-2 -->
<!-- rem-1: body_md -->
In our approach, we view the difference $ 
\left\lVert \Phi(t)u \right\rVert 
_{H^s}^2-  
\left\lVert u \right\rVert 
_{H^s}^2$ as the limit of continuous functions on $ H^{\sigma}(\mathbb{T})$, with $\sigma < s-\frac{1}{2}$ close enough to $s-\frac{1}{2}$. An alternative to give a meaning to this quantity (for $u \in H^{\sigma}(\mathbb{T})$) could have been to use a \textit{nonlinear smoothing} for the solutions of \eqref{NLS}. In the context of this paper, with $s>\frac{3}{2}$, the result in Theorem 1 from the interesting work \cite{mcconnell_nonlin_smoothing} implies that for  $\sigma < s-\frac{1}{2}$ (close enough to $s-\frac{1}{2}$), we have the following nonlinear smoothing (for $u \in H^{\sigma}(\mathbb{T})$):
    \begin{equation*}
       v(t) := \Phi(t)u - e^{it\partial_x^2} e^{-i\frac{3}{2\pi} \int_0^t  
\left\lVert \Phi(\tau)u \right\rVert 
_{\mathbb{L}^4}^4 d\tau} u \in \mathcal C([-T,T]; H^{\sigma + 1-\varepsilon}(\mathbb{T}))
    \end{equation*}
    for $0<\varepsilon < 1$, and at least for small time $T>0$.
    Hence, we could have tried to define the difference $ 
\left\lVert \Phi(t)u \right\rVert 
_{H^s}^2-  
\left\lVert u \right\rVert 
_{H^s}^2$ as :
    \begin{equation*}
         
\left\lVert \Phi(t)u \right\rVert 
_{H^s}^2-  
\left\lVert u \right\rVert 
_{H^s}^2 :=  
\left\lVert v(t) \right\rVert 
_{H^s}^2 + 2 \textnormal{Re} \bigl \langle \langle \nabla \rangle^{2s - \sigma} v(t),  \langle \nabla \rangle^\sigma \big(e^{it\partial_x^2} e^{-i\frac{3}{2\pi} \int_0^t  
\left\lVert \Phi(\tau)u \right\rVert 
_{\mathbb{L}^4}^4 d\tau} u\big) \bigr \rangle_{\mathbb{L}^2(\mathbb{T})}
    \end{equation*}
    since this formula is true when $u$ is smooth (with $\langle.,. \rangle_{\mathbb{L}^2(\mathbb{T})}$ the $\mathbb{L}^2(\mathbb{T})$-scalar product). With $\varepsilon$ close to 0, the $1-\varepsilon$ gain of regularity in the smoothing above implies that for $u \in H^{\sigma}(\mathbb{T})$, $ 
\left\lVert v(t) \right\rVert 
_{H^s(\mathbb{T})}^2<+\infty$ because $\sigma+1-\varepsilon$ is close to $s+\frac{1}{2}>s$. However, this smoothing is not enough to define the term $\langle \nabla \rangle^{2s-\sigma}v(t)$ because $\sigma + 1 - \varepsilon < 2s-\sigma$, no matter how close $\varepsilon$ and $\sigma$ are close to 0 and $s-\frac{1}{2}$ respectively. For  $\langle \nabla \rangle^{2s-\sigma}v(t)$ to be well-defined, we need a gain of $1+ \varepsilon'$ regularity, where $\varepsilon'>0$.
<!-- end rem-1 -->
<!-- rem-2: body_md -->
In this paper, we deal with the defocusing NLS, but it would have also been possible to consider the focusing NLS. However, in the focusing case, we would have needed an additional cut-off on small $\mathbb{L}^2(\mathbb{T})$-initial data, ensuring that the flow of \eqref{NLS} is global and a control on the $H^1(\mathbb{T})$-norm of the solutions.
<!-- end rem-2 -->
<!-- defns-1: body_md -->
\label{def normal form R and E}
    Let $N \in \mathbb{N}$. 
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item For $u \in \mathcal S'(\mathbb{T})$, we define:
    \begin{equation}
    R_{s,N}(u) := \frac{1}{6} \textnormal{Im} \sum_{\substack{k_1-k_2+...-k_6=0 \\ \Omega(\vec{k}) \neq 0}} \frac{\psi_{2s}(\vec{k})}{-i \Omega(\vec{k})} \left( \prod_{j=1}^6 \mathds{1}_{|k_j|\leq N}\right) u_{k_1} 
  \overline{u_{k_2}} 
  ... 
  \overline{u_{k_6}} 
  
\end{equation} and,
\begin{equation}\label{modified energy}
   E_{s,N}(u) := \frac{1}{2} {\left\vert\kern-0.25ex\left\vert\kern-0.25ex\left\vert \Pi_N u 
    \right\vert\kern-0.25ex\right\vert\kern-0.25ex\right\vert}_{H^s(\mathbb{T})}^2 + R_{s,N}(u)
\end{equation}
    \item For $u \in \mathcal C^{\infty}(\mathbb{T})$, we define:
    \begin{equation}\label{Rs,infty}
    R_{s,\infty}(u) := \frac{1}{6} \textnormal{Im} \sum_{\substack{k_1-k_2+...-k_6=0 \\ \Omega(\vec{k}) \neq 0}} \frac{\psi_{2s}(\vec{k})}{-i \Omega(\vec{k})}u_{k_1} 
  \overline{u_{k_2}} 
  ... 
  \overline{u_{k_6}} 
  
\end{equation}
and,
\begin{equation}
    E_{s,\infty} := \frac{1}{2}{\left\vert\kern-0.25ex\left\vert\kern-0.25ex\left\vert u 
    \right\vert\kern-0.25ex\right\vert\kern-0.25ex\right\vert}_{H^s(\mathbb{T})}^2 + R_{s,\infty}(u)
\end{equation}
    \end{enumerate}
For $N \in \mathbb{N} \cup \{ \infty \}$, $R_{s,N}$ and $E_{s,N}$ are respectively called the \textit{energy correction} and the \textit{modified energy}. Moreover, we will use interchangeably the notation $R_s$ and $E_s$ to refer respectively to $R_{s,\infty}$ and $E_{s,\infty}$.
<!-- end defns-1 -->
<!-- rem-3: body_md -->
In Section \ref{section Deterministic properties of the energy correction} (in Proposition \ref{prop R_s,N continuous}), we will see that for $s>\frac{3}{2}$ and $\sigma< s-\frac{1}{2}$ close enough to $s-\frac{3}{2}$, we can extend $R_s$ to $H^{\sigma}(\mathbb{T})$, because we will be able to prove that the sum in \eqref{Rs,infty} is absolutely convergent for every $u \in H^{\sigma}(\mathbb{T})$.
<!-- end rem-3 -->
<!-- defns-2: body_md -->
\label{def normal form Q} Let $N \in \mathbb{N}$. Let $\Phi_N(t)$ the flow of \eqref{truncated equation}. \\
\begin{enumerate}
    \item For $u \in \mathcal S'(\mathbb{T})$, we define:
    \begin{equation*}\label{def Qs,N in the normal form}
        Q_{s,N}(u) :=  \frac{d}{dt} E_{s,N}(\Pi_N \Phi_N(t)u) |_{t=0} = \text{(RHS)}|_{t=0} \hspace{0.1cm} \text{of \eqref{time derivative modified energy}}
    \end{equation*}
    \item For $u \in \mathcal C^{\infty}(\mathbb{T})$, we define:
    \begin{equation}\label{def Qs,infty normal form}
    \begin{split}
       Q_{s,\infty}(u) & := \text{(RHS)}|_{t=0} \hspace{0.1cm} \text{of \eqref{time derivative modified energy} with $N=\infty$} \\
       & = -\frac{1}{6} \textnormal{Im} \sum_{\substack{k_1-k_2+...-k_6=0 \\ \Omega(\vec{k}) = 0}} \psi_{2s}(\vec{k})u_{k_1} 
  \overline{u_{k_2}} 
  ... 
  \overline{u_{k_6}} 
   +\frac{1}{2} \textnormal{Im} \sum_{\substack{k_1-k_2+...-k_6=0 \\ p_1-p_2+...+p_5 =k_1 \\\Omega(\vec{k}) \neq 0}} \frac{\psi_{2s}(\vec{k})}{ \Omega(\vec{k})} u_{p_1} 
  \overline{u_{p_2}} 
  ...u_{p_5} 
  \overline{u_{k_2}} 
  ...  
  \overline{u_{k_6}} 
   \\ 
        & -\frac{1}{2} \textnormal{Im} \sum_{\substack{k_1-k_2+...-k_6=0 \\ q_1-q_2+...+q_5 =k_2 \\\Omega(\vec{k}) \neq 0}} \frac{\psi_{2s}(\vec{k})}{ \Omega(\vec{k})} u_{k_1} 
  \overline{u_{q_1}} 
  u_{q_2}... 
  \overline{u_{q_5}} 
  u_{k_3}...  
  \overline{u_{k_6}} 
   
    \end{split}
\end{equation}
\end{enumerate}
   For $N\in \mathbb{N} \cup \{ \infty \}$, $Q_{s,N}$ is called the \textit{derivative of the modified energy at 0}. Moreover, we will use interchangeably the notation $Q_s$ to refer to $Q_{s,\infty}$.
<!-- end defns-2 -->
<!-- rem-4: body_md -->
For $N \in \mathbb{N}$, note that from the additivity of the flow we have:
    \begin{equation}\label{Qs,N(phi_N(t)u)}
    \begin{split}
    Q_{s,N}(\Phi_N(\tau)u) = \frac{d}{dt} E_{s,N}\left( \Pi_N \Phi_N(t)\Phi_N(\tau)u \right) |_{t=0} &= \frac{d}{dt} E_{s,N}\left( \Pi_N \Phi_N(t+\tau)u \right) |_{t=0} \\
    &= \frac{d}{dt} E_{s,N}\left( \Pi_N \Phi_N(t)u \right) |_{t=\tau}
    \end{split}
\end{equation}
<!-- end rem-4 -->
<!-- rem-5: body_md -->
In Section \ref{section the modified energy derivative at 0} (in Proposition \ref{prop continuity of Qs,N and deterministic estimate}), we will see that for $s>\frac{3}{2}$ and $\sigma< s-\frac{1}{2}$ close enough to $s-\frac{1}{2}$, we can extend $Q_s$ to $H^{\sigma}(\mathbb{T})$, because we will be able to prove that the sum in \eqref{def Qs,infty normal form} is absolutely convergent for every $u \in H^{\sigma}(\mathbb{T})$.
<!-- end rem-5 -->
<!-- prop-1: body_md -->
\label{prop R_s,N continuous}
    Let $s>\frac{3}{2}$. For $\sigma < s - \frac{1}{2}$ close enough to $s-\frac{1}{2}$, there exists a constant $C>0$ such that for every $u^{(1)},...,u^{(6)} \in H^{\sigma}(\mathbb{T})$ :
    \begin{equation}\label{energy correction with absolute value}
        \sum_{\substack{k_1-k_2+...-k_6=0 \\ \Omega(\vec{k}) \neq 0}} \big| \frac{\psi_{2s}(\vec{k})}{\Omega(\vec{k})} \big| \big|u^{(1)}_{k_1} 
  \overline{u^{(2)}_{k_2}} 
  ... 
  \overline{u^{(6)}_{k_6}} 
   \big| \leq C \prod_{j=1}^6   
\left\lVert u^{(j)} \right\rVert_{H^{\sigma}}  

    \end{equation}
    Hence, the map:
    \begin{equation*}
        \begin{array}{cccc} \mathcal R : & H^{\sigma}(\mathbb{T})^6 & \longrightarrow & \mathbb{C} \\ & (u^{(1)},...,u^{(6)}) & \longmapsto & \mathlarger{\sum \limits_{\substack{k_1-k_2+...-k_6=0 \\ \Omega(\vec{k}) \neq 0}} \frac{\psi_{2s}(\vec{k})}{\Omega(\vec{k})}u^{(1)}_{k_1} 
  \overline{u^{(2)}_{k_2}} 
  ... 
  \overline{u^{(6)}_{k_6}} 
  } \end{array}
    \end{equation*}
    is a continuous multi-linear form.
    Then, for $N \in \mathbb{N} \cup \{ \infty \}$\footnote{Using the notation $\Pi_{\infty} = id $}, setting \footnote{By abuse of notation, we still denote by $R_{s,N}$ this new function, even though it has already been defined in Definition~\ref{def normal form R and E}. The $R_{s,N}$ of Definition~\ref{def normal form R and E} and the $R_{s,N}$ of this proposition coincide on $\mathcal C^{\infty}(\mathbb{T})$.}:
    \begin{equation}\label{R_s,N diag multilinear form}
        \begin{array}{cccc} R_{s,N} : & H^{\sigma}(\mathbb{T}) & \longrightarrow & \mathbb{C} \\ & u & \longmapsto & \frac{1}{6} \textnormal{Re} \hspace{0.1cm} \mathcal R(\Pi_N u,...,\Pi_N u) \end{array},
    \end{equation}
    we deduce that $R_{s,N}$ is a continuous map on $H^{\sigma}(\mathbb{T})$ that satisfies for all $u,v \in H^{\sigma}(\mathbb{T})$:
    \begin{equation*}
        \left| R_{s,N}(u)- R_{s,N}(v) \right| \leq C   
\left\lVert u-v \right\rVert_{H^{\sigma}}  
 (  
\left\lVert u \right\rVert_{H^{\sigma}}  
^5 +   
\left\lVert v \right\rVert_{H^{\sigma}}  
^5)
    \end{equation*}
    uniformly in $N \in \mathbb{N} \cup \{ \infty \}$.
<!-- end prop-1 -->
<!-- notn-1: body_md -->
We also use the notation $R_s$ to refer  to $R_{s,\infty}$.
<!-- end notn-1 -->
<!-- prop-2: body_md -->
\label{prop approx R_s by R_s,N on compact sets}
    Let $s>\frac{3}{2}$. Let $\sigma < s-\frac{1}{2}$ close enough to $s-\frac{1}{2}$ so that the conclusion of Proposition \ref{prop R_s,N continuous} holds. Then, for every compact set $K \subset H^{\sigma}(\mathbb{T})$,
    \begin{equation*}
        \sup_{u\in K} \left| R_s(u)-R_{s,N}(u) \right|  
\underset{N \rightarrow \infty}{\longrightarrow} 
 0
    \end{equation*}
    In other words, $R_{s,N}$ converges to $R_s$ uniformly on compact sets of $H^{\sigma}(\mathbb{T})$.
<!-- end prop-2 -->
<!-- proof-1: body_md -->
Here we assume the statements in Proposition~\ref{prop R_s,N continuous}. Thus, we invoke $\sigma<s-\frac{1}{2}$ close enough to $s-\frac{1}{2}$ along with the constant $C > 0$ from this proposition. Next, we observe that for all $N \in \mathbb{N}$:
    \begin{equation*}
        R_{s}(u) - R_{s,N}(u) = R_s(\Pi_N^{\perp}u)
    \end{equation*}
    Then, it follows from Proposition~\ref{prop R_s,N continuous} that:
    \begin{equation*}
        |R_{s}(u) - R_{s,N}(u)| = |R_s(\Pi_N^{\perp}u)| \leq C   
\left\lVert \Pi_N^{\perp}u \right\rVert_{H^{\sigma}}  
^6
    \end{equation*}
    On the other hand, we have that for every $u \in H^{\sigma}$, $ 
\left\lVert \Pi_N^\perp u \right\rVert 
_{H^{\sigma}}  
\underset{N\rightarrow \infty}{\longrightarrow} 
 0$ and $ 
\left\lVert \Pi_N^\perp \right\rVert 
_{H^{\sigma} \rightarrow H^{\sigma}} \leq 1$. So, using the following general abstract lemma in the inequality above finishes the proof:
    \begin{lem}\label{lem cvgce on compact set of bdd lin map}
        Let $E,F$ two Banach spaces. Let $\{ T_N\}_{N \in \mathbb{N}}$ be a sequence of bounded linear maps with the uniform (in $N \in \mathbb{N}$) bound $ 
\left\lVert T_N \right\rVert 
_{E \rightarrow F} \leq M$, for some constant $M>0$. If for every $u \in E$:
        \begin{equation*}
            
\left\lVert T(u)-T_N(u) \right\rVert 
_F  
\underset{N \rightarrow \infty}{\longrightarrow} 
 0
        \end{equation*}
        for some linear map $T : E \rightarrow F$, then for every compact set $K \subset E$, we have:
        \begin{equation*}
            \sup_{u \in K}  
\left\lVert T(u)-T_N(u) \right\rVert 
_F  
\underset{N \rightarrow \infty}{\longrightarrow} 
 0
        \end{equation*}
    \end{lem}
<!-- end proof-1 -->
<!-- lem-1: body_md -->
\label{lem cvgce on compact set of bdd lin map}
        Let $E,F$ two Banach spaces. Let $\{ T_N\}_{N \in \mathbb{N}}$ be a sequence of bounded linear maps with the uniform (in $N \in \mathbb{N}$) bound $ 
\left\lVert T_N \right\rVert 
_{E \rightarrow F} \leq M$, for some constant $M>0$. If for every $u \in E$:
        \begin{equation*}
            
\left\lVert T(u)-T_N(u) \right\rVert 
_F  
\underset{N \rightarrow \infty}{\longrightarrow} 
 0
        \end{equation*}
        for some linear map $T : E \rightarrow F$, then for every compact set $K \subset E$, we have:
        \begin{equation*}
            \sup_{u \in K}  
\left\lVert T(u)-T_N(u) \right\rVert 
_F  
\underset{N \rightarrow \infty}{\longrightarrow} 
 0
        \end{equation*}
<!-- end lem-1 -->
<!-- prop-3: body_md -->
\label{prop continuity of Qs,N and deterministic estimate}
    Let $s>\frac{3}{2}$. For $\sigma < s - \frac{1}{2}$ close enough to $s-\frac{1}{2}$, there exists a constant $C>0$ such that for every $u^{(1)},...,u^{(6)},v^{(1)},...,v^{(5)} \in H^{\sigma}(\mathbb{T})$ : 
    \begin{equation}\label{T0 with abs value}
        \sum_{\substack{k_1-k_2+...-k_6=0 \\ \Omega(\vec{k}) = 0}} \big| \psi_{2s}(\vec{k}) \big| \big| u^{(1)}_{k_1} 
  \overline{u^{(2)}_{k_2}} 
  ... 
  \overline{u^{(6)}_{k_6}} 
   \big| \leq C \prod_{j=1}^6  
\left\lVert u^{(j)} \right\rVert 
_{H^{\sigma}}
    \end{equation}
    and,
    \begin{equation}\label{T1 with abs value}
        \sum_{\substack{k_1-k_2+...-k_6=0 \\ p_1-p_2+...+p_5 =k_1 \\\Omega(\vec{k}) \neq 0}} \big|\frac{\psi_{2s}(\vec{k})}{ \Omega(\vec{k})} \big| \big| v^{(1)}_{p_1} 
  \overline{v^{(2)}_{p_2}} 
  ...v^{(5)}_{p_5} 
  \overline{u^{(2)}_{k_2}} 
  ... 
  \overline{u^{(6)}_{k_6}} 
   \big| \leq C \prod_{j \in \{2,...,6 \}}  
\left\lVert u^{(j)} \right\rVert 
_{H^{\sigma}} \prod_{l=1}^5  
\left\lVert v^{(l)} \right\rVert 
_{H^{\sigma}}
    \end{equation}
    and, 
    \begin{equation}\label{T2 with abs value}
        \sum_{\substack{k_1-k_2+...-k_6=0 \\ q_1-q_2+...+q_5 =k_2 \\\Omega(\vec{k}) \neq 0}} \big| \frac{\psi_{2s}(\vec{k})}{ \Omega(\vec{k})} \big| \big| u^{(1)}_{k_1} 
  \overline{v^{(1)}_{q_1}} 
  v^{(2)}_{q_2}... 
  \overline{v^{(5)}_{q_5}} 
  u^{(3)}_{k_3}...  
  \overline{u^{(6)}_{k_6}} 
  \big|\leq C \prod_{j \in \{1,3,...,6 \}}  
\left\lVert u^{(j)} \right\rVert 
_{H^{\sigma}} \prod_{l=1}^5  
\left\lVert v^{(l)} \right\rVert 
_{H^{\sigma}}
    \end{equation}
    Hence, the maps:
    \begin{equation*}
        \begin{array}{cccc} \mathcal T_0 : & H^{\sigma}(\mathbb{T})^6 & \longrightarrow & \mathbb{C} \\ & u^{(1)},...,u^{(6)} & \longmapsto & \mathlarger{\sum_{\substack{k_1-k_2+...-k_6=0 \\ \Omega(\vec{k}) = 0}} \psi_{2s}(\vec{k})u^{(1)}_{k_1} 
  \overline{u^{(2)}_{k_2}} 
  ... 
  \overline{u^{(6)}_{k_6}} 
  } \end{array},
    \end{equation*}
    \begin{equation*}
        \begin{array}{cccc} \mathcal T_1 : & H^{\sigma}(\mathbb{T})^{10} & \longrightarrow & \mathbb{C} \\ & u^{(2)},...,u^{(6)},v^{(1)},...,v^{(5)} & \longmapsto & \mathlarger{ \sum_{\substack{k_1-k_2+...-k_6=0 \\ p_1-p_2+...+p_5 =k_1 \\\Omega(\vec{k}) \neq 0}} \frac{\psi_{2s}(\vec{k})}{ \Omega(\vec{k})} v^{(1)}_{p_1} 
  \overline{v^{(2)}_{p_2}} 
  ...v^{(5)}_{p_5} 
  \overline{u^{(2)}_{k_2}} 
  ... 
  \overline{u^{(6)}_{k_6}} 
  } \end{array}
    \end{equation*}
    \begin{equation*}
        \begin{array}{cccc} \mathcal T_2 : & H^{\sigma}(\mathbb{T})^{10} & \longrightarrow & \mathbb{C} \\ & u^{(1)},u^{(3)},...,u^{(6)},v^{(1)},...,v^{(5)} & \longmapsto & \mathlarger{\sum_{\substack{k_1-k_2+...-k_6=0 \\ q_1-q_2+...+q_5 =k_2 \\\Omega(\vec{k}) \neq 0}} \frac{\psi_{2s}(\vec{k})}{ \Omega(\vec{k})} u^{(1)}_{k_1} 
  \overline{v^{(1)}_{q_1}} 
  v^{(2)}_{q_2}... 
  \overline{v^{(5)}_{q_5}} 
  u^{(3)}_{k_3}...  
  \overline{u^{(6)}_{k_6}} 
  } \end{array}
    \end{equation*}
    are continuous multi-linear forms. Then, for $j=0,1,2$, setting for $u\in H^{\sigma}(\mathbb{T})$:
    \begin{equation*}
        \mathcal Q_j(u) := \mathcal T_j(u,...,u)
    \end{equation*}
    we deduce that each $Q_j$ is continuous on $H^{\sigma}(\mathbb{T})$, and that for $N \in \mathbb{N} \cup \{ \infty \}$, the map\footnote{By abuse of notation, we still denote by $Q_{s,N}$ this new function, even though it has already been defined in Definition~\ref{def normal form Q}. The $Q_{s,N}$ of Definition~\ref{def normal form Q} and the $Q_{s,N}$ of this proposition coincide on $\mathcal C^{\infty}(\mathbb{T})$.}:
    \begin{equation}\label{def Qs,N = Q0 + Q1 +Q2}
       Q_{s,N} := \textnormal{Im}(-\frac{1}{6}\mathcal Q_0 \circ \Pi_N  + \frac{1}{2}\mathcal Q_1 \circ \Pi_N - \frac{1}{2}\mathcal Q_2\circ \Pi_N)
    \end{equation}
    is continuous on $H^{\sigma}(\mathbb{T})$ and satisfies for all $u,v \in H^{\sigma}(\mathbb{T})$:
        \begin{equation}\label{Qs,N almost Lipschitz}
    \begin{split}
       \left| Q_{s,N}(u) - Q_{s,N}(v)\right| & \leq C   
\left\lVert u-v \right\rVert_{H^{\sigma}}  
(  
\left\lVert u \right\rVert_{H^{\sigma}}  
^6+  
\left\lVert v \right\rVert_{H^{\sigma}}  
^6+  
\left\lVert u \right\rVert_{H^{\sigma}}  
^9+  
\left\lVert v \right\rVert_{H^{\sigma}}  
^9) \\
        & \leq C   
\left\lVert u-v \right\rVert_{H^{\sigma}}  
(1+  
\left\lVert u \right\rVert_{H^{\sigma}}  
 +   
\left\lVert v \right\rVert_{H^{\sigma}}  
)^9
    \end{split}
    \end{equation}
    uniformly in $N\in \mathbb{N} \cup \{\infty \}$.
<!-- end prop-3 -->
<!-- notn-2: body_md -->
We also use the notation $Q_s$ to refer to $Q_{s,\infty}$.
<!-- end notn-2 -->
<!-- rem-6: body_md -->
Note that we cannot a priori define $Q_{s}(u)$ on the support of $\mu_s$ as $\frac{d}{dt}E_{s}(\Phi(t)u)|_{t=0}$, because the expression
\begin{equation*}
    E_s(\Phi(t)u) = \frac{1}{2} {\left\vert\kern-0.25ex\left\vert\kern-0.25ex\left\vert \Phi(t)u 
    \right\vert\kern-0.25ex\right\vert\kern-0.25ex\right\vert}_{H^s(\mathbb{T})}^2 + R_s(\Phi(t)u)
\end{equation*}
is a priori ill defined for initial data $u$ in the support of $\mu_s$ since:
\begin{equation*}
    {\left\vert\kern-0.25ex\left\vert\kern-0.25ex\left\vert \Phi(t)u 
    \right\vert\kern-0.25ex\right\vert\kern-0.25ex\right\vert}_{H^s(\mathbb{T})}^2 = +\infty, \hspace{0.3cm} \text{$\mu_s$-almost surely.}
\end{equation*}
Indeed, for $\sigma < s- \frac{1}{2}$, it follows from the fact that the flow $\Phi(t)$ is a bijection from $H^{\sigma}(\mathbb{T})$ to itself that:
\begin{equation*}
	\mu_s(\{u \in H^{\sigma}(\mathbb{T}): \hspace{0.1cm} {\left\vert\kern-0.25ex\left\vert\kern-0.25ex\left\vert \Phi(t)u 
    \right\vert\kern-0.25ex\right\vert\kern-0.25ex\right\vert}_{H^s(\mathbb{T})}^2 < +\infty \}) = \mu_s(\{v \in H^{\sigma}(\mathbb{T}): \hspace{0.1cm} {\left\vert\kern-0.25ex\left\vert\kern-0.25ex\left\vert v 
    \right\vert\kern-0.25ex\right\vert\kern-0.25ex\right\vert}_{H^s(\mathbb{T})}^2 < +\infty \})= \mu_s(H^s(\mathbb{T})) = 0
\end{equation*}
<!-- end rem-6 -->
<!-- prop-4: body_md -->
\label{prop Qs,N tends to Qs uniformly on compact sets}
    Let $s>\frac{3}{2}$. Let $\sigma < s-\frac{1}{2}$ close enough to $s-\frac{1}{2}$ so that the conclusion of Proposition \ref{prop continuity of Qs,N and deterministic estimate} holds. Then, for every compact set $K \subset H^{\sigma}(\mathbb{T})$,
    \begin{equation*}
        \sup_{u \in K} \left| Q_s(u) - Q_{s,N}(u) \right|  
\underset{N \rightarrow \infty}{\longrightarrow} 
 0
    \end{equation*}
    In other words, $Q_{s,N}$ converges to $Q_s$ uniformly on compact sets of $H^{\sigma}(\mathbb{T})$.
<!-- end prop-4 -->
<!-- proof-2: body_md -->
Assuming the statements in Proposition~\ref{prop continuity of Qs,N and deterministic estimate}, the proof goes exactly the same as the proof of Proposition~\ref{prop approx R_s by R_s,N on compact sets}.
<!-- end proof-2 -->
<!-- prop-5: body_md -->
\label{prop trc invarianve of leb-low times Gauss-high}
The measure 
    \begin{equation*}
        \prod_{|k| \leq N} d \widehat{u}_k \otimes \mu_{s,N}^{\perp}
    \end{equation*}
    is invariant under the truncated flow. In other words, for every $N \in \mathbb{N}$ and $t \in \mathbb{R}$, 
    \begin{equation*}
        (\Phi_N(t))_{\#} \Bigg( \prod_{|k| \leq N} d \widehat{u}_k \otimes \mu_{s,N}^{\perp} \Bigg) = \prod_{|k| \leq N} d \widehat{u}_k \otimes \mu_{s,N}^{\perp}
    \end{equation*}
<!-- end prop-5 -->
<!-- cor-2: body_md -->
\label{change-of-variable formula}
    Let $A$ a Borel measurable set. Let $f : H^{\sigma}(\mathbb{T}) \longrightarrow \mathbb{R}_+ $ be a positive measurable function.
    Then, 
    \begin{equation*}
        \int_{\Phi_N(t)A} f(v) \prod_{|k| \leq N} d \widehat{v}_k \otimes \mu_{s,N}^{\perp}(v) = \int_A f(\Phi_N(t)u) \prod_{|k| \leq N} d \widehat{u}_k \otimes \mu_{s,N}^{\perp}(u)
    \end{equation*}
<!-- end cor-2 -->
<!-- proof-3: body_md -->
Let $\widetilde{\Phi}_N(t)$ be the restriction of the truncated flow $\Phi_N(t)$ on the finite-dimensional space $E_N$, which maps $E_N$ to itself (see Proposition~\ref{structure of the truncated flow}). We factorize $\Phi_N(t)$ as $(\widetilde{\Phi}_N(t), e^{it\partial_x^2})$ on $E_N \times E_N^{\perp}$, in the sense that $\Phi_N(t)u_0 = \widetilde{\Phi}_N(t) \Pi_N u_0 + e^{it\partial_x^2} \Pi_N^{\perp} u_0$ (see again Proposition~\ref{structure of the truncated flow}). Now, we provide a proof in two steps.
\bigskip

\underline{Step 1 :} Firstly, we show the formula 
\begin{equation}\label{formula truncated transport}
    (\Phi_N(t))_{\#} \Bigg( \prod_{|k| \leq N} d \widehat{u}_k \otimes \mu_{s,N}^{\perp} \Bigg) = \Bigg( \prod_{|k| \leq N} d \widehat{u}_k\Bigg) \otimes (e^{it\partial_x^2})_{\#} \mu_{s,N}^{\perp}
\end{equation}
To do so, we rely on the fact $\mathcal B(H^{\sigma}(\mathbb{T})) = \mathcal B(E_N) \otimes \mathcal B(E_N^{\perp})$\footnote{Indeed, whenever $X$ and $Y$ are two topological separable spaces, we have $\mathcal B(X \times Y) = \mathcal B(X) \otimes \mathcal B(Y)$, where $\otimes$ is the symbol for tensor-product of sigma-algebra}. Thanks to that point, if we show that for every $A_{low} \in \mathcal B(E_N)$ and $A_{high} \in \mathcal B(E_N^\perp)$, we have: 
\begin{equation}\label{equality on Alow x Ahigh}
        \Big( \prod_{|k| \leq N} d \widehat{u}_k \otimes \mu_{s,N}^{\perp} \Big) \big( \Phi_N(t)^{-1}(A_{low} \times A_{high})\big)
         = \Big( \prod_{|k| \leq N} d \widehat{u}_k\Big)( A_{low})\mu_{s,N}^{\perp}(e^{-it\partial_x^2}A_{high}), 
\end{equation}
then, the property of uniqueness of product measures\footnote{Both $\prod_{|k| \leq N} d \widehat{u}_k$ and  $(e^{it\partial_x^2})_{\#} \mu_{s,N}^{\perp}$ being $\sigma$-finite measures.} will ensure that the two measures in \eqref{formula truncated transport} coincide on $\mathcal B(E_N) \otimes \mathcal B(E_N^{\perp})$, that is on $\mathcal B(H^{\sigma}(\mathbb{T}))$. Hence, let us prove \eqref{equality on Alow x Ahigh}. Let $A_{low} \in \mathcal B(E_N)$ and $A_{high} \in \mathcal B(E_N^\perp)$. On the one hand, from the factorization of the truncated flow, we have:
\begin{equation*}
    \Phi_N(t)^{-1}(A_{low} \times A_{high}) = \widetilde{\Phi}_N(t)^{-1}(A_{low}) \times e^{-it\partial_x^2}A_{high} \subset E_N \times E_N^\perp
\end{equation*}
so, using the definition of product measures we obtain:
\begin{equation*}
        \Big( \prod_{|k| \leq N} d \widehat{u}_k \otimes \mu_{s,N}^{\perp} \Big) \left( \Phi_N(t)^{-1}(A_{low}   \times A_{high})\right) = \Big( \prod_{|k| \leq N} d \widehat{u}_k\Big)(\widetilde{\Phi}_N(t)^{-1}(A_{low}))\mu_{s,N}^{\perp}(e^{-it\partial_x^2}A_{high})
\end{equation*}
Thus, to prove \eqref{equality on Alow x Ahigh}, it remains to show that:
\begin{equation}\label{invariance of the Lebesgue measure under the truncated flow}
    \Big( \prod_{|k| \leq N} d \widehat{u}_k\Big)\big(\widetilde{\Phi}_N(t)^{-1}(A_{low})\big) = \Big( \prod_{|k| \leq N} d \widehat{u}_k\Big)\big(A_{low}\big)
\end{equation}
To do so, we recall that on the other hand, $\widetilde{\Phi}_N(t)$ is the flow of the Hamiltonian equation: 
\begin{equation}
    \begin{cases}
        i\partial_t u = \frac{\partial H_N}{\partial  
  \overline{u} 
  }(u) \\
        u|_{t=0} = u_0 \in E_N
    \end{cases}
    \tag{FNLS}
\end{equation}
on the finite-dimensional space $E_N$ (see Proposition~\ref{structure of the truncated flow}). So the equality \eqref{invariance of the Lebesgue measure under the truncated flow} follows from the application of Liouville's theorem, which states that the flow of finite-dimensional Hamiltonian equation preserves the Lebesgue measure. To sum up, we obtained \eqref{formula truncated transport}. Let us now turn to the second step of the proof:
\bigskip



\underline{Step 2 :} Secondly, we show the following invariance property:
\begin{equation*}
    (e^{it\partial_x^2})_{\#} \mu_{s,N}^{\perp} = \mu_{s,N}^{\perp}
\end{equation*}
We recall that the probability measure $\mu_{s,N}^{\perp}$ is the law of the random variable
\begin{equation*}
    \begin{split}
   X : \hspace{0.1cm} &  \Omega \longrightarrow H^{\sigma}(\mathbb{T}) \\
   & \omega \longmapsto \sum_{|n| > N} \frac{g_n(\omega)}{\langle n \rangle^s} e^{inx}
    \end{split}
\end{equation*}
where the sum converges in the space $\mathbb{L}^2(\Omega,H^{\sigma}(\mathbb{T}))$. Since $e^{it\partial_x^2}$ is a linear isometry on $\mathbb{L}^2(\mathbb{T})$, we deduce that 
\begin{equation*}
    e^{it\partial_x^2} \circ X (\omega) = \sum_{|n| > N} \frac{e^{-itn^2}g_n(\omega)}{\langle n \rangle^s} e^{inx}
\end{equation*}
where the sum still converges in $\mathbb{L}^2(\Omega,H^{\sigma}(\mathbb{T}))$. Moreover, the Gaussian  measures are invariant under rotations, so the family $\{e^{-itn^2}g_n \}_{n \in \mathbb{Z}}$ is still a family of independent standard complex Gaussian measures. Consequently, we obtain that $X$ and $e^{it\partial_x^2} \circ X$ have the same law, and this means that
\begin{equation*}
    (e^{it\partial_x^2})_{\#} \mu_{s,N}^{\perp} = \mu_{s,N}^{\perp}
\end{equation*}
which is the invariance property of Step 2.
\bigskip

\underline{Conclusion :} We get the desired result by combining Step 1 and Step 2.
<!-- end proof-3 -->
<!-- prop-6: body_md -->
\label{prop Radon-Nikodym derivative for the trc trspted GM}
    Let $s > \frac{3}{2}$, $R>0$ and $N \in \mathbb{N}$. For every $t \in \mathbb{R}$, we have
    \begin{equation*}
        \Phi_N(t)_\# \mu_s = \textnormal{exp}\bigl(-\frac{1}{2} ( 
\left\lVert \Pi_N \Phi_N(-t)u \right\rVert 
_{H^s}^2- 
\left\lVert \Pi_N u \right\rVert 
_{H^s}^2 )   \bigr) d\mu_s
    \end{equation*}
    Moreover, we can rewrite this formula as
    \begin{equation*}
        \Phi_N(t)_\# \mu_s = \textnormal{exp}\left(R_{s,N}(\Phi_N(-t)u) - R_{s,N}(u)-\int_0^{-t} Q_{s,N}(\Phi_N(\tau)u)d\tau \right) d\mu_s
    \end{equation*}
    where $R_{s,N}$ is defined in Definition~\ref{def normal form R and E} (see also \eqref{R_s,N diag multilinear form}) and $Q_{s,N}$ is defined in \eqref{def Qs,N = Q0 + Q1 +Q2}  (see also Definition~\ref{def normal form Q}).
<!-- end prop-6 -->
<!-- rem-7: body_md -->
Such a formula for the density has also been obtained for the different models in \cite{debussche2021quasi}, \cite{forlano_and_soeng2022transport}, \cite{genovese2023transport} and \cite{forlano2022quasi}.
<!-- end rem-7 -->
<!-- proof-4: body_md -->
Firstly, we decompose $\mu_s$ as:
\begin{equation*}
   d \mu_s = \left( \frac{1}{Z_N}e^{-\frac{1}{2} 
\left\lVert \Pi_N u \right\rVert 
_{H^s}^2} \prod_{|k| \leq N} d \widehat{u_k} \right) \otimes d\mu_{s,N}^{\perp}
\end{equation*}
(see \eqref{mu_s = mu_s,N times mu_s,N^perp} and \eqref{mu_s,N}).
    Then, thanks to a general feature for the transport of density measure, we have :
     \begin{equation*}
        \begin{split}
            \Phi_N(t)_\# d\mu_s &= \Phi_N(t)_\# \left( \frac{1}{Z_N}e^{-\frac{1}{2} 
\left\lVert \Pi_N u \right\rVert 
_{H^s}^2} \prod_{|k| \leq N} d \widehat{u_k} \right) \otimes d\mu_{s,N}^{\perp} \\
            & =  \frac{1}{Z_N}e^{-\frac{1}{2} 
\left\lVert \Pi_N(\Phi_N(t)^{-1}u) \right\rVert 
^2_{H^s}} \cdot \Phi_N(t)_\# \left( \prod_{|k| \leq N} d \widehat{u_k} \right) \otimes d\mu_{s,N}^{\perp} \\
            & =  \frac{1}{Z_N}e^{-\frac{1}{2} 
\left\lVert \Pi_N(\Phi_N(-t)(u) \right\rVert 
^2_{H^s}} \cdot  \left( \prod_{|k| \leq N} d \widehat{u_k} \right) \otimes d\mu_{s,N}^{\perp} \\
            &= e^{-\frac{1}{2}\left( 
\left\lVert \Pi_N(\Phi_N(-t)(u) \right\rVert 
^2_{H^s} -   
\left\lVert \Pi_N u \right\rVert 
^2_{H^s} \right)} d\mu_s
        \end{split}
    \end{equation*}
    where we used in the third line the invariance property from Proposition~\ref{prop trc invarianve of leb-low times Gauss-high}. Hence, the first statement of Proposition~\ref{prop Radon-Nikodym derivative for the trc trspted GM} is proven. To achieve the proof, we rewrite the term inside the exponential thanks to the definition of the modified energy \eqref{modified energy} and the identity \eqref{Qs,N(phi_N(t)u)}:
    \begin{equation*}
        \begin{split}
        -\frac{1}{2}\big( 
\left\lVert \Pi_N(\Phi_N(-t)(u) \right\rVert 
^2_{H^s} &-   
\left\lVert \Pi_N u \right\rVert 
^2_{H^s} \big) = \int_0^{-t} -\frac{1}{2}\frac{d}{d\tau}  
\left\lVert \Pi_N(\Phi_N(\tau)(u) \right\rVert 
^2_{H^s} d\tau \\
        & = \int_0^{-t} \big( \frac{d}{d\tau}\left( R_{s,N}(\Phi_N(\tau)u) \right) -\frac{d}{d\tau}( E_{s,N}(\Pi_N \Phi_N(\tau)u)) \big) d\tau \\
        & = \int_0^{-t} \big( \frac{d}{d\tau}\left( R_{s,N}(\Phi_N(\tau)u) \right)- Q_{s,N}(\Phi_N(\tau)u) \big) d\tau \\
        & = R_{s,N}(\Phi_N(-t)u) - R_{s,N}(u) - \int_0^{-t} Q_{s,N}(\Phi_N(\tau)u) d\tau
        \end{split} 
    \end{equation*}
    which is the desired rewriting.
<!-- end proof-4 -->
<!-- prop-7: body_md -->
\label{prop Radon-Nikodym derivative for the transported GM}
    Let $s>\frac{3}{2}$ and $R>0$. Let $t \in \mathbb{R}$. Then,
    \begin{equation*}
        \Phi(t)_\# \mu_s = G_s(t,u) d\mu_s
    \end{equation*}
    In particular, $\mu_s$ is quasi-invariant under the flow of \eqref{NLS}.
<!-- end prop-7 -->
<!-- rem-8: body_md -->
\label{rem continuity of the densities}
    For $\sigma < s-\frac{1}{2}$ close enough to $s-\frac{1}{2}$, we deduce from Proposition~\ref{prop R_s,N continuous}, Proposition~\ref{prop continuity of Qs,N and deterministic estimate} (whose proofs are provided in Section~\ref{section Proofs of the deterministic properties}), and from the continuity properties of the flow, that the map :
    \begin{equation*}
        (t,u) \in \mathbb{R} \times H^{\sigma}(\mathbb{T}) \mapsto \textnormal{exp} \left( R_s(\Phi(-t)u)-R_s(u) -\int_0^{-t} Q_{s,N}(\Phi_N(\tau)u) d\tau\right)
    \end{equation*}
    is continuous, for any $N\in \mathbb{N} \cup \{ \infty \}$. \\
    Moreover, on $H^{\sigma}(\mathbb{T})$, the a priori ill-defined object $-\frac{1}{2}( 
\left\lVert \Phi(-t)u \right\rVert 
_{H^s}^2- 
\left\lVert u \right\rVert 
_{H^s}^2)$ can be seen as the well-defined object:
    \begin{equation*}
        -\frac{1}{2}( 
\left\lVert \Phi(-t)u \right\rVert 
_{H^s}^2- 
\left\lVert u \right\rVert 
_{H^s}^2) := R_s(\Phi(-t)u)-R_s(u) - \int_0^{-t} Q_{s}(\Phi(\tau)u) d\tau
    \end{equation*}
<!-- end rem-8 -->
<!-- prop-8: body_md -->
\label{prop inner regularity of rho}Let $\mu$ be a finite measure on $(H^{\sigma}(\mathbb{T}),\mathcal B(H^{\sigma}(\mathbb{T})))$. Then, for any Borel set $A \subset H^\sigma(\mathbb{T})$, we have 
    \begin{equation*}
    \mu(A) = \sup \{ \mu(K) : \hspace{0.1cm} K \subset A, \hspace{0.1cm} K \hspace{0.1cm} \textnormal{compact set in} \hspace{0.1cm} H^{\sigma}(\mathbb{T}) \}
\end{equation*}
<!-- end prop-8 -->
<!-- proof-5: body_md -->
This follows from the general fact that finite measures on Polish spaces are regular.
<!-- end proof-5 -->
<!-- cor-3: body_md -->
\label{cor mu(K) = nu(K) for all compact sets}
    Let $\mu$ and $\nu$ be two finite measures on $(H^{\sigma}(\mathbb{T}), \mathcal B(H^{\sigma}(\mathbb{T})))$. Assume that for every compact set $K \subset H^{\sigma}(\mathbb{T})$, we have:
    \begin{equation*}
        \mu(K) = \nu(K)
    \end{equation*}
    Then, $\mu = \nu$.
<!-- end cor-3 -->
<!-- proof-6: body_md -->
Let $A \in \mathcal B(H^{\sigma}(\mathbb{T}))$. Let us prove that $\mu(A) = \nu(A)$. Let $\varepsilon > 0$. From the inner regularity of $\mu$ (see Proposition \ref{prop inner regularity of rho}), we invoke a compact set $K$ of $H^{\sigma}(\mathbb{T})$ such that $K \subset A$ and $\mu(A) - \varepsilon \leq \mu(K)$. Thus,
    \begin{equation*}
        \mu(A) - \varepsilon \leq \mu(K) = \nu(K) \leq \nu(A)
    \end{equation*}
    Since $\varepsilon >0$ is arbitrary, we conclude that $\mu(A) \leq \nu(A)$. By interchanging the roles of $\mu$ and $\nu$, we obtain the converse inequality.
<!-- end proof-6 -->
<!-- prop-9: body_md -->
\label{prop GsN cvg uniformly on cpcts to Gs} Let $s>\frac{3}{2}$. Let $K \subset H^{\sigma}(\mathbb{T})$ a compact set. Then, for every $t\in \mathbb{R}$:
\begin{equation*}
    \sup_{u \in K} \left|G_s(t,u) - G_{s,N}(t,u) \right|  
\underset{N\rightarrow \infty}{\longrightarrow} 
 0 
\end{equation*}
    In other words, $G_{s,N}(t,.)$ converges to $G_s(t,.)$ uniformly on compact sets.
<!-- end prop-9 -->
<!-- proof-7: body_md -->
Let $t\in \mathbb{R}$. Recall that $G_{s,N}(t,.)$ and $G_s(t,.)$ are respectively defined in \eqref{bis density trc trspted GM} and \eqref{density transported GM}. We prove separately that:
\begin{flushleft}
    \text{$(a):$ $ R_{s,N}(\Phi_N(t)u)-R_{s,N}(u)$ converges to $R_s(\Phi(t)u)-R_s(u)$ uniformly on compact sets as $N \rightarrow \infty$}
\end{flushleft}
    and,
\begin{flushleft}
   \text{ $(b):$ $\int_0^{t} Q_{s,N}(\Phi_N(\tau)u) d\tau$ converges to $ \int_0^{t} Q_{s}(\Phi(\tau)u) d\tau$ uniformly on compact sets as $N \rightarrow \infty$}. 
\end{flushleft}

Indeed, if we do so, we will obtain that: 
\begin{center}
$R_{s,N}(\Phi_N(t)u)-R_{s,N}(u) - \int_0^{t} Q_{s,N}(\Phi(_N\tau)u) d\tau $ converges to $R_s(\Phi(t)u)-R_s(u) - \int_0^{t} Q_{s}(\Phi(\tau)u) d\tau$ uniformly on compact sets as $N \rightarrow \infty$.  
\end{center}

Then, since the exponential is continuous, this will lead to the result. In order not to repeat the same argument, and since $(a)$ is similar to $(b)$ and a little bit easier, we will only prove $(b)$. Then, let $K \subset H^{\sigma}(\mathbb{T})$ be a compact set. Then,
\begin{equation}\label{diffce integrals on compatc set}
    \begin{split}
        &| \int_0^{t} Q_{s}(\Phi(\tau)u) d\tau - \int_0^{t} Q_{s,N}(\Phi_N(\tau)u) d\tau | \\
        & \leq \int_0^{t} |Q_{s}(\Phi(\tau)u) - Q_{s,N}(\Phi(\tau)u) | d\tau +  \int_0^{t} | Q_{s,N}(\Phi(\tau)u) - Q_{s,N}(\Phi_N(\tau)u) |
        d\tau \\
        & \leq |t| \sup_{\tau \in [0,t]} |Q_{s}(\Phi(\tau)u) - Q_{s,N}(\Phi(\tau)u)| + |t| \sup_{\tau \in [0,t]} |Q_{s,N}(\Phi(\tau)u) - Q_{s,N}(\Phi_N(\tau)u)|
    \end{split}
\end{equation}
On the one hand, from the continuity of $\Phi: \mathbb{R} \times H^{\sigma} \rightarrow H^{\sigma}$, the set $\{\Phi(\tau)u; \hspace{0.1cm} \tau \in [0,t], u \in K\}$ is compact. Combining this with the fact that $Q_{s,N}  
\underset{N}{\longrightarrow} 
 Q_s$ uniformly on compact sets (see Proposition~\ref{prop Qs,N tends to Qs uniformly on compact sets}) yields:
\begin{equation*}
   \sup_{u \in K} \sup_{\tau \in [0,t]} |Q_{s}(\Phi(\tau)u) - Q_{s,N}(\Phi(\tau)u)|  
\underset{N \rightarrow \infty}{\longrightarrow} 
 0
\end{equation*}
On the other hand, using \eqref{Qs,N almost Lipschitz} from Proposition~\ref{prop continuity of Qs,N and deterministic estimate} we can invoke a constant $C_s>0$ independent of $N$ such that:
\begin{equation}\label{Qs,N(phi) - Qs,N(phi_N) on compact sets}
    \begin{split}
   &\sup_{u \in K} \sup_{\tau \in [0,t]} |Q_{s,N}(\Phi(\tau)u) - Q_{s,N}(\Phi_N(\tau)u)| \\
   & \leq C_s \sup_{(\tau,u)\in [0,t]\times K}  
\left\lVert \Phi(\tau)u-\Phi_N(\tau)u \right\rVert_{H^{\sigma}}  
\left(1 +   
\left\lVert \Phi(\tau)u \right\rVert_{H^{\sigma}}  
+  
\left\lVert \Phi_N(\tau)u \right\rVert_{H^{\sigma}}  
\right)^9 
   \end{split}
\end{equation}
Besides, from the Cauchy theory, there exists a constant $C>0$ independent of $N$ such that:
\begin{equation*}
    \sup_{(\tau,u)\in [0,t]\times K}   
\left\lVert \Phi(\tau)u \right\rVert_{H^{\sigma}}  
 +   
\left\lVert \Phi_N(\tau)u \right\rVert_{H^{\sigma}}  
 \leq C
\end{equation*}
(see Proposition~\ref{prop exponential bound}). And, from Proposition~\ref{appendix second approximation prop}, we also have:
\begin{equation*}
    \sup_{(\tau,u)\in [0,t]\times K}  
\left\lVert \Phi(\tau)u-\Phi_N(\tau)u \right\rVert_{H^{\sigma}}  
  
\underset{N \rightarrow \infty}{\longrightarrow} 
 0
\end{equation*}
Using these two facts in \eqref{Qs,N(phi) - Qs,N(phi_N) on compact sets} yields:
\begin{equation*}
    \sup_{(\tau,u)\in [0,t]\times K}\ |Q_{s,N}(\Phi(\tau)u) - Q_{s,N}(\Phi_N(\tau)u)|  
\underset{N \rightarrow \infty}{\longrightarrow} 
 0 
\end{equation*}
Finally, coming back to \eqref{diffce integrals on compatc set}, we conclude that:
\begin{equation*}
    \sup_{u \in K}| \int_0^{t} Q_{s}(\Phi(\tau)u) d\tau - \int_0^{t} Q_{s,N}(\Phi_N(\tau)u) d\tau |  
\underset{N \rightarrow \infty}{\longrightarrow} 
 0
\end{equation*}
This completes the proof.
<!-- end proof-7 -->
<!-- rem-9: body_md -->
We will be able to use Corollary~\ref{cor mu(K) = nu(K) for all compact sets} with the measures $\Phi(t)_\# \mu_s$ and $G_s(t,.) d\mu_s$. Indeed, both are finite measures on $(H^{\sigma}(\mathbb{T}), \mathcal B(H^{\sigma}(\mathbb{T})))$. On the one hand, $\Phi(t)_\# \mu_s$ is a probability measure; on the other hand, Fatou's lemma provide the following a priori bound for $G_s(t,.) d\mu_s(H^{\sigma}(\mathbb{T}))$ :
    \begin{equation*}
        G_s(t,.) d\mu_s(H^{\sigma}(\mathbb{T})) = \int_{H^{\sigma}} G_s(t,u)d\mu_s =\int_{H^{\sigma}} \lim_N G_{s,N}(t,u)d\mu_s \leq \liminf_N \int_{H^{\sigma}}G_{s,N}(t,u)d\mu_s = 1
    \end{equation*}
<!-- end rem-9 -->
<!-- rem-10: body_md -->
The proof we provide below for Proposition \ref{prop Radon-Nikodym derivative for the transported GM} is similar to the one for Theorem 1.4 in \cite{planchon2022modified}. However, it is worth noting that our proof do not require any $\mathbb{L}^p$-integrability for the truncated densities $G_{s,N}(t,.)$.
<!-- end rem-10 -->
<!-- proof-8: body_md -->
Let $t \in \mathbb{R}$. Relying on Corollary \ref{cor mu(K) = nu(K) for all compact sets}, it suffices to prove that for every compact set $K$ of $H^{\sigma}(\mathbb{T})$, we have:
\begin{equation}\label{it suffices equality on K}
    G_s(t,u) d\mu_s (K) = \Phi(t)_\# \mu_s (K), \hspace{0.2cm} \text{that is}, \hspace{0.2cm} \int_K G_s(t,u) d\mu_s = \mu_s(\Phi(-t) K) 
\end{equation}
Fix $K$ a compact of $H^{\sigma}(\mathbb{T})$.\\
We invoke two real numbers $\sigma_1$ and $\sigma_2$ such that $\sigma < \sigma_1 < \sigma_2 < s -\frac{1}{2}$. Moreover, we invoke for $k \in \mathbb{N}$:
\begin{equation*}
    B^{H^{\sigma_2}}_k := \{ u \in H^{\sigma_2}(\mathbb{T}): \hspace{0.1cm}  
\left\lVert u \right\rVert 
_{H^{\sigma_2}(\mathbb{T})} \leq k  \}
\end{equation*}
the closed centered ball in $H^{\sigma_2}(\mathbb{T})$ of radius $k$. Note that $ B^{H^{\sigma_2}}_k$ is compact in $H^{\sigma_1}(\mathbb{T})$ because $\sigma_1 < \sigma_2$. To establish \eqref{it suffices equality on K}, it suffices to prove that for all $k \in \mathbb{N}$:
\begin{equation}\label{it suffices equality on K cap Ball stronger topology}
    \int_{K \cap B^{H^{\sigma_2}}_k} G_s(t,u) d\mu_s = \mu_s(\Phi(-t) (K \cap B^{H^{\sigma_2}}_k) )
\end{equation}
Indeed, if we do so, we will obtain that:
\begin{equation*}
    \begin{split}
    &\int_{K \cap H^{\sigma_2}(\mathbb{T})} G_s(t,u) d\mu_s  = \int_{ \bigcup_{k \in \mathbb{N}} (K \cap B^{H^{\sigma_2}}_k )} G_s(t,u) d\mu_s  = \lim_{k \rightarrow \infty} \nnearrow \int_{K \cap B^{H^{\sigma_2}}_k} G_s(t,u) d\mu_s \\
    & = \lim_{k \rightarrow \infty} \nnearrow  \mu_s(\Phi(-t) (K \cap B^{H^{\sigma_2}}_k) ) = \mu_s \big( \bigcup_{k \in \mathbb{N}} \Phi(-t) (K \cap B^{H^{\sigma_2}}_k) \big) = \mu_s\big(  \Phi(-t) (\bigcup_{k \in \mathbb{N}}(K \cap B^{H^{\sigma_2}}_k)) \big) \\
    & = \mu_s\big(\Phi(-t)(K \cap H^{\sigma_2}(\mathbb{T}))\big)
    \end{split}
\end{equation*}
Besides, since $\mu_s(H^{\sigma}(\mathbb{T}) \setminus  H^{\sigma_2}(\mathbb{T})) = 0$, we have: 
\begin{equation*}
    \int_K G_s(t,u) d\mu_s = \int_{K \cap H^{\sigma_2}(\mathbb{T})} G_s(t,u) d\mu_s
\end{equation*}
and,
\begin{equation*}
    \mu_s(\Phi(-t)K) = \mu_s\big((\Phi(-t)K) \cap H^{\sigma_2}(\mathbb{T})\big) = \mu_s\big(\Phi(-t)(K\cap H^{\sigma_2}(\mathbb{T}))\big)
\end{equation*}
Hence, if we prove \eqref{it suffices equality on K cap Ball stronger topology}, then we will obtain \eqref{it suffices equality on K}, and the proof will be complete. Thus, we now move on to the proof of \eqref{it suffices equality on K cap Ball stronger topology}. Let $k\in \mathbb{N}$ and denote $K_2 := K \cap B^{H^{\sigma_2}}_k $.\\

-- Firstly, we prove that:
\begin{equation}\label{first ineq}
    \int_{K_2} G_s(t,u) d\mu_s \leq \mu_s(\Phi(-t) (K_2) )
\end{equation}
Since $K_2$ is compact in $H^{\sigma}(\mathbb{T})$, we obtain from Proposition \ref{prop GsN cvg uniformly on cpcts to Gs} that:
\begin{equation}\label{int_K G_s = lim int_K Gs,N}
    \int_{K_2} G_s(t,u) d\mu_s = \lim_{N \rightarrow \infty} \int_{K_2} G_{s,N}(t,u) d\mu_s = \lim_{n\rightarrow \infty} \Phi_N(t)_\# \mu_s (K_2) = \lim_{N \rightarrow \infty} \mu_s(\Phi_N(-t)K_2)
\end{equation}
Let $\varepsilon >0$. Thanks to Corollary \ref{appendix set approximation}, we invoke $N_0 \in \mathbb{N}$ such that:
    \begin{equation*}
      N\geq N_0 \implies  \Phi_N(-t)(K_2) \subset \Phi(-t)(K_2) +  B^{H^{\sigma}}_{\varepsilon}
    \end{equation*}
    where $ B^{H^{\sigma}}_{\varepsilon}$ is the closed centered ball in $H^{\sigma}(\mathbb{T})$ of radius $\varepsilon$. As a consequence, we have:
    \begin{equation*}
        \limsup_N \mu_s(\Phi_N(-t)K_2) \leq \mu_s(\Phi(-t)(K_2) +  B^{H^{\sigma}}_{\varepsilon})
    \end{equation*}
    Plugging this into \eqref{int_K G_s = lim int_K Gs,N}, we obtain:
    \begin{equation*}
         \int_{K_2} G_s(t,u) d\mu_s \leq \mu_s(\Phi(-t)(K_2) +  B^{H^{\sigma}}_{\varepsilon})
    \end{equation*}
    Since $\varepsilon>0$ is arbitrary, we deduce that\footnote{Since $\Phi(-t) K_2$ is closed in $H^{\sigma}(\mathbb{T})$, we have $\bigcap_{\varepsilon > 0}(\Phi(-t)(K_2) +  B^{H^{\sigma}}_{\varepsilon}) = \Phi(-t) K_2$}:
        \begin{equation*}
         \int_{K_2} G_s(t,u) d\mu_s \leq \lim_{\varepsilon \rightarrow 0} \ssearrow \mu_s(\Phi(-t)(K_2) +  B^{H^{\sigma}}_{\varepsilon})  = \mu_s\big(\bigcap_{\varepsilon > 0}(\Phi(-t)(K_2) +  B^{H^{\sigma}}_{\varepsilon})\big) = \mu_s(\Phi(-t) K_2)
    \end{equation*}
    So we have proven \eqref{first ineq}. \\
    
-- Secondly, we prove that:
\begin{equation}\label{second ineq}
    \int_{K_2} G_s(t,u) d\mu_s \geq \mu_s(\Phi(-t) (K_2) )
\end{equation}
Let us first observe that $K_2$ is compact in $H^{\sigma_1}(\mathbb{T})$ : if $\{ u_n\}_{n \in \mathbb{N}} \in K_2^\mathbb{N}$ is a sequence in $K_2 = K \cap B^{H^{\sigma_2}}_k $, then, from the compactness of $B^{H^{\sigma_2}}_k$ in $H^{\sigma_1}(\mathbb{T})$ (because $\sigma_1 < \sigma_2$), there exists a subsequence $\{ u_{n_j}\}_{j \in \mathbb{N}}$ and an element $u \in B^{H^{\sigma_2}}_k$ such that:
\begin{equation*}
     
\left\lVert u_{n_j}-u \right\rVert 
_{H^{\sigma_1}}  
\underset{j \rightarrow \infty}{\longrightarrow} 
 0
\end{equation*}
In particular, we have $ 
\left\lVert u_{n_j}-u \right\rVert 
_{H^{\sigma}} 
\underset{j \rightarrow \infty}{\longrightarrow} 
 0$ because $\sigma < \sigma_1 $. Since $K$ is closed in $H^{\sigma}(\mathbb{T})$, it implies that $u \in K$. Then $u \in K \cap B^{H^{\sigma_2}}_k$, and $K_2$ is compact in $H^{\sigma_1}(\mathbb{T})$. \\

Now, let $\varepsilon >0$. Thanks to Corollary \ref{appendix set approximation}, and the fact that $K_2$ is compact in $H^{\sigma_1}(\mathbb{T})$ , we are able to invoke $N_1 \in \mathbb{N}$ such that:
    \begin{equation*}
       N \geq N_1 \implies  \Phi(-t)(K_2) \subset \Phi_N(-t)(K_2 + B^{H^{\sigma_1}}_{\varepsilon})
    \end{equation*}
    where $ B^{H^{\sigma_1}}_{\varepsilon}$ is the closed centered ball in $H^{\sigma_1}(\mathbb{T})$ of radius $\varepsilon$. It is now important to notice that  $K_2 + B^{H^{\sigma_1}}_{\varepsilon}$ is compact in $H^{\sigma}(\mathbb{T})$. It follows from the fact that both $K_2$ and $B^{H^{\sigma_1}}_{\varepsilon}$ are compact in $H^{\sigma}(\mathbb{T})$. As a consequence, we obtain from Proposition \ref{prop GsN cvg uniformly on cpcts to Gs} that for $N \geq N_1$: 
    \begin{equation*}
        \mu_s(\Phi(-t) (K_2)) \leq \mu_s( \Phi_N(-t)(K_2 + B^{H^{\sigma_1}}_{\varepsilon})) = \int_{K_2 + B^{H^{\sigma_1}}_{\varepsilon}} G_{s,N}(t,u) d\mu_s  
\underset{N \rightarrow \infty}{\longrightarrow} 
 \int_{K_2 + B^{H^{\sigma_1}}_{\varepsilon}} G_s(t,u) d\mu_s 
    \end{equation*}
    Since $\varepsilon >0$ is arbitrary, we obtain that:
    \begin{equation*}
        \mu_s(\Phi(-t) (K_2)) \leq \lim_{\varepsilon \rightarrow 0} \ssearrow \int_{K_2 + B^{H^{\sigma_1}}_{\varepsilon}} G_s(t,u) d\mu_s  = \int_{K_2} G_s(t,u) d\mu_s 
    \end{equation*}
    So we have proven \eqref{second ineq}. This completes the proof of Proposition \ref{prop Radon-Nikodym derivative for the transported GM}.
<!-- end proof-8 -->
<!-- notn-3: body_md -->
We also use the notations $\rho_{s,R,\infty}$ and $Z_{s,R,\infty}$ to respectively refer to $\rho_{s,R}$ and $Z_{s,R}$.
<!-- end notn-3 -->
<!-- rem-11: body_md -->
\label{rem cut-off H1}
We can rewrite $\mathcal C(u)$ as :
\begin{equation*}
    \mathcal C(u) = \frac{1}{2}  
\left\lVert u \right\rVert 
_{H^1}^2 + \frac{1}{6} 
\left\lVert u \right\rVert 
_{\mathbb{L}^6}^6
\end{equation*}
From the Sobolev embedding $H^1(\mathbb{T}) \hookrightarrow \mathbb{L}^6(\mathbb{T})$, we have
\begin{equation*}
    \frac{1}{2}  
\left\lVert u \right\rVert 
_{H^1}^2 \leq \mathcal C(u) \leq C(1+ 
\left\lVert u \right\rVert 
_{H^1})^6
\end{equation*}
It means that the cut-off $\1_{ \{\mathcal C(u) \leq R \}}$ is a $H^1(\mathbb{T})$ cut-off. In particular, (for $R\geq 2$)
\begin{equation*}
    \mathcal C(u) \leq R \implies  
\left\lVert u \right\rVert 
_{H^1} \leq \sqrt{2R} \leq R
\end{equation*}
so, 
\begin{equation*}
    \1_{ \{\mathcal C(u) \leq R \}} \leq \1_{B_R^{H^1}}(u)
\end{equation*}
where $B_R^{H^1}$ is the closed center ball of radius $R$ in $H^1(\mathbb{T})$.\\
The additional nice property is that the quantity $\mathcal C(u)$ is conserved by the flow of \eqref{NLS}.
<!-- end rem-11 -->
<!-- rem-12: body_md -->
(Passing from $\rho_{s,R,N}$ to $\mu_s$)\label{rem mu_s on balls}
Let $R>0$. The measure $\mu_s|_{\{ \mathcal C \leq R\}}$ coincide with the measure $ Z_{s,N,R}e^{R_{s,N}(u)}\rho_{s,R,N}|_{\{ \mathcal C \leq R\}}$.
    In other words, for every Borel set $A \subset H^1(\mathbb{T})$ such that $A \subset \{\mathcal C \leq R\}$, we have
    \begin{equation*}
        Z_{s,N,R} e^{R_{s,N}(u)} \rho_{s,R,N}(A) = \mu_s(A)
    \end{equation*}
    Indeed, it results from
    \begin{equation*}
        \begin{split}
        Z_{s,N,R} e^{R_{s,N}(u)}\rho_{s,R,N}(A) & = \int_A Z_{s,N,R}  e^{R_{s,N}(u)} d\rho_{s,R,N} (u) \\
        & = \int_A  Z_{s,N,R} e^{R_{s,N}(u)} \underbrace{\1_{ \{\mathcal C(u) \leq R \}}}_{=1} e^{-R_{s,N}(u)} \frac{1}{Z_{s,N,R}} d\mu_s(u) \\
        & = \int_A d\mu_s(u) = \mu_s(A)
        \end{split}
    \end{equation*}
<!-- end rem-12 -->
<!-- prop-10: body_md -->
\label{prop estimate for the weight of the weighted measure}
    Let $s > \frac{3}{2}$ and $R>0$. Then for any $p \in [1,+\infty)$, there exists a constant $C(s,p,R)>0$ such that for every $N \in \mathbb{N} \cup \{ \infty \}$, we have:
    \begin{equation}\label{estimate weight of wgm}
        
\left\lVert \1_{\{ \mathcal C(u) \leq R \} } e^{|R_{s,N}(u)|} \right\rVert 
_{\mathbb{L}^p(d\mu_s)} \leq C(s,p,R)
    \end{equation}
    Moreover, 
    \begin{equation*}
         
\left\lVert \1_{\{ \mathcal C(u) \leq R \} } e^{-R_s(u)}-\1_{\{ \mathcal C(u) \leq R \} } e^{-R_{s,N}(u)} \right\rVert 
_{\mathbb{L}^p(d\mu_s)}  
\underset{N \rightarrow \infty}{\longrightarrow} 
 0
    \end{equation*}
    In particular, $Z_{s,N,R}  
\underset{N}{\longrightarrow} 
 Z_{s,R}$ so that we also have:
        \begin{equation}\label{cvgce density rhoN to density rho}
         
\left\lVert \frac{1}{Z_{s,R}}\1_{\{ \mathcal C(u) \leq R \} } e^{-R_s(u)}-\frac{1}{Z_{s,R,N}}\1_{\{ \mathcal C(u) \leq R \} } e^{-R_{s,N}(u)} \right\rVert 
_{\mathbb{L}^p(d\mu_s)}  
\underset{N \rightarrow \infty}{\longrightarrow} 
 0
    \end{equation}
<!-- end prop-10 -->
<!-- rem-13: body_md -->
\label{rem well defined proba meas}
    The inequality \eqref{estimate weight of wgm} in  Proposition~\ref{prop estimate for the weight of the weighted measure} ensures that for all $N \in \mathbb{N} \cup \{ \infty\}$ :
    \begin{equation*}
       Z_{s,R,N} = \int_{H^{s-\frac{1}{2}}}  \1_{\{ \mathcal C(u) \leq R \} } e^{-R_{s,N}(u)}d\mu_s < +\infty
        \end{equation*}
        Besides, we also have $Z_{s,R,N}>0$ because one can show that $\mu_s (  \1_{\{ \mathcal C(u) \leq R \} } e^{-R_{s,N}(u)} > 0 ) > 0$. To see this, we write on the one hand:
    \begin{equation*}
        \mu_s \left(  \1_{\{ \mathcal C(u) \leq R \} } e^{-R_{s,N}(u)} > 0 \right) = \mu_s\left(\{ \mathcal C(u) \leq R \} \cap R_{s,N}<+\infty \right) = \mu_s\left(\{ \mathcal C(u) \leq R \} \right)
    \end{equation*}
    and on the other hand, we have that $\mu_s(\{ \mathcal C(u) \leq R \}) > 0$, for any $R>0$, since $\mu_s$ charges all open sets of $H^1(\mathbb{T})$. For this latter point, we refer to \cite{burq2013probabilistic}, Proposition 1.2.
  Note also that since $Z_{s,R,N} \rightarrow Z_{s,R}$, there exists a constant $C_{s,R}>0$ such that:
    \begin{equation}\label{1/Cs,R leq Zs,R,N leq Cs,R}
        \frac{1}{C_{s,R}} \leq Z_{s,R,N} \leq C_{s,R}
    \end{equation}
    uniformly in $N\in \mathbb{N} \cup \{ \infty \}$.
<!-- end rem-13 -->
<!-- prop-11: body_md -->
\label{prop Radon-Nikodym derivative for the transported wgm}
    Let $s > \frac{3}{2}$, $R>0$ and $N \in \mathbb{N} \cup\{ \infty \}$. For every $t \in \mathbb{R}$, we have:
    \begin{equation*}
        \Phi_N(t)_\# \rho_{s,R,N} = F_{s,N}(t,u) d\rho_{s,R,N}
    \end{equation*}
    for a function $F_{s,N}(t,.)$ given by the explicit formula:
    \begin{equation*}
        F_{s,N}(t,u)=\textnormal{exp}\left(-\int_0^{-t} Q_{s,N}(\Phi_N(\tau)u)d\tau \right)
    \end{equation*}
    where $Q_{s,N}$ is defined in \eqref{def Qs,N = Q0 + Q1 +Q2} (see also Definition~\ref{def normal form Q}). In particular, $\rho_{s,R}$ is quasi-invariant along the flow of \eqref{NLS}; and when $N \in \mathbb{N}$, $\rho_{s,R,N}$ is quasi-invariant along the flow of \eqref{truncated equation}.
<!-- end prop-11 -->
<!-- rem-14: body_md -->
When $N \in \mathbb{N}$, we have:
    \begin{equation*}
        \int_0^{t} Q_{s,N}(\Phi_N(\tau)u)d\tau  = E_{s,N}(\Pi_N \Phi_N(t)u) - E_{s,N}(\Pi_N u)
    \end{equation*}
    Hence, the a priori ill-defined object $E_s(\Phi(t)u)-E_s(u)$ (on the support of $\mu_s$) can be seen as:
    \begin{equation*}
        E_s(\Phi(t)u)-E_s(u) := \int_0^{t} Q_s(\Phi(\tau)u)d\tau
    \end{equation*}
    which is a continuous function on $H^{\sigma}(\mathbb{T})$ for $\sigma <s-\frac{1}{2}$ close enough to $s-\frac{1}{2}$.
<!-- end rem-14 -->
<!-- proof-9: body_md -->
Let $N \in \mathbb{N} \cup \{ \infty \}$. We start by applying a general feature for the transport of density measures:
    \begin{equation*}
    \begin{split}
        \Phi_N(t)_\# \rho_{s,R,N} &=  \Phi_N(t)_\# \left(\frac{1}{Z_{s,R,N}}\1_{ \{\mathcal C(u) \leq R \}} e^{-R_{s,N}(u)} d\mu_s \right)\\
        &= \frac{1}{Z_{s,R,N}}\1_{ \{\mathcal C(\Phi_N(t)^{-1}u) \leq R \}} e^{-R_{s,N}(\Phi_N(t)^{-1}u)} \Phi_N(t)_\# d\mu_s
    \end{split}
    \end{equation*}
    Next, thanks to Proposition~\ref{prop Radon-Nikodym derivative for the trc trspted GM} and \ref{prop Radon-Nikodym derivative for the transported GM}, along with the facts that $\Phi_N(t)^{-1}=\Phi_N(-t)$ and that $\mathcal C$ is conserved by the flows, we obtain:
    \begin{equation*}
        \begin{split}
        \Phi_N(t)_\# \rho_{s,R,N} &= \frac{1}{Z_{s,R,N}}\1_{ \{\mathcal C(u) \leq R \}} \textnormal{exp}\left(-R_{s,N}(u) - \int_0^{-t} Q_{s,N}(\Phi_N(\tau)u) d\tau\right)d\mu_s \\
        &=  \textnormal{exp}\left( - \int_0^{-t} Q_{s,N}(\Phi_N(\tau)u) d\tau\right) d\rho_{s,R,N
        }
        \end{split}
    \end{equation*}
    which completes the proof.
<!-- end proof-9 -->
<!-- rem-15: body_md -->
\label{rem FsN cvg uniformly on cpcts to Fs} Let $s>\frac{3}{2}$ and $\sigma<s-\frac{1}{2}$. Then, for every $t\in \mathbb{R}$, $F_{s,N}(t,.)$ converges to $F_s(t,.)$ uniformly on compact sets of $H^{\sigma}(\mathbb{T})$ (see the proof of Proposition~\ref{prop GsN cvg uniformly on cpcts to Gs}).
<!-- end rem-15 -->
<!-- rem-16: body_md -->
Since $\mathcal C$ is conserved by the flow, we still have:
    \begin{align}\label{transport restricted GM}
    \Phi_N(t)_\# \mu_{s,R}& = G_{s,N}(t,.)\mu_{s,R}, & &\text{and,} & \Phi(t)_\# \mu_{s,R} & = G_s(t,.)\mu_{s,R}
\end{align}
<!-- end rem-16 -->
<!-- prop-12: body_md -->
\label{prop Qs,N L^p estimate wrt mu_s}
    Let $s > \frac{3}{2}$. There exists $\beta \in (0,1)$ such that for every $R>0$, there exists a constant $C(s,R) > 0$, such that for any $p \in [2,+\infty)$,
    \begin{equation}\label{Qs,N L^p estimate wrt mu_s}
          
\left\lVert \1_{\{ \mathcal C{u} \leq R \}} Q_{s,N}(u) \right\rVert 
_{\mathbb{L}^p(d\mu_s)} \leq C(s,R)p^\beta
    \end{equation}
    uniformly in $N \in \mathbb{N} \cup \{\infty \}$.\\
<!-- end prop-12 -->
<!-- prop-13: body_md -->
\label{prop Qs,N L^p estimate wrt rho_s,R,N}
    Let $s > \frac{3}{2}$. There exists $\beta \in (0,1)$ such that for every $R>0$, there exists a constant $C(s,R) > 0$, such that for any $p \in [1,+\infty)$,
    \begin{equation}\label{Qs,N L^p estimate wrt rho_s,R,N}
         
\left\lVert  Q_{s,N}(u) \right\rVert 
_{\mathbb{L}^p(d\rho_{s,R,N})} \leq C(s,R)p^\beta
    \end{equation}
    uniformly in $N \in \mathbb{N} \cup \{\infty \}$.\\
<!-- end prop-13 -->
<!-- proof-10: body_md -->
It results from Cauchy-Schwarz that:
\begin{equation*}
    \begin{split}
     
\left\lVert  Q_{s,N}(u) \right\rVert 
_{\mathbb{L}^p(d\rho_{s,R,N})} &=  
\left\lVert \frac{1}{Z_{s,R,N}}\1_{\{ \mathcal C{u} \leq R \}} |Q_{s,N}(u)|^p e^{-R_{s,N}(u)} \right\rVert 
_{\mathbb{L}^1(d\mu_s)}^{1/p} \\
    & \leq\frac{1}{Z_{s,R,N}}   
\left\lVert \1_{\{ \mathcal C{u} \leq R \}} Q_{s,N}(u) \right\rVert 
_{\mathbb{L}^{2p}(d\mu_s)}  
\left\lVert \1_{\{ \mathcal C{u} \leq R \}}e^{-R_{s,N}(u)} \right\rVert 
_{\mathbb{L}^2(d\mu_s)}^{1/p} \\
    & \leq C(s,R)2^{\beta} p^\beta \cdot C(s,R,2)^{1/p} \leq C(s,R) p^\beta
    \end{split}
\end{equation*}
    where the constant $C(s,R)$ has changed but still depends only on $s$ and $R$. Note also that we used \eqref{1/Cs,R leq Zs,R,N leq Cs,R}.
<!-- end proof-10 -->
<!-- prop-14: body_md -->
\label{prop formula d/dt rho(phi(t)(A)) wrt to Qs} Let $s > \frac{3}{2}$, $R>0$, $N \in \mathbb{N} \cup \{ \infty\}$ and $t \in \mathbb{R}$. For every Borel set $A \subset H^\sigma(\mathbb{T})$, we have :
\begin{equation}\label{formula d/dt rho(phi_N(t)(A)) wrt to Qs,N}
    \frac{d}{dt} \rho_{s,R,N}\left(\Phi_N(t)(A) \right) = - \int_{\Phi_N(t)A} Q_{s,N}(u) d\rho_{s,R,N}
\end{equation}
<!-- end prop-14 -->
<!-- proof-11: body_md -->
We use the explicit formula for the density from Proposition~\ref{prop Radon-Nikodym derivative for the transported wgm}, so that we obtain:
\begin{equation*}
    \begin{split}
         & \frac{d}{dt} \rho_{s,R,N}\left(\Phi_N(t)(A) \right) = \frac{d}{dt} \left( \Phi_N(-t)_\# \rho_{s,R,N} \right)(A) = \frac{d}{dt} \int_A e^{-\int_0^t Q_{s,N}(\Phi_N(\tau)u) d\tau} d\rho_{s,R,N} \\
         & = - \int_A Q_{s,N}(\Phi_N(t)u) d \left( \Phi_N(-t)_\# \rho_{s,R,N} \right)(u) = -\int_{\Phi_N(t)A} Q_{s,N}(u) d\rho_{s,R,N}
    \end{split}
\end{equation*}
where the last equality follows from the definition of a push-forward measure.
<!-- end proof-11 -->
<!-- prop-15: body_md -->
\label{prop quantitative quasi-invariance for rho_s,R}
    Let $s>\frac{3}{2}$, $R>0$ and $t\in \mathbb{R}$. Then, there exists $\beta \in (0,1)$ such that for every $\alpha \in (0,1)$, there exists a constant $C=C_{s,R,\alpha,\beta} > 0$ such that for all Borel set $A \subset H^\sigma(\mathbb{T})$ :
    \begin{equation}\label{ineq quantitative quasi-invariance for rho_s,R}
        \rho_{s,R,N}(\Phi_N(t)A) \leq \rho_{s,R,N}(A)^{1-\alpha} \textnormal{exp}\left( C(1+|t|)^{\frac{1}{1-\beta}}\right)
    \end{equation}
    uniformly in $N \in \mathbb{N} \cup \{ \infty \}$.
<!-- end prop-15 -->
<!-- proof-12: body_md -->
Let $s>\frac{3}{2}$, $R>0$ and $N \in \mathbb{N} \cup \{ \infty \}$. Let $A \subset H^\sigma(\mathbb{T})$ be a Borel set. Using \eqref{formula d/dt rho(phi_N(t)(A)) wrt to Qs,N}, Hölder inequality and the energy estimate from Proposition~\ref{prop Qs,N L^p estimate wrt rho_s,R,N}, we obtain :
     \begin{equation*}
         \big| \frac{d}{dt}\rho_{s,R,N}(\Phi_N(t)A) \big| \leq  
\left\lVert Q_{s,N} \right\rVert 
_{\mathbb{L}^p(d\rho_{s,R,N})} \rho_{s,R,N}(\Phi_N(t)A)^{1-\frac{1}{p}} \leq C_{s,R} \hspace{0.1cm} p^\beta  \rho_{s,R,N}(\Phi_N(t)A)^{1-\frac{1}{p}}
     \end{equation*}
     for all $p \in [1,+\infty)$. It means that the function $F(t):=\rho_{s,R,N}(\Phi_N(t)A)$ satisfies the differential inequality :
     \begin{equation*}
        | F'(t) | \leq C_{s,R} \hspace{0.1cm} p^\beta F(t)^{1-\frac{1}{p}}
     \end{equation*}
     Integrating this yields :
     \begin{equation*}
        \begin{split}
         F(t) \leq \left( F(0)^{\frac{1}{p}} + C_{s,R}|t| p^{\beta -1} \right)^p &= F(0) \left( 1 + C_{s,R}|t| F(0)^{-\frac{1}{p}}p^{\beta -1} \right)^p \\
         &= F(0) \textnormal{exp}\left(p\textnormal{log}(1+ C_{s,R}|t| F(0)^{-\frac{1}{p}}p^{\beta -1}) \right)
         \end{split}
     \end{equation*}
     Then, using the inequality $\textnormal{log}(1+x)\leq x$ implies : 
     \begin{equation*}
          F(t) \leq F(0) \textnormal{exp}\left( C_{s,R}|t| F(0)^{-\frac{1}{p}}p^\beta) \right)
     \end{equation*}
     Now, we choose $p:=1+\textnormal{log}(\frac{1}{F(0)})$ so that $F(0)^{-\frac{1}{p}} = \textnormal{exp}(\frac{\textnormal{log}(F(0))}{\textnormal{log}(F(0))-1}) \leq \textnormal{exp}(1)$. Hence,
          \begin{equation}\label{ineq optimized in p}
          F(t) \leq F(0) \textnormal{exp}\left( C_{s,R}|t| (1-\textnormal{log}F(0))^\beta \right)
     \end{equation}
     Let us mention the following elementary lemma, whose proof is provided afterwards.
\begin{lem}\label{lem qualitative elementary estimate}
    For every $\alpha \in (0,1)$, there exists a constant $C_{s,R,\alpha,\beta}>0$ such that for all $x \geq 0$ :
    \begin{equation*}
        C_{s,R}|t| \left( 1+x \right)^\beta \leq \alpha x + C_{s,R,\alpha,\beta} \left( 1+|t| \right)^{\frac{1}{1-\beta}}
    \end{equation*}
\end{lem}
Using Lemma~\ref{lem qualitative elementary estimate} in \eqref{ineq optimized in p} with $x=-\textnormal{log}(F(0)) \geq 0$ yields :
\begin{equation*}
    F(t) \leq F(0)^{1-\alpha} \textnormal{exp} \left( C_{s,R,\alpha,\beta} (1+|t|)^{\frac{1}{1-\beta}} \right)
\end{equation*}
which is the desired inequality, so the proof is completed.
<!-- end proof-12 -->
<!-- lem-2: body_md -->
\label{lem qualitative elementary estimate}
    For every $\alpha \in (0,1)$, there exists a constant $C_{s,R,\alpha,\beta}>0$ such that for all $x \geq 0$ :
    \begin{equation*}
        C_{s,R}|t| \left( 1+x \right)^\beta \leq \alpha x + C_{s,R,\alpha,\beta} \left( 1+|t| \right)^{\frac{1}{1-\beta}}
    \end{equation*}
<!-- end lem-2 -->
<!-- proof-13: body_md -->
Let $\alpha \in (0,1)$. We invoke the function $f(x) := C_{s,R}|t|(1+x)^\beta - \alpha x$. We aim to show that $f(x) \leq C_{s,R,\alpha,\beta} \left( 1+|t| \right)^{\frac{1}{1-\beta}}$. Recall that $\beta \in (0,1)$. We have :
    \begin{equation*}
        f'(x) = \beta C_{s,R}|t|(1+x)^{\beta-1} -\alpha \geq 0 \iff (1+x)^{\beta-1}  \geq \frac{\alpha}{\beta C_{s,R}|t|} \iff x \leq \left( \frac{\beta C_{s,R}|t|}{\alpha} \right)^{\frac{1}{1-\beta}} -1
    \end{equation*}
    This implies that $f$ has a maximum at the point $x=\left( \frac{\beta C_{s,R}|t|}{\alpha} \right)^{\frac{1}{1-\beta}} -1$. Thus, for all $x\geq 0$ :
    \begin{equation*}
        \begin{split}
        f(x) &\leq C_{s,R}|t| \left( \frac{\beta C_{s,R}|t|}{\alpha} \right)^{\frac{\beta}{1-\beta}} -\alpha \left( \frac{\beta C_{s,R}|t|}{\alpha} \right)^{\frac{1}{1-\beta}} +\alpha \\
        & = \alpha + (C_{s,R}|t|)^{\frac{1}{1-\beta}} \left( \left( \frac{\beta}{\alpha} \right)^{\frac{\beta}{1-\beta}} - \alpha \left(\frac{\beta}{\alpha} \right)^{\frac{1}{1-\beta}} \right) \\
        & \leq C_{s,R,\alpha,\beta}(1+|t|)^{\frac{1}{1-\beta}}
        \end{split}
    \end{equation*}
    This completes the proof of Lemma~\ref{lem qualitative elementary estimate}.
<!-- end proof-13 -->
<!-- prop-16: body_md -->
\label{prop quantitative quasi-invariance for mu_s,R}
     Let $s>\frac{3}{2}$, $R>0$ and $t\in \mathbb{R}$. Then, there exists $\beta \in (0,1)$ such that for every $\alpha \in (0,1)$, there exists a constant $C=C_{s,R,\alpha,\beta} > 0$ such that for all Borel set $A \subset H^1(\mathbb{T})$ :
    \begin{equation}\label{ineq quantitative quasi-invariance for mu_s,R}
        \mu_{s,R}(\Phi_N(t)A) \leq \mu_{s,R}(A)^{1-\alpha} \textnormal{exp}\left( C(1+|t|)^{\frac{1}{1-\beta}}\right)
    \end{equation}
    uniformly in $N \in \mathbb{N} \cup \{ \infty \}$.
<!-- end prop-16 -->
<!-- proof-14: body_md -->
Let $N\in \mathbb{N} \cup \{ \infty \}$. Recall that $\mu_{s,R}$ is defined in \eqref{mu_s,R}, and observe that we have:
     \begin{equation*}
         \mu_{s,R}=Z_{s,N,R} e^{R_{s,N}(u)} d\rho_{s,R,N}
     \end{equation*}
    (see also Remark \ref{rem mu_s on balls}). Let $\alpha \in (0,1)$. Let us invoke the $\beta \in (0,1)$ and the constant $C>0$ from Proposition~\ref{prop quantitative quasi-invariance for rho_s,R}. Then, for every $q_1 \in (1,\infty)$:
    \begin{equation*}
        \begin{split}
        \mu_{s,R}(\Phi_N(t)A)= Z_{s,R,N} \int_{\Phi(t)A} e^{R_{s,N}(u)} d\rho_{s,R,N} &\leq Z_{s,R,N}  
\left\lVert e^{R_{s,N}} \right\rVert 
_{\mathbb{L}^{q_1}(d\rho_{s,R,N})}\rho_{s,R,N}(\Phi(t)A)^{1-\frac{1}{q_1}} \\
        & \leq C_{s,R,q_1} \rho_{s,R,N}(\Phi(t)A)^{1-\frac{1}{q_1}}
        \end{split}
    \end{equation*}
    where in the last inequality we used \eqref{1/Cs,R leq Zs,R,N leq Cs,R} and Proposition~\ref{prop estimate for the weight of the weighted measure}. Using now Proposition~\ref{prop quantitative quasi-invariance for rho_s,R}, we obtain:
    \begin{equation}\label{first ineq mu_s(phi(t)A)}
        \mu_{s,R}(\Phi_N(t)A) \leq \rho_{s,R,N}(A)^{(1-\alpha)(1-\frac{1}{q_1})} \textnormal{exp}\left( C(1+|t|)^{\frac{1}{1-\beta}}\right)
    \end{equation}
    where the constant $C>0$ depends on $s,R,\alpha$ and $q_1$ (and also $\beta$). On the other hand, for every $q_2 \in (1,\infty)$:
    \begin{equation*}
        \begin{split}
        \rho_{s,R,N}(A) = \frac{1}{Z_{s,R,N}} \int_A e^{-R_{s,N}} d\mu_{s,R} &\leq \frac{1}{Z_{s,R,N}}  
\left\lVert e^{-R_{s,N}} \right\rVert 
_{\mathbb{L}^{q_2}(d\mu_{s,R})} \mu_{s,R}(A)^{1-\frac{1}{q_2}} \\ &\leq C_{s,R,q_2} \mu_{s,R}(A)^{1-\frac{1}{q_2}} 
        \end{split}
    \end{equation*}
     where again in the last inequality we used \eqref{1/Cs,R leq Zs,R,N leq Cs,R} and Proposition~\ref{prop estimate for the weight of the weighted measure}. Then, plugging this into \eqref{first ineq mu_s(phi(t)A)} yields:
    
    \begin{equation*}
        \mu_{s,R}(\Phi_N(t)A) \leq \rho_{s,R,N}(A)^{(1-\alpha)(1-\frac{1}{q_1})(1-\frac{1}{q_2})} \textnormal{exp}\left( C(1+|t|)^{\frac{1}{1-\beta}}\right)
    \end{equation*}
    where now, the constant $C>0$ depends on $s,R,\alpha,q_1$ and $q_2$. Finally, since $\alpha \in (0,1)$ and $q_1,q_2 \in (1,\infty)$ are arbitrary, we have that $(1-\alpha)(1-\frac{1}{q_1})(1-\frac{1}{q_2})$ takes all the values in $(0,1)$. This completes the proof.
<!-- end proof-14 -->
<!-- prop-17: body_md -->
\label{prop Gs,N uniformly bounded in Lp}
    Let $s>\frac{3}{2}$, $R>0$ and $t \in \mathbb{R}$.  For every $p\in [1,+\infty)$, there exists a constant $C(s,R,p,t) \in (0,+\infty)$ such that :
    \begin{equation*}
         
\left\lVert G_{s,N,t} \right\rVert 
_{\mathbb{L}^p(d\mu_{s,R})} \leq C(s,R,p,t)
    \end{equation*}
    uniformly in $N\in \mathbb{N} \cup \{ \infty \}$.
<!-- end prop-17 -->
<!-- proof-15: body_md -->
Let $p \in [1,+\infty)$ and let us prove that $G_{s,N,t}$ belongs to $\mathbb{L}^p(d\mu_{s,R})$. To do so, we use Cavalieri's principle :
    \begin{equation}\label{cavalieri's principle}
         
\left\lVert G_{s,N,t} \right\rVert 
_{L^p(d\mu_{s,R})}^p = p \int_0^{\infty} \lambda^{p-1} \mu_{s,R}(G_{s,N,t} > \lambda) d\lambda
    \end{equation}
    We can estimate $\mu_{s,R}(G_{s,N,t} > \lambda)$ as follows :
    \begin{equation*}
        \begin{split}
           & \mu_{s,R}(G_{s,N,t} > \lambda)= \int \1_{\{G_{s,N,t} > \lambda\} } d\mu_{s,R} = \int \frac{1}{G_{s,N,t}}\1_{\{G_{s,N,t} > \lambda\} }  G_{s,N,t} d\mu_{s,R}\\
            &= \int \frac{1}{G_{s,N,t}}\1_{\{G_{s,N,t} > \lambda\} }   d\left( \Phi_N(t)_\#\mu_{s,R} \right)
            \leq \frac{1}{\lambda} \int \1_{\{G_{s,N,t} > \lambda\} }   d\left( \Phi_N(t)_\#\mu_{s,R} \right) = \frac{1}{\lambda}\mu_{s,R}(\Phi_N(-t)(G_{s,N,t} > \lambda))
        \end{split}
    \end{equation*}
    Here, we can make use of estimate \eqref{ineq quantitative quasi-invariance for mu_s,R} and deduce that for any $\alpha \in (0,1)$, there exists $C=C_{s,R,\alpha}>0$ such that
    \begin{equation*}
        \mu_{s,R}(G_{s,N,t} > \lambda) \leq \frac{1}{\lambda} \mu_{s,R}(G_{s,N,t} > \lambda)^{1-\alpha} \textnormal{exp}\left( C(1+|t|)^{\frac{1}{1-\beta}}\right)
    \end{equation*}
    So, 
        \begin{equation*}
        \mu_{s,R}(G_{s,N,t} > \lambda) \leq \lambda^{-1/\alpha} \textnormal{exp}\left(C'(1+|t|)^{\frac{1}{1-\beta}}\right) =: \lambda^{-1/\alpha} C_{s,R,\alpha,t} 
    \end{equation*}
    (Where $C'=\frac{C}{\alpha}$ still depends only on $s,R$ and $\alpha$). Plugging this into \eqref{cavalieri's principle} yields
    \begin{equation*}
          
\left\lVert G_{s,N,t} \right\rVert 
_{L^p(d\mu_{s,R})}^p \leq p + \int_1^{\infty} \lambda^{p-1} \mu_{s,R}(G_{s,N,t} > \lambda) d\lambda \leq p + C_{s,R,\alpha,t} \int_1^{\infty} \lambda^{p-1-1/ \alpha} d\lambda
    \end{equation*}
    Choosing $\alpha \in (0,1)$ such that $p-1-\frac{1}{\alpha}<-1$, that is $\alpha < \frac{1}{p}$, we have that the integral $\int_1^{\infty} \lambda^{p-1-1/ \alpha} d\lambda$ is finite. Hence, denoting by
    \begin{equation*}
        C(s,R,p,t) :=  p + C_{s,R,\alpha,t} \int_1^{\infty} \lambda^{p-1-1/ \alpha} d\lambda
    \end{equation*}
    leads the result.
<!-- end proof-15 -->
<!-- prop-18: body_md -->
\label{prop Gs,N cvg Gs in Lp}
    Let $s> \frac{3}{2}$ and $R>0$. Then, for every $t\in \mathbb{R}$ and every $p \in [1,+\infty)$, $G_{s,N}(t,.)$ converges to $G_s(t,.)$ in $\mathbb{L}^p(d\mu_{s,R})$.
<!-- end prop-18 -->
<!-- proof-16: body_md -->
Let $q\in (1,+\infty)$. From Proposition~\ref{prop Gs,N uniformly bounded in Lp} and \ref{prop GsN cvg uniformly on cpcts to Gs}, we know that the two following facts hold:
    \begin{equation*}
        \begin{cases}
            \sup_{N \in \mathbb{N}}  
\left\lVert G_{s,N}(t,.) \right\rVert 
_{L^q(d\mu_{s,R})} < +\infty \\
             \text{$G_{s,N}(t,.)$ converges in measure to $G_s(t,.)$ (with respect to $\mu_{s,R}$)}
        \end{cases}
    \end{equation*}
    Then -- see for example \cite{tzvetkov2008invariant} Remark 3.8 -- it implies that for every $p \in [1,q)$, $G_{s,N}(t,.)$ converges in $\mathbb{L}^p(d\mu_{s,R})$ to $G_s(t,.)$. Since $q \in (1,+\infty)$ is arbitrary, we deduce that this convergence holds for every $p \in [1,+\infty)$.
<!-- end proof-16 -->
<!-- rem-17: body_md -->
\label{rem density wrt wgm in L^p and cvgce}
Starting from Proposition~\ref{prop quantitative quasi-invariance for rho_s,R}, it would have also been possible to prove (with the notations of Proposition~\ref{prop Radon-Nikodym derivative for the transported wgm}) that the densities $F_{s,N}(t,.)$, $F_s(t,.)$ of the transported weighted Gaussian measures belongs to $\mathbb{L}^p(d\rho_{s,R})$ and that $F_{s,N}(t,.)$ converges to $F_s(t,.)$ in $\mathbb{L}^p(d\rho_{s,R})$.
<!-- end rem-17 -->
<!-- notns-1: body_md -->
We will intensively use the following notations:
\begin{itemize} 
    \item Given a set of frequencies $k_1,...,k_m \in \mathbb{Z}$, we denote by $k_{(1)},...,k_{(m)}$ a rearrangement of the $k_j's$ such that 
    \begin{equation*}
        |k_{(1)}| \geq |k_{(2)}| \geq ... \geq |k_{(m)}| 
    \end{equation*}
    \item Similarly, given a set of dyadic integers $N_1,...,N_m \in 2^{\mathbb{N}}$, we denote by $N_{(1)},...,N_{(m)}$ a non-decreasing rearrangement of the $N_j$.
\end{itemize}
<!-- end notns-1 -->
<!-- exmps-1: body_md -->
For example, we have :
    \begin{itemize}
        \item If $k_1 = -1$, $k_2=0$, $k_3=2$ then $k_{(1)} = k_3$, $k_{(2)}=k_1$, and $k_{(3)}=k_2$
        \item If $N_1 = 8$, $N_2=2$, $N_3=4$ then $N_{(1)}=N_1$, $N_{(2)}=N_3$, and $N_{(3)}= N_2$
    \end{itemize}
<!-- end exmps-1 -->
<!-- lem-3: body_md -->
\label{lem counting bound}
    There exists a constant $C>0$ such that for every dyadic integers $N_1,...,N_m$, every $\varepsilon_1,...,\varepsilon_m \in \{-1,+1\}$, and every $\kappa \in \mathbb{Z}$,
    \begin{equation}\label{elementary counting bound}
        \sum_{k_1,...,k_m \in \mathbb{Z}} \1_{\varepsilon_1 k_1 +\varepsilon_2 k_2 +...+\varepsilon_m k_m = \kappa} \cdot \left( \prod_{j=1}^{m} \1_{|k_j| \sim N_j} \right) \leq C N_{(2)}N_{(3)}...N_{(m)}
    \end{equation}
<!-- end lem-3 -->
<!-- proof-17: body_md -->
Without loss of generality, we assume that $N_j = N_{(j)}$. The idea of the proof is to let free the variables $k_{2},...,k_{m}$ and to freeze the variable $k_{1}$ thanks to the constraint $\varepsilon_1 k_1 = \kappa -\varepsilon_2 k_2 -...-\varepsilon_m k_m$:
    \begin{equation*}
        \sum_{\substack{k_1,...,k_m \\ |k_j| \sim N_j}} \1_{\varepsilon_1 k_1 +\varepsilon_2 k_2 +...+\varepsilon_m k_m = \kappa} = \sum_{\substack{k_1,...,k_m \\ |k_j| \sim N_j, j\geq2}}  \underbrace{\sum_{|k_1| \sim N_1} \1_{\varepsilon_1 k_1 = \kappa -\varepsilon_2 k_2 -...-\varepsilon_m k_m}}_{\leq 1} \leq \sum_{\substack{k_1,...,k_m \\ |k_j| \sim N_j, j\geq2}} 1 \lesssim N_2 N_3...N_m
    \end{equation*}
<!-- end proof-17 -->
<!-- lem-4: body_md -->
\label{lemma psi estimate}
    Set 
    \begin{align*}
        \psi_{2s}(\vec{k}) &:= \sum_{j=1}^{6} (-1)^{j-1}|k_j|^{2s}, & \Omega(\vec{k}) &= \sum_{j=1}^6 (-1)^{j-1} k_j^2
    \end{align*}
There exists a constant $C(s)>0$ such that for every $k_1-k_2+k_3-k_4+k_5-k_6 = 0$,
\begin{equation*}
    | \psi_{2s}(\vec{k}) | \leq C(s) | k_{(1)} |^{2s-2} \left( | \Omega(\vec{k}) |+| k_{(3)} |^2\right)
\end{equation*}
<!-- end lem-4 -->
<!-- proof-18: body_md -->
Essentially, we have to consider two cases : when $k_{(1)}=k_1$, $k_{(2)}=k_2$ and $k_{(1)}=k_1$, $k_{(2)}=k_3$. In any case, we can assume that $|k_{(3)}| \leq \frac{1}{2} |k_{(2)}|$. Otherwise, using the fact that the constraint $k_1-k_2+k_3-k_4+k_5-k_6 = 0$ implies that $|k_{(2)}| \sim |k_{(1)}|$, we would deduce that $|k_{(3)}| \sim |k_{(1)}|$. Therefore, the a priori bound $ | \psi_{2s}(\vec{k}) | \lesssim |k_{(1)}|^{2s}$ would guarantee the desired inequality. \\

    \underline{Case 1} : Firstly, we consider the case $k_{(1)}=k_1$ and $k_{(2)}=k_2$. We use the mean value theorem :
    \begin{equation*}
        \begin{split}
            |\psi_{2s}(\vec{k})| & \leq k_1^{2s} - k_2^{2s} + |k_3^{2s}-k_4^{2s}+k_5^{2s}-k_6^{2s}| \\
            & \leq \sup_{t \in [k_2^2,k_1^2]} \frac{d}{dt}(t^s) (k_1^2 - k_2^2) + 4 k_{(3)}^{2s} \\
            & \leq s |k_{(1)}|^{2(s-1)}(\Omega(\vec{k}) - k_3^2+k_4^2-k_5^2+k_6^2)  + 4 k_{(1)}^{2(s-1)} k_{(3)}^2 \\
            & \leq C(s) |k_{(1)}|^{2(s-1)} (|\Omega(\vec{k})| + |k_{(3)}|^2)
        \end{split}
    \end{equation*}
which is the desired inequality. \\

    \underline{Case 2} : Secondly, we consider the case  $k_{(1)}=k_1$ and $k_{(2)}=k_3$. Since we assume that $k_{(3)} \leq \frac{1}{2} |k_{(2)}| = \frac{1}{2} |k_{3}|$, we have
    \begin{equation*}
            \Omega(\vec{k}) \geq k_1^2 + k_3^2 -|k_2^2 +k_4^2 -k_5^2+k_6^2| \geq k_1^2 + k_3^2 - 4 k_{(3)}^2 \geq k_1^2
    \end{equation*}
    Therefore, the a priori bound $ | \psi_{2s}(\vec{k}) | \lesssim |k_{(1)}|^{2s}$ guarantees the desired inequality.
<!-- end proof-18 -->
<!-- thm-3: body_md -->
\label{Strichartz estimate}
    For any $\varepsilon >0$, there exists a constant $C_{\varepsilon} > 0$ such that for any function $g$ on $\mathbb{T}$ : 
    \begin{equation*}
         
\left\lVert e^{it\partial_x^2}g \right\rVert 
_{\mathbb{L}^6(\mathbb{T}_t \times \mathbb{T}_x)} \leq C_{\varepsilon}  
\left\lVert g \right\rVert 
_{H^{\varepsilon}(\mathbb{T})}
    \end{equation*}
<!-- end thm-3 -->
<!-- lem-5: body_md -->
\label{Strichartz's trick}
    Let $\varepsilon > 0$. There exists a constant $C_{\varepsilon} > 0$ such that for any dyadic integers $N_1,...,N_6$ and any sequences $\left( f_{k_1}^{(1)} \right)_{k_1 \in \mathbb{Z}}$,...,$\left( f_{k_6}^{(6)} \right)_{k_6 \in \mathbb{Z}}$ of complex numbers that satisfy $f^{(j)}_{k_j} = \1_{|k_j| \sim N_j} f^{(j)}_{k_j} $, we have for any $\kappa \in \mathbb{Z}$ :
    \begin{equation*}
        \sum_{\substack{k_1-k_2+...-k_6=0 \\ \Omega(\vec{k})= \kappa}} \prod_{j=1}^6 |f_{k_j}^{(j)}| \leq C_{\varepsilon} N_{(1)}^{\varepsilon} \prod_{j=1}^6  
\left\lVert f^{(j)} \right\rVert 
_{l^2}
    \end{equation*}
<!-- end lem-5 -->
<!-- proof-19: body_md -->
We set
    \begin{align*}
        F_0^{(1)}(x) &:= \sum_{k_1 \in \mathbb{Z}} |f_{k_1}^{(1)} |e^{i k_1 x}, &  F^{(1)}(t,x) & := e^{it\partial_x^2}e^{it \kappa}F_0^{(1)}(x)
    \end{align*}
    and for $j \geq 2$, 
    \begin{align*}
         F_0^{(j)}(x) &:= \sum_{k_j \in \mathbb{Z}} |f_{k_j}^{(j)}| e^{i k_j x}, &  F^{(j)}(t,x) & := e^{it\partial_x^2}F_0^{(j)}(x)
    \end{align*}
    Let us now prove the identity : 
    \begin{equation}\label{sum as an integral}
        \sum_{\substack{k_1-k_2+...-k_6=0 \\ \Omega(\vec{k})= \kappa}} \prod_{j=1}^6 |f_{k_j}^{(j)}| = \int_{\mathbb{T}_t} \int_{\mathbb{T}_x} \left( F^{(1)} 
  \overline{F^{(2)}} 
  F^{(3)} 
  \overline{F^{(4)}} 
  F^{(5)} 
  \overline{F^{(6)}} 
   \right) (t,x) \frac{dxdt}{(2\pi)^2}
    \end{equation}
    Firstly, we expand
    \begin{equation*}
        \left( F^{(1)} 
  \overline{F^{(2)}} 
  F^{(3)} 
  \overline{F^{(4)}} 
  F^{(5)} 
  \overline{F^{(6)}} 
   \right) (t,x) = \sum_{k_1,...,k_6 \in \mathbb{Z}} |f_{k_1}^{(1)}...f_{k_6}^{(6)}| e^{ix(k_1-k_2+...-k_6)} e^{-it (\Omega(\vec{k}) - \kappa)}
    \end{equation*}
    Secondly, we integrate with respect to $x$ and $t$ 
    \begin{equation*}
        \begin{split}
            \int_{\mathbb{T}_t} \int_{\mathbb{T}_x}   F^{(1)} 
  \overline{F^{(2)}} 
  & F^{(3)} 
  \overline{F^{(4)}} 
  F^{(5)} 
  \overline{F^{(6)}} 
   (t,x) \frac{dxdt}{(2\pi)^2} \\
            & =   \sum_{k_1,...,k_6 \in \mathbb{Z}} |f_{k_1}^{(1)}...f_{k_6}^{(6)}| \left( \int_{\mathbb{T}_t} \int_{\mathbb{T}_x} e^{ix(k_1-k_2+...-k_6)} e^{-it (\Omega(\vec{k})-\kappa)} \frac{dxdt}{(2\pi)^2} \right)
       \end{split}
    \end{equation*}
    Then, the formula \eqref{sum as an integral} follows from the fact that 
    \begin{equation*}
        \int_{\mathbb{T}_t} \int_{\mathbb{T}_x} e^{ix(k_1-k_2+...-k_6)} e^{-it (\Omega(\vec{k}) -\kappa)} \frac{dxdt}{(2\pi)^2} = \1_{k_1-k_2+...-k_6=0} \1_{\Omega(\vec{k}) = \kappa}
    \end{equation*}
    Starting now from \eqref{sum as an integral} and using the Hölder's inequality and Theorem~\ref{Strichartz estimate} we get that 
    \begin{equation*}
       \sum_{\substack{k_1-k_2+...-k_6=0 \\ \Omega(\vec{k})= \kappa}} \prod_{j=1}^6 |f_{k_j}^{(j)}| \leq \prod_{j=1}^6  
\left\lVert F^{(j)} \right\rVert 
_{\mathbb{L}^6(\mathbb{T}_t \times \mathbb{T}_x)} \leq C_{\varepsilon} \prod_{j=1}^6  
\left\lVert F_0^{(j)} \right\rVert 
_{H^{\frac{\varepsilon}{6}}(\mathbb{T}_x)}
    \end{equation*}
    We also used the fact that $ 
\left\lVert F^{(1)} \right\rVert 
_{\mathbb{L}^6(\mathbb{T}_t \times \mathbb{T}_x)} =  
\left\lVert e^{it\kappa}e^{it\partial_x^2}F^{(1)}_0 \right\rVert 
_{\mathbb{L}^6(\mathbb{T}_t \times \mathbb{T}_x)} =  
\left\lVert e^{it\partial_x^2}F^{(1)}_0 \right\rVert 
_{\mathbb{L}^6(\mathbb{T}_t \times \mathbb{T}_x)}$. \\

    On the other hand, with the localizations of the sequences $\left( f^{(j)}_{k_j}\right)_{k_j \in \mathbb{Z}}$, we can write 
    \begin{equation*}
         
\left\lVert F_0^{(j)} \right\rVert 
_{H^{\frac{\varepsilon}{6}}(\mathbb{T}_x)} \lesssim N_j^{\frac{\varepsilon}{6}} 
\left\lVert f^{(j)} \right\rVert 
_{l^2}  \lesssim N_{(1)}^{\frac{\varepsilon}{6}} 
\left\lVert f^{(j)} \right\rVert 
_{l^2}
    \end{equation*}
    Coming back to the previous estimate we obtain 
    \begin{equation*}
        \sum_{\substack{k_1-k_2+...-k_6=0 \\ \Omega(\vec{k})= \kappa}} \prod_{j=1}^6 |f_{k_j}^{(j)}| \leq C'_{\varepsilon} N_{(1)}^{\varepsilon}\prod_{j=1}^6  
\left\lVert f^{(j)} \right\rVert 
_{l^2}
    \end{equation*}
    which is the desired estimate.
<!-- end proof-19 -->
<!-- lem-6: body_md -->
\label{an estimate using Strichartz's trick}
       Let $s\in\mathbb{R}$ and $\varepsilon > 0$. There exists a constant $C_{\varepsilon,s} > 0$ such that for any dyadic integers $N_1,...,N_6$ and any sequences $\left( f_{k_1}^{(1)} \right)_{k_1 \in \mathbb{Z}}$,...,$\left( f_{k_6}^{(6)} \right)_{k_6 \in \mathbb{Z}}$ of complex numbers that satisfy $f^{(j)}_{k_j} = \1_{|k_j| \sim N_j} f^{(j)}_{k_j} $, we have
        \begin{equation*}
