            \sum_{\substack{k_1-k_2+...-k_6=0 \\ \Omega(\vec{k}) \neq 0}} \left| \frac{\psi_{2s}(\vec{k})}{\Omega(\vec{k})}\right| \prod_{j=1}^6 | f_{k_j}^{(j)} | \leq C_{\varepsilon,s} N_{(1)}^{2s-2+\varepsilon} N_{(3)}^{2} \prod_{j=1}^6  
\left\lVert f^{(j)} \right\rVert 
_{l^2}
        \end{equation*}
<!-- end lem-6 -->
<!-- proof-20: body_md -->
We start by applying Lemma~\ref{lemma psi estimate} :
    \begin{equation*}
        \begin{split}
            \sum_{\substack{k_1-k_2+...-k_6=0 \\ \Omega(\vec{k}) \neq 0}} \left| \frac{\psi_{2s}(\vec{k})}{\Omega(\vec{k})}\right| \prod_{j=1}^6 | f_{k_j}^{(j)} | & \lesssim \sum_{\substack{k_1-k_2+...-k_6=0 \\ \Omega(\vec{k}) \neq 0}} |k_{(1)}|^{2s-2} \left( 1 + \frac{|k_{(3)}|^2}{|\Omega(\vec{k})|} \right)  \prod_{j=1}^6 | f_{k_j}^{(j)} | \\
            & \lesssim \hspace{.5cm} \textbf{I} + \textbf{II}
        \end{split}
    \end{equation*}
    where we denote 
    \begin{equation*}
        \textbf{I} := N_{(1)}^{2s-2}\sum_{\substack{k_1-k_2+...-k_6=0 \\ \Omega(\vec{k}) \neq 0}} \prod_{j=1}^6 | f_{k_j}^{(j)} |
    \end{equation*}
    and,
    \begin{equation*}
        \textbf{II} := N_{(1)}^{2s-2} N_{(3)}^2\sum_{\substack{k_1-k_2+...-k_6=0 \\ \Omega(\vec{k}) \neq 0}} \frac{1}{|\Omega(\vec{k})|}\prod_{j=1}^6 | f_{k_j}^{(j)} |
    \end{equation*}
    We estimate separately \textbf{I} and \textbf{II}. \\

    \textbullet \textbf{Estimate of I :} Removing the constraint $\Omega(\vec{k}) \neq 0$ and using the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality in the $k_{(1)},k_{(2)}$ summations, we get that
    \begin{equation*}
        \begin{split}
            \textbf{I} & \leq N_{(1)}^{2s-2}  
\left\lVert f^{\left( (1)\right)} \right\rVert 
_{l^2}  
\left\lVert f^{\left( (2)\right)} \right\rVert 
_{l^2} \prod_{j=3}^6  
\left\lVert f^{\left( (j)\right)} \right\rVert 
_{l^1} \\
            & \leq N_{(1)}^{2s-2} \left( N_{(3)} N_{(4)}N_{(5)} N_{(6)} \right)^{\frac{1}{2}} \prod_{j=1}^6  
\left\lVert f^{(j)} \right\rVert 
_{l^2} \\
            & \leq N_{(1)}^{2s-2}  N_{(3)}^2 \prod_{j=1}^6  
\left\lVert f^{(j)} \right\rVert 
_{l^2}
        \end{split} 
    \end{equation*}
    which is even better than the desired bound. \\
    
    \textbullet \textbf{Estimate of II :} Firstly, we observe that $|\Omega(\vec{k})|\lesssim N_{(1)}^2$ so we can write
    \begin{equation*}
        \textbf{II} \leq N_{(1)}^{2s-2} N_{(3)}^2 \sum_{ N_{(1)}^2 \gtrsim |\kappa| \geq 1} \frac{1}{|\kappa|} \sum_{\substack{k_1-k_2+...-k_6=0 \\ \Omega(\vec{k}) = \kappa}} \prod_{j=1}^6 |f_{k_j}^{(j)}|
    \end{equation*}
    Secondly, we use Lemma~\ref{Strichartz's trick} that says
    \begin{equation*}
            \sum_{\substack{k_1-k_2+...-k_6=0 \\ \Omega(\vec{k}) = \kappa}} \prod_{j=1}^6 |f_{k_j}^{(j)}| \leq C_{\varepsilon} N_{(1)}^{\frac{\varepsilon}{2}}\prod_{j=1}^6  
\left\lVert f^{(j)} \right\rVert 
_{l^2}
    \end{equation*}
    Finally, we invoke the well-known estimate 
    \begin{equation*}
        \sum_{ N_{(1)}^2 \gtrsim |\kappa| \geq 1} \frac{1}{|\kappa|} \lesssim \textnormal{log} \left( N_{(1)}\right) \leq C'_{\varepsilon}N_{(1)}^{\frac{\varepsilon}{2}}
    \end{equation*}
    and the combination of those inequalities yields 
    \begin{equation*}
        \textbf{II} \leq C''_{\varepsilon} N_{(1)}^{2s-2+\varepsilon} N_{(3)}^2 \prod_{j=1}^6  
\left\lVert f^{(j)} \right\rVert 
_{l^2}
    \end{equation*}
    which is the desired bound. 
    This completes the proof of Lemma~\ref{an estimate using Strichartz's trick}.
<!-- end proof-20 -->
<!-- lem-7: body_md -->
Let $s\in \mathbb{R}$ and $\sigma < s-\frac{1}{2}$. Then, there exists $C=C(s,\sigma)>0$ such that for all $m \geq 1$ :
    \begin{equation}\label{Gaussian moments}
       \Big( \int_{H^{\sigma}}   
\left\lVert u \right\rVert_{H^{\sigma}}  
^m d\mu_s \Big)^{\frac{1}{m}} \leq C m^{\frac{1}{2}} 
    \end{equation}
<!-- end lem-7 -->
<!-- proof-21: body_md -->
From Fernique's theorem (see for example \cite{kuo2006gaussian}, \cite{bogachev1998gaussian}), there exists $\alpha>0$ such that:
\begin{equation*}
    \int_{H^{\sigma}} e^{\alpha  
\left\lVert u \right\rVert 
_{H^{\sigma}}^2} d\mu_s < + \infty
\end{equation*}
Then, by Markov's inequality, we obtain the following large deviation estimate:
\begin{equation*}
    \mu_s(  
\left\lVert u \right\rVert_{H^{\sigma}}  
 > \lambda) = \mu_s(e^{\alpha   
\left\lVert u \right\rVert_{H^{\sigma}}  
^2} > e^{\alpha \lambda^2}) \leq e^{-\alpha \lambda^2} \int_{H^{\sigma}} e^{\alpha  
\left\lVert u \right\rVert 
_{H^{\sigma}}^2} d\mu_s \leq C e^{-\alpha \lambda^2}
\end{equation*}
Combining this estimate with Cavalieri's principle, we have:
\begin{equation*}
    \int_{H^{\sigma}}   
\left\lVert u \right\rVert_{H^{\sigma}}  
^m d\mu_s = m \int_0^{+\infty} \lambda^{m-1} \mu_s({  
\left\lVert u \right\rVert_{H^{\sigma}}  
>\lambda}) d\lambda \leq C m \int_0^{+\infty} \lambda^{m-1} e^{-\alpha \lambda^2} d\lambda
\end{equation*}
To conclude, we perform $\lfloor \frac{m}{2}\rfloor -1$ integration by parts on the integral on the right hand side:
\begin{equation*}
    \begin{split}
   \int_0^{+\infty} \lambda^{m-1} e^{-\alpha \lambda^2} d\lambda &= \frac{m-2}{2\alpha} \int_0^{+\infty} \lambda^{m-3} e^{-\alpha \lambda^2} d\lambda \\
   &=...= \frac{(m-2)(m-4)...(m-2(\lfloor \frac{m}{2}\rfloor-1))}{(2\alpha)^{\lfloor \frac{m}{2}\rfloor-1} }\int_0^{+\infty}\lambda^{m- 2(\lfloor \frac{m}{2}\rfloor-1)-1} e^{-\alpha \lambda^2}d\lambda \\
  & \leq \left( \frac{m}{2\alpha}\right)^{\lfloor \frac{m}{2}\rfloor-1} \sup_{\widetilde{m} \in [0,2]} \int_0^{+\infty} \lambda^{\widetilde{m}}e^{-\alpha \lambda^2} d\lambda
   \end{split}
\end{equation*}
<!-- end proof-21 -->
<!-- lem-8: body_md -->
\label{lem Wiener chaos}
    Let $(\Omega,\mathcal A,\mathbb{P})$ be a probability space and $\mathcal B$ be a $\sigma$-algebra on $\Omega$ such that $\mathcal B \subset \mathcal A$. Let $m \in \mathbb{N}$ and $\iota_1,...,\iota_m \in \{-,+ \}$. We consider the following expression :
    \begin{equation*}
        F(\omega) := \sum_{k_1,...,k_m} c_{k_1,...,k_m}(\omega) \cdot \prod_{j=1}^m g_{k_j}^{\iota_j}(\omega), \hspace{1cm} \omega \in \Omega
    \end{equation*}
    where, the $g_{k_j}(\omega)$ are complex standard i.i.d Gaussians, independent of the $\sigma$-algebra $\mathcal B$, and the $c_{k_1,...,k_m}(\omega)$ are $\mathcal B$-mesurable complex random variables. Then, there exists $C>0$ such that for every $p\geq 2$, we have :
    \begin{equation*}
         
\left\lVert F \right\rVert 
_{\mathbb{L}^p(\Omega | \mathcal B)} \leq C p^{\frac{m}{2}}  
\left\lVert F \right\rVert 
_{\mathbb{L}^2(\Omega | \mathcal B)}
    \end{equation*}
    where $\mathbb{L}^p(\Omega | \mathcal B)$ is the $\mathbb{L}^p$-norm conditioned to the $\sigma$- algebra $\mathcal B$.
<!-- end lem-8 -->
<!-- lem-9: body_md -->
\label{L2 estimate with orthogonality}
    Let $(\Omega,\mathcal A,\mathbb{P})$ be a probability space. Let $m\in \mathbb{N}$, $\iota_1,...,\iota_m \in \{-,+ \}$, and $g_{k_1},...,g_{k_m}$ be complex standard i.i.d Gaussians. We consider the following multi-linear expression of Gaussians:
    \begin{equation}\label{mult lin gauss}
        G(\omega) := \sum_{\substack{k_1,...,k_m \\ \forall \iota_i \neq \iota_j, \hspace{0.1cm} k_i \neq k_j}} c_{k_1,...,k_m} \cdot \prod_{j=1}^m g_{k_j}^{\iota_j}(\omega), \hspace{1cm} \omega \in \Omega 
    \end{equation}
    where $c_{k_1,...,k_m}$ is a sequence of $l^2(\mathbb{Z}^m;\mathbb{C})$. Then, there exists $C>0$ such that:
    \begin{equation}\label{ineq L2 estimate orhtogonality}
         
\left\lVert G \right\rVert 
_{\mathbb{L}^2(\Omega)} \leq C \biggl( \sum_{\substack{k_1,...,k_m \\ \forall \iota_i \neq \iota_j, \hspace{0.1cm} k_i \neq k_j}} | c_{k_1,...,k_m} |^2 \biggr)^{\frac{1}{2}}
    \end{equation}
<!-- end lem-9 -->
<!-- proof-22: body_md -->
For more readability, we perform the proof only for $m=3$ (and that is the value of $m$ we will use with this lemma). In addition, we assume that $\iota_1, \iota_3=1$ and $\iota_2=-1$ (the other cases are similar). Thus, we want to prove that:
    \begin{equation*}
        \big\|  \sum_{\substack{k_1,k_2,k_3 \\  k_2 \neq k_1,k_3}} c_{k_1,k_2,k_3} g_{k_1}  
  \overline{g_{k_2}} 
   g_{k_3} \big\|_{\mathbb{L}^2(\Omega)}^2 \leq C \sum_{\substack{k_1,k_2,k_3 \\  k_2 \neq k_1,k_3}} | c_{k_1,k_2,k_3} |^2 
    \end{equation*}
    We start by expanding the left hand side:
    \begin{equation}\label{expanding L^2 norm}
         \big\|  \sum_{\substack{k_1,k_2,k_3 \\  k_2 \neq k_1,k_3}} c_{k_1,k_2,k_3} g_{k_1}  
  \overline{g_{k_2}} 
   g_{k_3} \big\|_{\mathbb{L}^2(\Omega)}^2 =  \sum_{\substack{k_1,k_2,k_3,l_1,l_2,l_3 \\  k_2 \neq k_1,k_3 \hspace{0.1cm} \& \hspace{0.1cm} l_2 \neq l_1,l_3}} c_{k_1,k_2,k_3}  
  \overline{c_{l_1,l_2,l_3}} 
   \hspace{0.1cm} \mathbb{E}[g_{k_1}  
  \overline{g_{k_2}} 
   g_{k_3}  
  \overline{g_{l_1}} 
   g_{l_2}  
  \overline{g_{l_3}} 
  ]
    \end{equation}
    From the independence of the Gaussians $g_n$, and the fact that for a complex standard Gaussian variable $g$ we have $\mathbb{E}[g]=\mathbb{E}[g^2]=\mathbb{E}[g^3]=0$, the only non-zero contributions in the sum above is when for each $g_{k_j}^{\pm}$ there exists an $g_{l_i}^{\mp}$, with the opposite signature, such that $k_j = l_i$. Hence, the only non-zero contributions are of the form:
    \begin{center}
    $c_{k_1,k_2,k_3}  
  \overline{c_{l_1,l_2,l_3}} 
   \hspace{0.1cm}   \mathbb{E}[|g_{k_1}|^2|g_{k_2}|^2|g_{k_3}|^2]$ with $k_2=l_2$, $\{ k_1 , k_3\} = \{ l_1, l_3\}$ and $k_2 \neq k_1,k_3$
    \end{center}
    Then, we invoke the following set of indices:
    \begin{equation*}
        \begin{split}
        D_1 &:= \{ (k_1,k_2,k_3,l_1,l_2,l_3) \in \mathbb{Z}^6 \hspace{0.1cm} : \hspace{0.1cm} k_2 = l_2, \hspace{0.1cm} k_1 = l_1,\hspace{0.1cm} k_3 = l_3, \hspace{0.1cm}   k_2 \neq k_1,k_3, \hspace{0.1cm} k_1 \neq k_3 \} \\
        D_2 &:= \{ (k_1,k_2,k_3,l_1,l_2,l_3) \in \mathbb{Z}^6 \hspace{0.1cm} : \hspace{0.1cm} k_2 = l_2, \hspace{0.1cm} k_1 = l_3,\hspace{0.1cm} k_3 = l_1, \hspace{0.1cm}   k_2 \neq k_1,k_3, \hspace{0.1cm} k_1 \neq k_3 \} \\
        D_3 &:= \{ (k_1,k_2,k_3,l_1,l_2,l_3) \in \mathbb{Z}^6 \hspace{0.1cm} : \hspace{0.1cm} k_2 = l_2, \hspace{0.1cm} k_1 = k_3 = l_1 = l_3, \hspace{0.1cm}   k_2 \neq k_1,k_3\}
        \end{split}
    \end{equation*}
    so that, coming back to \eqref{expanding L^2 norm}, we have (for any complex standard Gaussian $g$):
    \begin{equation*}
        \begin{split}
        \big\|  \sum_{\substack{k_1,k_2,k_3 \\  k_2 \neq k_1,k_3}} c_{k_1,k_2,k_3} g_{k_1}  
  \overline{g_{k_2}} 
   g_{k_3} \big\|_{\mathbb{L}^2(\Omega)}^2 &= \mathbb{E}[|g|^2]^3\sum_{D_1} |c_{k_1,k_2,k_3}|^2  + \mathbb{E}[|g|^2]^3\sum_{D_2} c_{k_1,k_2,k_3}  
  \overline{c_{k_3,k_2,k_1}} 
   \\
        & +\mathbb{E}[|g|^2]\mathbb{E}[|g|^4] \sum_{D_3}  |c_{k_1,k_2,k_1}|^2 
        \end{split}
    \end{equation*}
    This concludes the proof since:
    \begin{equation*}
        \sum_{D_1} |c_{k_1,k_2,k_3}|^2 + \sum_{D_3}  |c_{k_1,k_2,k_1}|^2  = \sum_{\substack{k_1,k_2,k_3 \\ k_2\neq k_1,k_3 \hspace{0.1cm} \& \hspace{0.1cm} k_1 \neq k_3}}|c_{k_1,k_2,k_3}|^2 + \sum_{\substack{k_1,k_2 \\ k_2 \neq k_1}}|c_{k_1,k_2,k_1}|^2 =  \sum_{\substack{k_1,k_2,k_3 \\  k_2 \neq k_1,k_3}} | c_{k_1,k_2,k_3} |^2
    \end{equation*}
    and,
    \begin{equation*}
        \sum_{D_2} c_{k_1,k_2,k_3}  
  \overline{c_{k_3,k_2,k_1}} 
   \leq \frac{1}{2} \sum_{\substack{k_1,k_2,k_3 \\ k_2\neq k_1,k_3 \hspace{0.1cm} \& \hspace{0.1cm} k_1 \neq k_3}} |c_{k_1,k_2,k_3}|^2 + \frac{1}{2} \sum_{\substack{k_1,k_2,k_3 \\ k_2\neq k_1,k_3 \hspace{0.1cm} \& \hspace{0.1cm} k_1 \neq k_3}} |c_{k_3,k_2,k_1}|^2 \leq \sum_{\substack{k_1,k_2,k_3 \\  k_2 \neq k_1,k_3}} | c_{k_1,k_2,k_3} |^2
    \end{equation*}
<!-- end proof-22 -->
<!-- rem-18: body_md -->
When $\iota_i \neq \iota_j$  \textbf{and} $\hspace{0.1cm} k_i = k_j$, we say that $k_i$ and $k_j$ are paired. If one allows such parings in the sum in \eqref{mult lin gauss}, then the inequality \eqref{ineq L2 estimate orhtogonality} does not hold anymore in general. In our analysis in the upcoming sections, we will not encounter such pairings. However, in \cite{sun2023quasi}, this situation occurred, and the authors needed to study these pairing contributions separately.
<!-- end rem-18 -->
<!-- proof-23: body_md -->
Let $\sigma < s-\frac{1}{2}$ and let $u^{(1)},...,u^{(6)} \in H^{\sigma}(\mathbb{T})$. First, we decompose the sum in \eqref{energy correction with absolute value} dyadically:
    \begin{equation}\label{starting estimate R}
        \sum_{\substack{k_1-k_2+...-k_6=0 \\ \Omega(\vec{k}) \neq 0}} \big| \frac{\psi_{2s}(\vec{k})}  {\Omega(\vec{k})}\big||u^{(1)}_{k_1}u^{(2)}_{k_2}...u^{(6)}_{k_6}| = \sum_{N_1,...,N_6} \mathfrak{R}(N_1,...,N_6)
    \end{equation}
    where the summations are performed on the dyadic values of $N_1,...,N_6$ and,
    \begin{equation*}
        \mathfrak{R}(N_1,...,N_6) := \sum_{\substack{k_1-k_2+...-k_6=0 \\ \Omega(\vec{k}) \neq 0}} \big| \frac{\psi_{2s}(\vec{k})}  {\Omega(\vec{k})}\big| \prod_{j=1}^6 \1_{|k_j| \sim N_j} |u^{(j)}_{k_j}|
    \end{equation*}
    Now, using Lemma~\ref{an estimate using Strichartz's trick} yields:
    \begin{equation}\label{R dyadic estimate L2}
         \mathfrak{R}(N_1,...,N_6) \lesssim_{\varepsilon} N_{(1)}^{2s-2+\varepsilon} N_{(3)}^2 \prod_{j=1}^{6}  
\left\lVert P_{N_j}u^{(j)} \right\rVert 
_{\mathbb{L}^2(\mathbb{T})} \lesssim_{\varepsilon}N_{(1)}^{2s-2+\varepsilon} N_{(3)}^2 (N_{(1)} ... N_{(6)})^{-\sigma}\prod_{j=1}^6   
\left\lVert u^{(j)} \right\rVert_{H^{\sigma}}  
 
    \end{equation}
    where $P_{N}$ is the projector onto frequencies $|k| \sim N$. Note that we have $N_{(1)} \sim N_{(2)}$ because the constraint $k_1-k_2+...-k_6 = 0$ implies that $ |k_{(2)}|  \sim |k_{(1)}|$. Besides, we crudely estimate $(N_{(4)}N_{(5)}N_{(3)})^{-\sigma} \lesssim 1$. Then, we rewrite the inequality above as: 
    \begin{equation}\label{R dyadic estimate Hsig}
         \mathfrak{R}(N_1,...,N_6) \lesssim_{\varepsilon} N_{(1)}^{2(s-1-\sigma)+\varepsilon} N_{(3)}^{2-\sigma} \prod_{j=1}^6   
\left\lVert u^{(j)} \right\rVert_{H^{\sigma}}  
  
    \end{equation}
    Next, let us observe that for $\sigma < s -\frac{1}{2}$ and $\varepsilon>0$: 

\begin{align*}
    &\begin{cases}
        2(s-1-\sigma)+\varepsilon > -1 \\
        2(s-1-\sigma)+\varepsilon \longrightarrow -1 \hspace{0.2cm} \text{as} \begin{cases}
            \sigma \rightarrow s-\frac{1}{2} \\
            \varepsilon \rightarrow 0
        \end{cases}
    \end{cases} 
    & &\text{and,} & &\begin{cases}
        2-\sigma > \frac{5}{2} -s \\
        2-\sigma \longrightarrow \frac{5}{2} -s \hspace{0.2cm} \text{as}  \begin{cases}
            \sigma \rightarrow s-\frac{1}{2} \\
            \varepsilon \rightarrow 0
        \end{cases}
    \end{cases}
\end{align*}
In particular, in \eqref{R dyadic estimate Hsig}, $N_{(1)}$ is accompanied by a negative exponent\footnote{In dimension $d\geq 2$, we have $\sigma <s-\frac{d}{2}$, and this scenario would be worse because we would have $2(s-1-\sigma)>0$, so $N_{(1)}$ would be accompanied by a positive exponent. This scenario is encountered in \cite{sun2023quasi}, with $d=3$.}. \\
Finally, if:
\begin{align*}
    &-1 + (\frac{5}{2} - s) < 0, & & \text{that is if:} & & s>\frac{3}{2}, 
\end{align*}
then, for $\sigma<s-\frac{1}{2}$ and $\varepsilon>0$ respectively close enough to $s-\frac{1}{2}$ and 0, we deduce from \eqref{R dyadic estimate Hsig} that\footnote{The notation $N^{-}$ means that the power of $N$ is $-\gamma$ for a certain $\gamma>0$.}:
\begin{equation*}
    \mathfrak{R}(N_1,...,N_6) \lesssim N_{(1)}^{-}  \cdot \prod_{j=1}^6   
\left\lVert u^{(j)} \right\rVert_{H^{\sigma}}  

\end{equation*}
which is summable in the $N_j$. Coming back to \eqref{starting estimate R} finishes the proof.
<!-- end proof-23 -->
<!-- proof-24: body_md -->
Let $\sigma < s-\frac{1}{2}$. \\
    \textbullet \textbf{Estimate for $\mathcal T_0$ :} The analysis is similar to the one for $\mathcal R$. Indeed, let us fix $u^{(1)},...,u^{(6)} \in H^{\sigma}(\mathbb{T})$. Then, decomposing the sum in \eqref{T0 with abs value} dyadically and using Lemma~\ref{lemma psi estimate} (with $\Omega(\vec{k}) = 0$), leads to:
     \begin{equation*}
        \begin{split}
             \sum_{\substack{k_1-k_2+...-k_6=0 \\ \Omega(\vec{k}) = 0}} | \psi_{2s} (\vec{k})| |u^{(1)}_{k_1}u^{(2)}_{k_2}...u^{(6)}_{k_6}|  & \lesssim \sum_{\substack{k_1-k_2+...-k_6=0 \\ \Omega(\vec{k}) = 0}} |k_{(1)}|^{2s-2} |k_{(3)}|^2 |u^{(1)}_{k_1}u^{(2)}_{k_2}...u^{(6)}_{k_6}| \\
            & \lesssim \sum_{N_1,...,N_6} \mathfrak{T}_0(N_1,...,N_6)
        \end{split}
    \end{equation*}
     where,
    \begin{equation*}
        \mathfrak{T}_0(N_1,...,N_6) := \sum_{\substack{k_1-k_2+...-k_6=0 \\ \Omega(\vec{k}) = 0}} N_{(1)}^{2s-2} N_{(3)}^2 \prod_{j=1}^6 \1_{|k_j| \sim N_j} |u^{(j)}_{k_j}|
    \end{equation*}
    Next, from Lemma~\ref{Strichartz's trick} (with $f^{j}_{k_j} = \1_{|k_j| \sim N_j} |u^{(j)}_{k_j}|$), we have:  
    \begin{equation*}
         \mathfrak{T}_0(N_1,...,N_6) \lesssim_{\varepsilon}  N_{(1)}^{2s-2+\varepsilon} N_{(3)}^2 \prod_{j=1}^{6}  
\left\lVert P_{N_j}u^{(j)} \right\rVert 
_{\mathbb{L}^2(\mathbb{T})}
    \end{equation*}
From that point the proof goes the same as the one for $\mathcal R$ (see the estimate \eqref{R dyadic estimate L2}).\\

\textbullet \textbf{Estimate of $\mathcal T_j$ for $j=1,2$:} We only prove the estimate \eqref{T1 with abs value} since the analysis for the estimate \eqref{T2 with abs value} is similar. Here, the computations are a little more delicate. For the sake of readability, we restrict ourselves to prove the estimate:
\begin{equation*}
    \sum_{\substack{k_1-k_2+...-k_6=0 \\ p_1-p_2+...+p_5 =k_1 \\\Omega(\vec{k}) \neq 0}} \big| \frac{\psi_{2s}(\vec{k})}{ \Omega(\vec{k})} \big| | u_{p_1} 
  \overline{u_{p_2}} 
  ...u_{p_5} 
  \overline{u_{k_2}} 
  ... 
  \overline{u_{k_6}} 
  | \leq C_s   
\left\lVert u \right\rVert_{H^{\sigma}}  
^{10}
\end{equation*}
In other words, we just prove the estimate \eqref{T1 with abs value} where all the $u^{(j)}$ and $v^{(l)}$ are equal to a single $u$.
To do so, we will use the following lemma:
\begin{lem}\label{technical lem Q estimate}
    There exists a constant $C > 0$ such that for any dyadic integers $P_1,...,P_5$ and any sequences $\left(g^{P_1}_{p_1} \right)_{p_1 \in \mathbb{Z}}, ... , \left(g^{P_5}_{p_5} \right)_{p_5 \in \mathbb{Z}} $ of complex numbers that satisfy for $j=1,...,5$, $g^{P_j}_{p_j} = \1_{|p_j| \sim P_j} g_{p_j}$, if we set for $k_1 \in \mathbb{Z}$ :
    \begin{equation*}
        f_{k_1} := \sum_{p_1-p_2+...+p_5 =k_1}  g_{p_1}^{P_1}g_{p_2}^{P_2}g_{p_3}^{P_3}g_{p_4}^{P_4}g_{p_5}^{P_5}
    \end{equation*}
    Then,
    \begin{equation*}
         
\left\lVert f \right\rVert 
_{l^2(\mathbb{Z})} \leq C \left( P_{(2)} P_{(3)}P_{(4)} P_{(5)} \right)^{\frac{1}{2}} \prod_{j=1}^5 
\left\lVert g^{P_j} \right\rVert 
_{l^2(\mathbb{Z})}
    \end{equation*}
\end{lem}
For clarity, we postpone the proof of this lemma for the end of this section. Now we are ready to prove the estimate. Once again, we start by decomposing the sum as:
\begin{equation*}
    \sum_{\substack{k_1-k_2+...-k_6=0 \\ p_1-p_2+...+p_5 =k_1 \\\Omega(\vec{k}) \neq 0}} \big| \frac{\psi_{2s}(\vec{k})}{ \Omega(\vec{k})} \big| | u_{p_1} 
  \overline{u_{p_2}} 
  ...u_{p_5} 
  \overline{u_{k_2}} 
  ... 
  \overline{u_{k_6}} 
  | = \sum_{\substack{M_1,...,M_6 \\ P_1,...,P_5}} \mathfrak{T}_1(M_1,...,M_6,P_1,...,P_5)
\end{equation*}
 where $M_1,...,M_6,P_1,...,P_5$ are dyadic-valued and
    \begin{equation}\label{T_1 dyadic block}
        \mathfrak{T}_1(M_1,...,M_6,P_1,...,P_5) := \sum_{\substack{k_1-k_2+...-k_6=0 \\ p_1-p_2+...+p_5 =k_1 \\\Omega(\vec{k}) \neq 0}} \big| \frac{\psi_{2s}(\vec{k})}{ \Omega(\vec{k})} \big| |u_{p_1}^{P_1}...u_{p_5}^{P_5}u_{k_2}^{M_2}...u_{k_6}^{M_6}| \cdot \1_{|k_1| \sim M_1}
    \end{equation}
    with the practical notation $u_l^N := \1_{|l| \sim N} u_l$. Next, we rewrite $\mathfrak{T}_1$ as:
    \begin{equation}\label{T_1 rewritten}
        \mathfrak{T}_1(M_1,...,P_5) =  \sum_{\substack{k_1-k_2+...-k_6=0 \\ \Omega(\vec{k}) \neq 0}} \big| \frac{\psi_{2s}(\vec{k})}{\Omega(\vec{k})}\big| \prod_{j=1}^6 | f_{k_j}^{(j)} |
    \end{equation}
     where, for $j=2,...,6$ we denote $f_{k_j}^{M_j} := u_{k_j}^{M_j}$, and:
    \begin{equation*}
        f_{k_1}^{(1)} := \1_{|k_1| \sim M_1} \cdot \sum_{p_1-p_2+...+p_5 =k_1}  |u_{p_1}^{P_1}...u_{p_5}^{P_5}|
    \end{equation*}
    At this stage, let us recall that $M_{(1)}\geq... \geq M_{(6)}$ and $P_{(1)} \geq ... \geq P_{(5)}$ are respectively a non-increasing rearrangement of $M_1,...,M_6$ and $P_1,...,P_5$. We also introduce:
    \begin{center}
        $N_{(1)} \geq N_{(2)} \geq ... \geq N_{(10)}$ a non-increasing rearrangement of $M_2,...,M_6,P_1,...,P_5$
    \end{center}
    Note that the constraints in the sum in $\mathfrak{T}_1$ imply that 
    \begin{center}
    $M_{(1)} \sim M_{(2)}$, and: $P_{(1)} \sim P_{(2)}$ or $P_{(1)} \sim M_1$, and: $N_{(1)}\sim N_{(2)}$.
    \end{center}
    Now, we use Lemma~\ref{an estimate using Strichartz's trick} to estimate $\mathfrak{T}_1$ in \eqref{T_1 rewritten}; we obtain that for any $\varepsilon>0$:
    \begin{equation*}
            \mathfrak{T}_1(M_1,...,P_5)  \lesssim_{\varepsilon} M_{(1)}^{2s-2+\varepsilon} M_{(3)}^{2} \prod_{j=1}^6  
\left\lVert f^{(j)} \right\rVert 
_{l^2}
              \lesssim_{\varepsilon} M_{(1)}^{2s-2+\varepsilon} M_{(3)}^{2} 
\left\lVert f^{(1)} \right\rVert 
_{l^2} \prod_{j=2}^6  
\left\lVert u^{M_j} \right\rVert 
_{\mathbb{L}^2}
    \end{equation*}
    Applying the well-suited estimate of $ 
\left\lVert f^{(1)} \right\rVert 
_{l^2}$ from Lemma~\ref{technical lem Q estimate} leads to
    \begin{equation}\label{dyadic estimate T_1}
        \mathfrak{T}_1(M_1,...,P_5)  \lesssim_{\varepsilon}  M_{(1)}^{2s-2+\varepsilon} M_{(3)}^{2} (P_{(2)} P_{(3)} P_{(4)} P_{(5)})^{\frac{1}{2}} \prod_{j=1}^5  
\left\lVert u^{P_j} \right\rVert 
_{\mathbb{L}^2} \prod_{j=2}^6  
\left\lVert u^{M_j} \right\rVert 
_{\mathbb{L}^2}
    \end{equation}
    and it follows that
    \begin{equation*}
        \mathfrak{T}_1(M_1,...,P_5)  \lesssim_{\varepsilon}  M_{(1)}^{2s-2+\varepsilon} M_{(3)}^{2} \left( M_2 M_3 M_4 M_5 M_6\right)^{- \sigma} P_{(1)}^{-\sigma} \left( P_{(2)} P_{(3)} P_{(4)}P_{(5)}\right)^{\frac{1}{2} - \sigma}   
\left\lVert u \right\rVert_{H^{\sigma}}  
^{10} 
    \end{equation*}
    In the remaining part of the proof, we show that it implies that:
    \begin{equation}\label{T_1 desired dyadic estimate}
        \mathfrak{T}_1(M_1,...,P_5) \lesssim_{\varepsilon} N_{(1)}^{-}   
\left\lVert u \right\rVert_{H^{\sigma}}  
^{10}
    \end{equation}
   for $\sigma < s-\frac{1}{2}$ close enough to $s-\frac{1}{2}$, which will complete the estimate for $\mathcal T_1$. We start from the inequality above and we use the fact that $M_1 \lesssim P_{(1)}$ due to the constraint $p_1-p_2+...+p_5 =k_1$, along with the rough estimates $( M_{(4)}M_{(5)}M_{(6)})^{-\sigma} \leq 1$ and $( P_{(3)} P_{(4)} P_{(5)})^{\frac{1}{2}-\sigma} \leq 1$, in order to obtain:
    \begin{equation}\label{T_1 dyadic estimate in hisg}
        \begin{split}
        \mathfrak{T}_1(M_1,...,P_5) &\lesssim_{\varepsilon} M_{(1)}^{2s-2+\varepsilon} M_{(3)}^{2} (M_1 M_2 M_3 M_4 M_5 M_6)^{- \sigma} (M_1^{\sigma}P_{(1)}^{-\sigma}) ( P_{(2)} P_{(3)} P_{(4)}P_{(5)})^{\frac{1}{2} - \sigma}   
\left\lVert u \right\rVert_{H^{\sigma}}  
^{10} \\
        & \lesssim_{\varepsilon} M_{(1)}^{2(s-1-\sigma)+\varepsilon} M_{(3)}^{2-\sigma} P_{(2)}^{\frac{1}{2} - \sigma}   
\left\lVert u \right\rVert_{H^{\sigma}}  
^{10}
        \end{split}
    \end{equation}
    Besides, when $\sigma < s - \frac{1}{2}$ and $\varepsilon > 0$ are respectively arbitrarily close to $s - \frac{1}{2}$ and $0$, we have that $2(s-1-\sigma) + \varepsilon$, $2-\sigma$ and $\frac{1}{2} - \sigma$ are respectively arbitrarily close to 
\begin{align*}
    2(s-1-(s-\frac{1}{2})) &= -1, & 2-(s - \frac{1}{2}) &= \frac{5}{2} -s, & \frac{1}{2} - (s - \frac{1}{2}) = 1-s
\end{align*}
    Hence, $M_{(1)}$ is accompanied by a negative exponent, $P_{(2)}$ is accompanied by a negative exponent (since $s>\frac{3}{2}>1$), and $M_{(3)}$ is accompanied by a negative exponent when $s\geq\frac{5}{2}$ and  by a non-negative one when $s<\frac{5}{2}$. \\
    
    --In the situation where $M_{(1)} \sim N_{(1)}$, we use the rough estimate $P_{(2)}^{\frac{1}{2}-\sigma}\leq 1 $ in \eqref{T_1 dyadic estimate in hisg}, and we obtain:
     \begin{equation*}
         \mathfrak{T}_1(M_1,...,P_5)\lesssim_{\varepsilon} N_{(1)}^{2(s-1-\sigma)+\varepsilon} M_{(3)}^{2-\sigma}  
\left\lVert u \right\rVert_{H^{\sigma}}  
^{10}
     \end{equation*}
    which is conclusive as far as 
\begin{equation*}
    2(s-1-(s-\frac{1}{2})) + 2 - (s-\frac{1}{2}) < 0
\end{equation*}
that is, as far as $s > \frac{3}{2}$. \\
--In the other situation, where $M_{(1)} \ll N_{(1)}$, we necessarily have $P_{(1)} \sim P_{(2)} \sim N_{(1)}$, so we deduce from \eqref{T_1 dyadic estimate in hisg} that:
\begin{equation*}
    \mathfrak{T}_1(M_1,...,P_5) \lesssim_{\varepsilon} N_{(1)}^{\frac{1}{2}-\sigma} M_{(3)}^{2(s-1-\sigma) + 2-\sigma +\varepsilon}   
\left\lVert u \right\rVert_{H^{\sigma}}  
^{10}
\end{equation*}
Then, for $\sigma < s - \frac{1}{2}$ and $\varepsilon > 0$ respectively arbitrarily close to $s - \frac{1}{2}$ and $0$, we have:
\begin{equation*}
    \mathfrak{T}_1(M_1,...,P_5) \lesssim N_{(1)}^{(1-s)+} M_{(3)}^{(\frac{3}{2}-s)+}   
\left\lVert u \right\rVert_{H^{\sigma}}  
^{10} \lesssim N_{(1)}^{-}   
\left\lVert u \right\rVert_{H^{\sigma}}  
^{10}
\end{equation*}
since $s>\frac{3}{2}$.\\ 
In conclusion, \eqref{T_1 desired dyadic estimate} is proven and the proof of Proposition~\ref{prop continuity of Qs,N and deterministic estimate} is completed.
<!-- end proof-24 -->
<!-- lem-10: body_md -->
\label{technical lem Q estimate}
    There exists a constant $C > 0$ such that for any dyadic integers $P_1,...,P_5$ and any sequences $\left(g^{P_1}_{p_1} \right)_{p_1 \in \mathbb{Z}}, ... , \left(g^{P_5}_{p_5} \right)_{p_5 \in \mathbb{Z}} $ of complex numbers that satisfy for $j=1,...,5$, $g^{P_j}_{p_j} = \1_{|p_j| \sim P_j} g_{p_j}$, if we set for $k_1 \in \mathbb{Z}$ :
    \begin{equation*}
        f_{k_1} := \sum_{p_1-p_2+...+p_5 =k_1}  g_{p_1}^{P_1}g_{p_2}^{P_2}g_{p_3}^{P_3}g_{p_4}^{P_4}g_{p_5}^{P_5}
    \end{equation*}
    Then,
    \begin{equation*}
         
\left\lVert f \right\rVert 
_{l^2(\mathbb{Z})} \leq C \left( P_{(2)} P_{(3)}P_{(4)} P_{(5)} \right)^{\frac{1}{2}} \prod_{j=1}^5 
\left\lVert g^{P_j} \right\rVert 
_{l^2(\mathbb{Z})}
    \end{equation*}
<!-- end lem-10 -->
<!-- proof-25: body_md -->
We have to estimate : 
    \begin{equation*}
         
\left\lVert f \right\rVert 
_{l^2(\mathbb{Z})}^2 = \sum_{k_1 \in \mathbb{Z}} \bigg|  \sum_{p_1-p_2+...+p_5 =k_1} g_{p_1}^{P_1}g_{p_2}^{P_2}g_{p_3}^{P_3}g_{p_4}^{P_4}g_{p_5}^{P_5}  \bigg|^2
    \end{equation*}
    Using the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality we obtain:
    \begin{equation*}
             
\left\lVert f \right\rVert 
_{l^2(\mathbb{Z})}^2 \leq \sum_{k_1 \in \mathbb{Z}} \bigl( \sum_{p_1,...,p_5} \1_{p_1-p_2+...+p_5 =k_1}  \prod_{j=1}^5 \1_{|p_j| \sim P_j} \bigr)
            \bigl( \sum_{p_1,...,p_5}  \1_{p_1-p_2+...+p_5 =k_1} |g_{p_1}^{P_1}g_{p_2}^{P_2}g_{p_3}^{P_3}g_{p_4}^{P_4}g_{p_5}^{P_5}|^2\bigr)
    \end{equation*}
    Plugging the counting bound \eqref{elementary counting bound} into this formula yields 
    \begin{equation*}
         
\left\lVert f \right\rVert 
_{l^2(\mathbb{Z})}^2 \lesssim P_{(2)}P_{(3)}P_{(4)}P_{(5)}  \sum_{p_1,...,p_5}  |g_{p_1}^{P_1}g_{p_2}^{P_2}g_{p_3}^{P_3}g_{p_4}^{P_4}g_{p_5}^{P_5}|^2  \underbrace{\big( \sum_{k_1 \in \mathbb{Z}} \1_{p_1-p_2+...+p_5 =k_1} \big)}_{\leq 1}
    \end{equation*}
    Thus,
    \begin{equation*}
         
\left\lVert f \right\rVert 
_{l^2(\mathbb{Z})}^2 \lesssim P_{(2)}P_{(3)}P_{(4)}P_{(5)} \prod_{j=1}^5  
\left\lVert g^{P_j} \right\rVert 
_{l^2(\mathbb{Z})}^2
    \end{equation*}
    which is the desired estimate.
<!-- end proof-25 -->
<!-- lem-11: body_md -->
\label{lem R_s,N L^p estimate}
    Let $s > \frac{3}{2}$. Then, there exists $\beta \in (0,1)$ such that for every $R>0$, there exists $C(s,R)>0$, such that for any $p \in [2,+\infty)$,
    \begin{equation*}
        
\left\lVert \1_{\{ \mathcal C(u) \leq R \} } R_{s,N} \right\rVert 
_{\mathbb{L}^p(d\mu_s)} \leq C(s,R)p^\beta
    \end{equation*}
    uniformly in $N \in \mathbb{N} \cup \{ \infty \}$.
<!-- end lem-11 -->
<!-- lem-12: body_md -->
\label{csqce control on all Lp norm}
    Let $(X,\mathcal A,d\nu)$ be a probability space and let $F : X \longrightarrow \mathbb{C}$ be a mesurable function. Assume that there exist constants $C_0 > 0$ and $\beta \in (0,1)$ such that for every $p \in [2,+\infty)$,
    \begin{equation*}
         
\left\lVert F \right\rVert 
_{\mathbb{L}^p(d\nu)} \leq C_0 p^\beta
    \end{equation*}
    Then, there exist $\delta > 0$ and $C_1>0$ only depending on $\beta$ and $C_0$ such that :
    \begin{equation*}
        \int_X e^{\delta |F(v)|^{\frac{1}{\beta}}} d\nu(v) \leq C_1
    \end{equation*}
<!-- end lem-12 -->
<!-- proof-26: body_md -->
Here, we assume the statements in Lemma~\ref{lem R_s,N L^p estimate} and Lemma~\ref{csqce control on all Lp norm}.\\
--We start by proving the first statement in Proposition~\ref{prop estimate for the weight of the weighted measure}. Lemma~\ref{lem R_s,N L^p estimate} shows that $F:=\1_{\{ \mathcal C(u) \leq R \} } R_{s,N}(u) : H^{\sigma}(\mathbb{T}) \longrightarrow \mathbb{C}$ satisfies the assumptions of Lemma~\ref{csqce control on all Lp norm} (with $\nu = \mu_s$). Then, applying Lemma~\ref{csqce control on all Lp norm}, we obtain that there exist $\delta = \delta(s,R) > 0$ and $C_1(s,R) > 0$ such that :
\begin{equation*}
    \int_{H^{\sigma}} e^{\delta \left|  \1_{\{ \mathcal C(u) \leq R \} } R_{s,N}(u) \right|^{\frac{1}{\beta}}} d\mu_s \leq C_1(s,R)
\end{equation*}
A fortiori we have, 
\begin{equation*}
    \int_{H^{\sigma}} \1_{\{ \mathcal C(u) \leq R \} } e^{\delta \left|  R_{s,N}(u) \right|^{\frac{1}{\beta}}} d\mu_s \leq C_1(s,R)
\end{equation*}
Thanks to the fact that $\frac{1}{\beta} > 1$, we deduce from the above inequality that for every $p\in [1,+\infty)$ : 
\begin{equation*}
      
\left\lVert \1_{\{ \mathcal C(u) \leq R \} } e^{|R_{s,N}(u)|} \right\rVert 
^p_{\mathbb{L}^p(d\mu_s)} = \int_{H^{\sigma}} \1_{\{ \mathcal C(u) \leq R \} } e^{p |R_{s,N}(u)|} d\mu_s \leq C(s,R,p) < +\infty
\end{equation*}
for a certain constant $C(s,R,p)>0$.\\
--As a consequence, we are now able to prove the second statement of Proposition~\ref{prop estimate for the weight of the weighted measure}, that is:  
\begin{equation*}
         
\left\lVert \1_{\{ \mathcal C(u) \leq R \} } e^{-R_s(u)}-\1_{\{ \mathcal C(u) \leq R \} } e^{-R_{s,N}(u)} \right\rVert 
_{\mathbb{L}^p(d\mu_s)}  
\underset{N \rightarrow \infty}{\longrightarrow} 
 0
    \end{equation*}
Firstly, we know from Proposition \ref{prop approx R_s by R_s,N on compact sets} that we have the pointwise convergence:
\begin{equation*}
    \1_{ \{\mathcal C(u) \leq R\}}R_s(u) = \1_{ \{\mathcal C(u) \leq R\}} \cdot \frac{1}{6} \textnormal{Re} \sum_{\substack{k_1-k_2+...-k_6=0 \\ \Omega(\vec{k}) \neq 0}} \frac{\psi_{2s}(\vec{k})}{ \Omega(\vec{k})} u_{k_1} 
  \overline{u_{k_2}} 
  ... 
  \overline{u_{k_6}} 
   = \lim_{N\rightarrow \infty} \1_{ \{\mathcal C(u) \leq R\}} R_{s,N}(u)
\end{equation*}
Consequently, from the continuity of the exponential, we also have the pointwise convergence:
\begin{equation*}
   \1_{\{ \mathcal C(u) \leq R \} } e^{-R_s(u)}  = \lim_{N \rightarrow \infty} \1_{\{ \mathcal C(u) \leq R \} } e^{-R_{s,N}(u)}
\end{equation*}
In particular, $\1_{\{ \mathcal C(u) \leq R \} } e^{-R_{s,N}(u)}$ converges to $\1_{\{ \mathcal C(u) \leq R \} } e^{-R_s(u)}$ in measure. In addition, for a fixed $q\in(1,+\infty)$, we just proved that the functions $\1_{\{ \mathcal C(u) \leq R \} } e^{-R_{s,N}(u)}$ are uniformly bounded in $\mathbb{L}^q(d\mu_s)$ (with respect to $N \in \mathbb{N}$). Then, (using the same argument as the one from the proof of Proposition \ref{prop Gs,N cvg Gs in Lp}) we can conclude that $\1_{\{ \mathcal C(u) \leq R \} } e^{-R_{s,N}(u)}$ converges to $\1_{\{ \mathcal C(u) \leq R \} } e^{-R_s(u)}$ in $\mathbb{L}^p(d\mu_s)$ for any $p\in [1,q)$; and since $q \in (1,+\infty)$ is arbitrary, the convergence holds for any $p\in[1,+\infty)$. This completes the proof of Proposition~\ref{prop estimate for the weight of the weighted measure}.
<!-- end proof-26 -->
<!-- defn-1: body_md -->
\label{def pairing}
    Consider a constraint under the form :
    \begin{equation*}
        \varepsilon_1 k_1 + \varepsilon_2 k_2 + ... + \varepsilon_m k_m = 0 
    \end{equation*}
    where $k_j \in \mathbb{Z}$ and $\varepsilon_j \in \{-,+ \}$. We say that $k_j$ and $k_l$ are paired if 
    \begin{equation*}
        \varepsilon_j k_j + \varepsilon_l k_l = 0
    \end{equation*}
<!-- end defn-1 -->
<!-- rem-19: body_md -->
\label{rem no high freq pairing, first generation}
    In $\Lambda_W$ (see \eqref{Lambda_W} above), there is (for $k_{(1)}$ large enough) no pairing within the three highest frequencies (relatively to the constraint $k_1 - k_2 + ... -k_6 = 0$). Indeed, suppose there is a pairing between two of the three highest frequencies. Then, the constraint would take the form:
    \begin{center}
        the remaining high frequency = sum of three low frequencies
    \end{center}
    which is impossible because in $\Lambda_W$ we have:
    \begin{center}
        $|$high frequencies$|$ $\gg$ $|$low frequencies$|$
    \end{center}
<!-- end rem-19 -->
<!-- proof-27: body_md -->
We organize the proof in two steps. In the first step, we provide a (deterministic) estimate for $\1_{\{ \mathcal C(u) \leq R \} } \mathcal R$. In the second step, we show that this estimate is only conclusive for the contribution $\mathcal R^{(D)}$, and that for the remaining contribution $\mathcal R^{(W)}$, further analysis using Wiener chaos is required.\\


    \underline{Step 1, Deterministic estimate :}  We rely on the estimate \eqref{R dyadic estimate L2} we obtained in Section~\ref{section Proofs of the deterministic properties} (which we do not reprove here). Thus, we start our analysis from the following estimates:
    \begin{align}\label{bound R_N1...N6}
        \left| \mathcal R(w) \right| &\lesssim \sum_{N_1,...,N_6} \mathfrak{R}(N_1,...,N_6) & &\text{and:} & \mathfrak{R}(N_1,...,N_6) & \lesssim_{\varepsilon} N_{(1)}^{2s-2+\varepsilon}N_{(3)}^2 \prod_{j=1}^6  
\left\lVert P_{N_j}w \right\rVert 
_{\mathbb{L}^2(\mathbb{T})}
    \end{align}
    where $N_1,...,N_6$ are dyadic valued, $P_N$ is the projector onto frequencies $|k| \sim N$, and:
    \begin{equation*}
        \mathfrak{R}(N_1,...,N_6) := \sum_{\substack{k_1-k_2+...-k_6=0 \\ \Omega(\vec{k}) \neq 0}} \Big| \frac{\psi_{2s}(\vec{k})}{\Omega(\vec{k}) } \Big| \prod_{j=1}^6 \1_{|k_j| \sim N_j} |w_{k_j}|
    \end{equation*}
    We decompose $\mathfrak{R}$ as $\mathfrak{R} = \mathfrak{R}^{(D)} + \mathfrak{R}^{(W)}$, according to the decomposition of $\mathcal R$.  \\
    
 Now, let $1<\sigma'<\sigma<s-\frac{1}{2}$. We have: 
    \begin{equation}\label{P_Nj w L2}
       \prod_{j=1}^6  
\left\lVert P_{N_j}w \right\rVert 
_{\mathbb{L}^2(\mathbb{T})} \lesssim \prod_{j=1}^6  
\left\lVert P_{N_j}u \right\rVert 
_{\mathbb{L}^2(\mathbb{T})} \lesssim (N_{(1)}^{-\sigma}  
\left\lVert u \right\rVert_{H^{\sigma}}  
)(N_{(2)}^{-\sigma'}  
\left\lVert u \right\rVert 
_{H^{\sigma'}})(N_{(3)}N_{(4)}N_{(5)}N_{(6)})^{-1}  
\left\lVert u \right\rVert 
_{H^1}^4
    \end{equation}
   Recall that the constraints in the sum in $\mathfrak{R}$ above implies that $N_{(1)} \sim N_{(2)}$. Moreover, if we write: 
    \begin{equation*}
        \sigma' = \alpha 1 + (1-\alpha) \sigma
    \end{equation*}
    for $\alpha \in (0,1)$, then, by interpolating $H^{\sigma'}$ between $H^1$ and $H^{\sigma}$, we obtain from \eqref{P_Nj w L2} that:
    \begin{equation*}
        \begin{split}
            \prod_{j=1}^6  
\left\lVert P_{N_j}u \right\rVert 
_{\mathbb{L}^2(\mathbb{T})} & \lesssim N_{(1)}^{-2\sigma +\alpha(\sigma-1)}(N_{(3)}N_{(4)}N_{(5)}N_{(6)})^{-1}  
\left\lVert u \right\rVert 
_{H^1}^{4+\alpha}  
\left\lVert u \right\rVert 
^{2-\alpha}_{H^{\sigma}} \\
            & \lesssim N_{(1)}^{-2\sigma +\alpha(s-\frac{3}{2})}(N_{(3)}N_{(4)}N_{(5)}N_{(6)})^{-1}  
\left\lVert u \right\rVert 
_{H^1}^{4+\alpha}  
\left\lVert u \right\rVert 
^{2-\alpha}_{H^{\sigma}}, \hspace{0.3cm} (\textnormal{because $\alpha(\sigma-1) < \alpha(s-3/2)$ })
        \end{split}
    \end{equation*}
    Plugging this into \eqref{bound R_N1...N6}, we obtain 
    \begin{equation*}
        \mathfrak{R}(N_1,...,N_6) \lesssim_{\varepsilon} N_{(1)}^{2(s-\sigma-1)+\varepsilon+\alpha(s-\frac{3}{2})}N_{(3)} (N_{(4)}N_{(5)}N_{(6)})^{-1}  
\left\lVert u \right\rVert 
_{H^1}^{4+\alpha}  
\left\lVert u \right\rVert 
^{2-\alpha}_{H^{\sigma}}
    \end{equation*}
    In particular, thanks to Remark \ref{rem cut-off H1},
    \begin{equation*}
        \1_{\{ \mathcal C(u) \leq R \}} \mathfrak{R}(N_1,...,N_6) \lesssim_{\varepsilon} N_{(1)}^{2(s-\sigma-1)+\varepsilon+\alpha(s-\frac{3}{2})}N_{(3)} (N_{(4)}N_{(5)}N_{(6)})^{-1} R^{4+\alpha}  
\left\lVert u \right\rVert 
^{2-\alpha}_{H^{\sigma}}
    \end{equation*}
    And since we will not need the smallness provided by $(N_{(5)}N_{(6)})^{-1}$, we simply write :
      \begin{equation*}
        \1_{\{ \mathcal C(u) \leq R \}} \mathfrak{R}(N_1,...,N_6) \lesssim_{\varepsilon,R} N_{(1)}^{2(s-\sigma-1)+\varepsilon+\alpha(s-\frac{3}{2})}N_{(3)} N_{(4)}^{-1}  
\left\lVert u \right\rVert 
^{2-\alpha}_{H^{\sigma}}
    \end{equation*}
    Using now \eqref{Gaussian moments}, we conclude that 
    \begin{equation}\label{cR deterministic estimate}
         
\left\lVert \1_{\{ \mathcal C(u) \leq R \}} \mathfrak{R}(N_1,...,N_6) \right\rVert 
_{\mathbb{L}^p(d\mu_s)} \leq C N_{(1)}^{2(s-\sigma-1)+\varepsilon+\alpha(s-\frac{3}{2})}N_{(3)} N_{(4)}^{-1} p^{\frac{2-\alpha}{2}}
    \end{equation}
    Where the constant $C>0$ depends on $R$, $s$, $\sigma$ and $\varepsilon$.
    This is the estimate we will work with later in the proof. We stress the fact that \eqref{cR deterministic estimate} is true for $\mathfrak{R}$ and also for $\mathfrak{R}^{(D)}$ and $\mathfrak{R}^{(W)}$ (with the exact same proof). \bigskip

    \underline{Step 2, Estimates for $\mathcal R^{(D)}$ and $\mathcal R^{(W)}$:} \\
    \textbullet We start with $\mathcal R^{(D)}$. Recalling that $\sigma < s -\frac{1}{2}$, we see that the exponent of $N_{(1)}$ in \eqref{cR deterministic estimate} satisfies:
    \begin{equation}\label{power of N(1)}
        \begin{cases}
            2(s-\sigma-1)+\varepsilon+\alpha(s-\frac{3}{2}) > -1 \\
            2(s-\sigma-1)+\varepsilon+\alpha(s-\frac{3}{2}) \longrightarrow -1 \hspace{0.2cm} \text{as} \begin{cases}
                \varepsilon \rightarrow 0 \\
                \alpha \rightarrow 0 \\
                \sigma \rightarrow s -\frac{1}{2}
            \end{cases}
        \end{cases}
    \end{equation}
    Moreover, for a fixed $\delta_0 \in (0,1)$, the conditions on the indices lying in $\Lambda_D$ imply that $N_{(3)} \lesssim N_{(1)}^{1-\delta_0}$ or $N_{(4)} \gtrsim N_{(3)}^{\delta_0}$. In both cases, we deduce from \eqref{cR deterministic estimate} that for $\varepsilon$ and $\alpha$ close enough to $0$ and $\sigma$ close enough to $s-\frac{1}{2}$, we have\footnote{The notation $N^{-}$ means that the power of $N$ is $-\gamma$ for a certain $\gamma>0$.}
    \begin{equation*}
         
\left\lVert \1_{\{ \mathcal C(u) \leq R \}} \mathfrak{R}^{(D)}(N_1,...,N_6) \right\rVert 
_{\mathbb{L}^p(d\mu_s)} \leq C N_{(1)}^-p^{\frac{2-\alpha}{2}}
    \end{equation*}
    Consequently,
        \begin{equation*}
         
\left\lVert \1_{\{ \mathcal C(u) \leq R \}} \mathcal R^{(D)} \right\rVert 
_{\mathbb{L}^p(d\mu_s)} \leq C p^{\frac{2-\alpha}{2}}
    \end{equation*}
   
\textbullet We continue our analysis with the term $\mathcal R^{(W)}$. Once again, we start by decomposing $\mathcal R^{(W)}$ dyadically as $\mathcal R^{(W)}(w) = \sum_{N_1,...,N_6}  \mathcal R_{N_1,...,N_6}^{(W)}(w)$, where\footnote{For the analysis below, we need to keep the complex conjugation bars, so here we don't use $\mathfrak{R}^{(W)}$}:
    \begin{equation*}
        \mathcal R_{N_1,...,N_6}^{(W)}(w) := \sum_{\substack{k_1-k_2+...-k_6=0 \\ \Omega(\vec{k}) \neq 0 \\ |k_{(4)}| \leq |k_{(3)}|^{\delta_0} }} \frac{\psi_{2s}(\vec{k})}{\Omega(\vec{k})}w_{k_1} 
  \overline{w_{k_2}} 
  ... 
  \overline{w_{k_6}} 
   \prod_{j=1}^6 \1_{|k_j| \sim N_j}
    \end{equation*}

Henceforth, we denote $w_{k_j}^{N_j} := \1_{|k_j|\sim N_j} w_{k_j}$ for better readability. \\
    
    Without loss of generality, we assume that $\{N_1,N_2,N_3 \} = \{N_{(1)}, N_{(2)}, N_{(3)} \}$, meaning that the three highest frequencies are $k_1,k_2,k_3$. The other cases are similar or simpler. \\
    We denote $\mathcal B_{\ll N_{(3)}}$ the $\sigma$-algebra generated by the Gaussians $\left( g_k \right)_{|k|\leq N_{(3)}/100}$. We only need to consider the contribution when $N_{(1)}$ is large because when $N_{(1)}$ is small, all the $N_j$'s are small, and we can use \eqref{cR deterministic estimate} without fearing issues of summability in the $N_j$'s. In particular, we assume that $N_{(1)}$ is sufficiently large so that $N_{(3)}$ (which is $\gtrsim N_{(1)}^{1-\delta_0}$) is large enough to ensure that $N_{(4)}$ (which is $\lesssim N_{(3)}^{\delta_0}$) is $\leq N_{(3)}/100$. As a consequence, we have that the random variables :
    \begin{equation*}
        \begin{split}
           & w_{k_4}^{N_4},w_{k_4}^{N_4},w_{k_5}^{N_6} \hspace{0.2cm} \textnormal{are $\mathcal B_{\ll N_{(3)}}$mesurable} \\
           & w_{k_1}^{N_1},w_{k_2}^{N_2},w_{k_3}^{N_3} \hspace{0.2cm} \textnormal{are independent of $\mathcal B_{\ll N_{(3)}}$}
        \end{split}
    \end{equation*}
    With this set up, we can now begin the analysis. Thanks to Remark \ref{rem cut-off H1}, we have 
    \begin{equation*}
        \begin{split}
             
\left\lVert \1_{\{ \mathcal C(u) \leq R \}} \mathcal R_{N_1,...,N_6}^{(W)} \right\rVert 
_{\mathbb{L}^p(d\mu_s)} & \leq  
\left\lVert \1_{ B_R^{H^1}}(u) \cdot \mathcal R_{N_1,...,N_6}^{(W)} \right\rVert 
_{\mathbb{L}^p(d\mu_s)} \\
            & \leq  
\left\lVert \1_{ B_R^{H^1} } (P_{N_{(3)/100}}u) \cdot \mathcal R_{N_1,...,N_6}^{(W)} \right\rVert 
_{\mathbb{L}^p(d\mu_s)}
        \end{split}
    \end{equation*}
    And, $\1_{ B_R^{H^1} } (P_{N_{(3)/100}}u)$ is $\mathcal B_{\ll N_{(3)}}$ mesurable. So, using the $\mathbb{L}^p$-norm conditioned to the $\sigma$-algebra $\mathcal B_{\ll N_{(3)}}$, denoted $\mathbb{L}^p(d\mu_s|\mathcal B_{\ll N_{(3)}})$, we obtain :
    \begin{equation}\label{R L^p less than L^p_cond Linfty}
        \begin{split}
             
\left\lVert \1_{\{ \mathcal C(u) \leq R \}} \mathcal R_{N_1,...,N_6}^{(W)} \right\rVert 
_{\mathbb{L}^p(d\mu_s)} & \leq \Big\| \big\| \1_{ B_R^{H^1}}(P_{N_{(3)/100}}u) \cdot \mathcal R_{N_1,...,N_6}^{(W)} \big\|_{\mathbb{L}^p(d\mu_s|\mathcal B_{\ll N_{(3)}})}\Big\|_{\mathbb{L}^\infty(d\mu_s)} \\
            & \leq  \Big\| \big\| \mathcal R_{N_1,...,N_6}^{(W)}\big\|_{\mathbb{L}^p(d\mu_s|\mathcal B_{\ll N_{(3)}})} \cdot \1_{ B_R^{H^1}}(P_{N_{(3)/100}}u)\Big\|_{\mathbb{L}^\infty(d\mu_s)}
        \end{split}
    \end{equation}
    Now, the conditional Wiener-chaos estimate from Lemma~\ref{lem Wiener chaos} (with $m=3$), followed by  Lemma~\ref{L2 estimate with orthogonality} combined with the absence of paring (see Remark \ref{rem no high freq pairing, first generation}), allows us to obtain : 
    \begin{equation}\label{R application Wiener chaos}
        \begin{split}
             
\left\lVert  \mathcal R_{N_1,...,N_6}^{(W)} \right\rVert 
_{\mathbb{L}^p(d\mu_s|\mathcal B_{\ll N_{(3)}})} & \lesssim p^{\frac{3}{2}}  
\left\lVert  \mathcal R_{N_1,...,N_6}^{(W)} \right\rVert 
_{\mathbb{L}^2(d\mu_s|\mathcal B_{\ll N_{(3)}})} \\
            & \lesssim p^{\frac{3}{2}} (N_{(1)} N_{(2)} N_{(3)})^{-s} \bigg( \sum_{k_1,k_2,k_3} \Big| \sum_{k_4,k_5,k_6} C(\vec{k}) \cdot \frac{\psi_{2s}(\vec{k})}{\Omega(\vec{k})} 
  \overline{w_{k_4}^{N_4}} 
  w_{k_5}^{N_5} 
  \overline{w_{k_6}^{N_6}} 
    \Big|^2 \bigg)^{\frac{1}{2}}
        \end{split}
    \end{equation}
    where we gathered all the constraints into the term :
    \begin{equation*}
        C(\vec{k}) := \1_{k_1-k_2+...-k_6=0} \cdot \1_{\Omega(\vec{k}) \neq 0} \cdot \prod_{j=1}^6 \1_{|k_j| \sim N_j}
    \end{equation*}
    Next, by Cauchy-Schwarz,
    \begin{equation*}
         \sum_{k_1,k_2,k_3} \Big| \sum_{k_4,k_5,k_6} C(\vec{k}) \cdot \frac{\psi_{2s}(\vec{k})}{\Omega(\vec{k})} 
  \overline{w_{k_4}^{N_4}} 
  w_{k_5}^{N_5} 
  \overline{w_{k_6}^{N_6}} 
    \Big|^2 \lesssim  \sum_{k_1,k_2,k_3} \Big( \sum_{k_4,k_5,k_6} C(\vec{k}) \cdot \Big| \frac{\psi_{2s}(\vec{k})}{\Omega(\vec{k})} \Big|^2 |w_{k_4}^{N_4}w_{k_5}^{N_5}|^2 \Big) \Big( \sum_{k_4,k_5,k_6} C(\vec{k}) |w_{k_6}^{N_6}|^2 \Big) 
    \end{equation*}
    From Lemma~\ref{lemma psi estimate} we get $\left| \frac{\psi_{2s}(\vec{k})}{\Omega(\vec{k})} \right| \lesssim |k_{(1)}|^{2s-2}(1+\frac{|k_{(3)}|^2}{|\Omega(\vec{k})|}) \lesssim |k_{(1)}|^{2s-2} |k_{(3)}|^2 \lesssim N_{(1)}^{2s-2} N_{(3)}^2$. Then, on the one hand :
    \begin{equation*}
        \begin{split}
            \sum_{k_4,k_5,k_6} C(\vec{k}) \cdot \Big| \frac{\psi_{2s}(\vec{k})}{\Omega(\vec{k})} \Big|^2 |w_{k_4}^{N_4}w_{k_5}^{N_5}|^2 & \lesssim (N_{(1)}^{2s-2} N_{(3)}^2)^2  \sum_{k_4,k_5,k_6} C(\vec{k}) \cdot |w_{k_4}^{N_4}w_{k_5}^{N_5}|^2 \\
            & \lesssim (N_{(1)}^{2s-2} N_{(3)}^2)^2 \sum_{k_4,k_5} |w_{k_4}^{N_4}w_{k_5}^{N_5}|^2 \cdot \underbrace{\sum_{k_6} \1_{k_6=k_1-k_2...+k_5}}_{\leq 1} \\
            & \lesssim (N_{(1)}^{2s-2} N_{(3)}^2  
\left\lVert w^{N_4} \right\rVert 
_{\mathbb{L}^2} 
\left\lVert w^{N_5} \right\rVert 
_{\mathbb{L}^2})^2
        \end{split}
    \end{equation*}
    and on the other hand,
    \begin{equation*}
    \begin{split}
            \sum_{k_1,k_2,k_3} \Big( \sum_{k_4,k_5,k_6} C(\vec{k}) |w_{k_6}^{N_6}|^2 \Big) = \sum_{k_6} |w_{k_6}^{N_6}|^2 \sum_{k_1,k_2,k_3,k_4,k_5} C(\vec{k})
            \lesssim N_{(2)}N_{(3)}N_{(4)}N_{(5)} \cdot  
\left\lVert w^{N_6} \right\rVert 
_{\mathbb{L}^2}^2
    \end{split}
    \end{equation*}
    where we used the counting bound from Lemma~\ref{lem counting bound}. We deduce from the two inequalities above that
    \begin{equation*}
    \begin{split}
        \bigg( \sum_{k_1,k_2,k_3} \Big| \sum_{k_4,k_5,k_6} C(\vec{k}) \cdot \frac{\psi_{2s}(\vec{k})}{\Omega(\vec{k})} 
  \overline{w_{k_4}^{N_4}} 
  w_{k_5}^{N_5} 
  \overline{w_{k_6}^{N_6}} 
    \Big|^2 \bigg)^{\frac{1}{2}} & \lesssim N_{(1)}^{2s-2} N_{(3)}^2 N_{(1)}^{\frac{1}{2}} N_{(3)}^{\frac{1}{2}}  (N_{(4)}N_{(5})^{\frac{1}{2}} 
\left\lVert w^{N_4} \right\rVert 
_{\mathbb{L}^2} 
\left\lVert w^{N_5} \right\rVert 
_{\mathbb{L}^2} 
\left\lVert w^{N_6} \right\rVert 
_{\mathbb{L}^2} \\
        & \lesssim N_{(1)}^{2s-2+\frac{1}{2}} N_{(3)}^{\frac{5}{2}} (N_{(4)}N_{(5})^{-\frac{1}{2}}N_{(6)}^{-1} 
\left\lVert w^{N_4} \right\rVert 
_{H^1} 
\left\lVert w^{N_5} \right\rVert 
_{H^1} 
\left\lVert w^{N_6} \right\rVert 
_{H^1} \\
        & \lesssim N_{(1)}^{2s-\frac{3}{2}} N_{(3)}^{\frac{5}{2}}  
\left\lVert w^{N_4} \right\rVert 
_{H^1} 
\left\lVert w^{N_5} \right\rVert 
_{H^1} 
\left\lVert w^{N_6} \right\rVert 
_{H^1} 
    \end{split}
    \end{equation*}
    Coming back to \eqref{R application Wiener chaos}, we deduce that 
    \begin{equation*}
          
\left\lVert  \mathcal R_{N_1,...,N_6}^{(W)} \right\rVert 
_{\mathbb{L}^p(d\mu_s|\mathcal B_{\ll N_{(3)}})} \lesssim p^{\frac{3}{2}} N_{(1)}^{-\frac{3}{2}} N_{(3)}^{\frac{5}{2}-s}  
\left\lVert w^{N_4} \right\rVert 
_{H^1} 
\left\lVert w^{N_5} \right\rVert 
_{H^1} 
\left\lVert w^{N_6} \right\rVert 
_{H^1} 
    \end{equation*}
    And plugging this into \eqref{R L^p less than L^p_cond Linfty}, we obtain:
    \begin{equation*}
         
\left\lVert \1_{\{ \mathcal C(u) \leq R \}} \mathcal R_{N_1,...,N_6}^{(W)} \right\rVert 
_{\mathbb{L}^p(d\mu_s)} \lesssim_R p^{\frac{3}{2}}  N_{(1)}^{-\frac{3}{2}} N_{(3)}^{\frac{5}{2}-s}
    \end{equation*}
    Interpolating the above inequality with \eqref{cR deterministic estimate} (more precisely \eqref{cR deterministic estimate} with $\mathfrak{R}^{(W)}$ instead of $\mathfrak{R}$), we have that for any $\theta \in (0,1)$ : 
    \begin{equation}\label{R interpolation}
         
\left\lVert \1_{\{ \mathcal C(u) \leq R \}} \mathcal R_{N_1,...,N_6}^{(W)} \right\rVert 
_{\mathbb{L}^p(d\mu_s)} \lesssim p^{\frac{3}{2}\theta +\frac{2-\alpha}{2}(1-\theta)}N_{(1)}^{-\frac{3}{2}\theta + \left(2(s-1-\sigma) + \varepsilon + \alpha(s-\frac{3}{2})\right)(1-\theta)}N_{(3)}^{(\frac{5}{2}-s)\theta + (1-\theta)}
    \end{equation}
Finally, we use the following lemma to finish the proof of Lemma~\ref{lem R_s,N L^p estimate}:

    \begin{lem}\label{lem theta exponent < 1 on p and negative exponent on N_{(1)}}
        There exist $\sigma<s-\frac{1}{2}$ close enough to $s-\frac{1}{2}$, $\varepsilon>0$ close enough to $0$, $\theta \in (0,1)$ and $\alpha \in (0,1)$, such that 
        \begin{align*}
                \frac{3}{2}\theta +\frac{2-\alpha}{2}(1-\theta) &< 1, & 
                N_{(1)}^{-\frac{3}{2}\theta + \left(2(s-1-\sigma) + \varepsilon + \alpha(s-\frac{3}{2})\right)(1-\theta)}N_{(3)}^{(\frac{5}{2}-s)\theta + (1-\theta)} &\lesssim N_{(1)}^{-}
        \end{align*}
    \end{lem}
Let us provide a proof of this lemma:

    \begin{proof}[Proof of Lemma~\ref{lem theta exponent < 1 on p and negative exponent on N_{(1)}}]
Firstly, we have:
\begin{equation}\label{cd theta power of p}
    \begin{split}
    \frac{3}{2}\theta +\frac{2-\alpha}{2}(1-\theta) < 1 & \iff  \theta \left(\frac{1+\alpha}{2}\right) < 1 + \frac{\alpha -2 }{2} = \frac{\alpha}{2} \\
    & \iff \theta < \frac{\alpha}{1+\alpha}
    \end{split}
\end{equation}

Secondly, regarding the exponent of $N_{(3)}$, we have:
\begin{equation}\label{cd theta positive power of N3}
    (\frac{5}{2}-s)\theta + (1-\theta) \geq 0 \iff \theta \leq \frac{1}{s-\frac{3}{2}}
\end{equation}

Let us take $\theta \leq \frac{1}{s-\frac{3}{2}}$ (always true when $s \leq \frac{5}{2}$). Then,
\begin{equation*}
    N_{(1)}^{-\frac{3}{2}\theta + \left(2(s-1-\sigma) + \varepsilon + \alpha(s-\frac{3}{2})\right)(1-\theta)}N_{(3)}^{(\frac{5}{2}-s)\theta + (1-\theta)} \lesssim N_{(1)}^{-\frac{3}{2}\theta + \left(2(s-1-\sigma) + \varepsilon + \alpha(s-\frac{3}{2})\right)(1-\theta)}N_{(1)}^{(\frac{5}{2}-s)\theta + (1-\theta)}
\end{equation*}
We want to have appropriate parameters such that the conditions on $\theta$ given in \eqref{cd theta power of p} and \eqref{cd theta positive power of N3} are satisfied along with the following one: 
\begin{equation*}
    -\frac{3}{2}\theta + \left(2(s-1-\sigma) + \varepsilon + \alpha(s-\frac{3}{2})\right)(1-\theta) + (\frac{5}{2}-s)\theta + (1-\theta) < 0 
\end{equation*}
Since $2(s-1-\sigma) + \varepsilon \longrightarrow -1$ as $\sigma \rightarrow s-\frac{1}{2}$ and $\varepsilon \rightarrow 0$, the previous condition will be true for $\sigma$ and $\varepsilon$ respectively close enough to $s-\frac{3}{2}$ and $0$ if:
\begin{equation*}
    -\frac{3}{2}\theta + \left(-1 + \alpha(s-\frac{3}{2})\right)(1-\theta) + (\frac{5}{2}-s)\theta + (1-\theta) < 0 
\end{equation*}
And this condition is equivalent to the following one:
\begin{equation}\label{cd power of N1}
\begin{split}
    & \theta \left( 1-s - \alpha(s-\frac{3}{2}) \right) < - \alpha(s-\frac{3}{2}) \\
   \iff &\theta > \frac{\alpha(s-\frac{3}{2})}{s-1 + \alpha(s-\frac{3}{2})} = \frac{\alpha}{\frac{s-1}{s-\frac{3}{2}} + \alpha} =  \frac{\alpha}{1 + \frac{1}{2(s-\frac{3}{2})} + \alpha}
\end{split}
\end{equation}

To conclude, if we first take $\alpha$ small enough such that $\frac{\alpha}{1+\alpha}<\frac{1}{s-\frac{3}{2}}$, and then $\theta$ such that
\begin{equation*}
    \frac{\alpha}{1 + \frac{1}{2(s-3/2)} + \alpha}<\theta<\frac{\alpha}{1+\alpha},
\end{equation*}
the conditions given in \eqref{cd theta power of p}, \eqref{cd theta positive power of N3} and \eqref{cd power of N1} are satisfied. We illustrate this with the following drawing :

\begin{center}
\begin{tikzpicture}
    \draw[line width=1.pt] (0,0) -- (14,0);
    \draw[line width=1.pt] (0, -0.1) -- (0, 0) node[above] {$0$} -- (0, 0.1);
    \draw[line width=1.pt] (14, -0.1) -- (14, 0) node[above] {$\frac{1}{s-3/2}$} -- (14, 0.1);
    \draw[line width=1.pt] (3.5, -0.1) -- (3.5, 0) node[below] {$\frac{\alpha}{1 + \frac{1}{2(s-3/2)} + \alpha}$} -- (3.5, 0.1);
    \draw[line width=1.pt] (7, -0.1) -- (7, 0) node[below] {$\frac{\alpha}{1 + \alpha}$} -- (7, 0.1);
    \draw[line width=1.pt] (5, -0.1) -- (5, 0) node[above] {$\theta$} -- (5, 0.1);
\end{tikzpicture}
\end{center}
With those parameters, Lemma~\ref{lem theta exponent < 1 on p and negative exponent on N_{(1)}} is proven.
    \end{proof}
    Hence, coming back to \eqref{R interpolation}, the proof of Lemma~\ref{lem R_s,N L^p estimate} is completed.
