Secondly, regarding the exponent of $N_{(3)}$, we have:
\begin{equation}\label{cd theta positive power of N3}
    (\frac{5}{2}-s)\theta + (1-\theta) \geq 0 \iff \theta \leq \frac{1}{s-\frac{3}{2}}
\end{equation}

Let us take $\theta \leq \frac{1}{s-\frac{3}{2}}$ (always true when $s \leq \frac{5}{2}$). Then,
\begin{equation*}
    N_{(1)}^{-\frac{3}{2}\theta + \left(2(s-1-\sigma) + \varepsilon + \alpha(s-\frac{3}{2})\right)(1-\theta)}N_{(3)}^{(\frac{5}{2}-s)\theta + (1-\theta)} \lesssim N_{(1)}^{-\frac{3}{2}\theta + \left(2(s-1-\sigma) + \varepsilon + \alpha(s-\frac{3}{2})\right)(1-\theta)}N_{(1)}^{(\frac{5}{2}-s)\theta + (1-\theta)}
\end{equation*}
We want to have appropriate parameters such that the conditions on $\theta$ given in \eqref{cd theta power of p} and \eqref{cd theta positive power of N3} are satisfied along with the following one: 
\begin{equation*}
    -\frac{3}{2}\theta + \left(2(s-1-\sigma) + \varepsilon + \alpha(s-\frac{3}{2})\right)(1-\theta) + (\frac{5}{2}-s)\theta + (1-\theta) < 0 
\end{equation*}
Since $2(s-1-\sigma) + \varepsilon \longrightarrow -1$ as $\sigma \rightarrow s-\frac{1}{2}$ and $\varepsilon \rightarrow 0$, the previous condition will be true for $\sigma$ and $\varepsilon$ respectively close enough to $s-\frac{3}{2}$ and $0$ if:
\begin{equation*}
    -\frac{3}{2}\theta + \left(-1 + \alpha(s-\frac{3}{2})\right)(1-\theta) + (\frac{5}{2}-s)\theta + (1-\theta) < 0 
\end{equation*}
And this condition is equivalent to the following one:
\begin{equation}\label{cd power of N1}
\begin{split}
    & \theta \left( 1-s - \alpha(s-\frac{3}{2}) \right) < - \alpha(s-\frac{3}{2}) \\
   \iff &\theta > \frac{\alpha(s-\frac{3}{2})}{s-1 + \alpha(s-\frac{3}{2})} = \frac{\alpha}{\frac{s-1}{s-\frac{3}{2}} + \alpha} =  \frac{\alpha}{1 + \frac{1}{2(s-\frac{3}{2})} + \alpha}
\end{split}
\end{equation}

To conclude, if we first take $\alpha$ small enough such that $\frac{\alpha}{1+\alpha}<\frac{1}{s-\frac{3}{2}}$, and then $\theta$ such that
\begin{equation*}
    \frac{\alpha}{1 + \frac{1}{2(s-3/2)} + \alpha}<\theta<\frac{\alpha}{1+\alpha},
\end{equation*}
the conditions given in \eqref{cd theta power of p}, \eqref{cd theta positive power of N3} and \eqref{cd power of N1} are satisfied. We illustrate this with the following drawing :

\begin{center}
\begin{tikzpicture}
    \draw[line width=1.pt] (0,0) -- (14,0);
    \draw[line width=1.pt] (0, -0.1) -- (0, 0) node[above] {$0$} -- (0, 0.1);
    \draw[line width=1.pt] (14, -0.1) -- (14, 0) node[above] {$\frac{1}{s-3/2}$} -- (14, 0.1);
    \draw[line width=1.pt] (3.5, -0.1) -- (3.5, 0) node[below] {$\frac{\alpha}{1 + \frac{1}{2(s-3/2)} + \alpha}$} -- (3.5, 0.1);
    \draw[line width=1.pt] (7, -0.1) -- (7, 0) node[below] {$\frac{\alpha}{1 + \alpha}$} -- (7, 0.1);
    \draw[line width=1.pt] (5, -0.1) -- (5, 0) node[above] {$\theta$} -- (5, 0.1);
\end{tikzpicture}
\end{center}
With those parameters, Lemma~\ref{lem theta exponent < 1 on p and negative exponent on N_{(1)}} is proven.
<!-- end proof-28 -->
<!-- proof-29: body_md -->
We decompose $\mathcal Q_0$ dyadically and we use Lemma~\ref{lemma psi estimate} (with $\Omega(\vec{k}) = 0$), and we obtain :
    \begin{equation*}
            \left| \mathcal Q_0(w) \right| \lesssim \sum_{N_1,...,N_6} \mathfrak{Q}_0 (N_1,...,N_6)
    \end{equation*}
    where,
    \begin{equation*}
        \mathfrak{Q}_0(N_1,...,N_6) := \sum_{\substack{k_1-k_2+...-k_6=0 \\ \Omega(\vec{k}) = 0}} N_{(1)}^{2s-2} N_{(3)}^2 \prod_{j=1}^6 \1_{|k_j| \sim N_j} |w_{k_j}|
    \end{equation*}     
    To estimate $\mathfrak{Q}_0(N_1,...,N_6)$, we use Lemma~\ref{Strichartz's trick} (with $f^{j}_{k_j} = \1_{|k_j| \sim N_j} |w_{k_j}|$), which yields:
    \begin{equation*}
         \mathfrak{Q}_0(N_1,...,N_6) \lesssim_{\varepsilon} N_{(1)}^{2s-2+\varepsilon} N_{(3)}^2 \prod_{j=1}^{6}  
\left\lVert P_{N_j}w \right\rVert 
_{\mathbb{L}^2(\mathbb{T})}
    \end{equation*}
with $P_{N}$ the projector onto frequencies $|k| \sim N$. This estimate is the analogue of \eqref{bound R_N1...N6}. And from this point, the proof of \eqref{Q0 estimate} goes exactly the same as the proof of Lemma~\ref{lem R_s,N L^p estimate}.
<!-- end proof-29 -->
<!-- lem-14: body_md -->
\label{lem Q1,Q2 estimate}
Let $s > \frac{3}{2}$. Then, there exists $\beta \in (0,1)$ such that for every $R>0$, there exists a constant $C(s,R) > 0$, such that for any $p \in [2,+\infty)$,
\begin{equation}
     
\left\lVert \1_{\{\mathcal C(u) \leq R\}} \mathcal Q_j \right\rVert 
_{\mathbb{L}^p(d\mu_s)} \leq C(s,R)p^\beta
\end{equation}
for $j=1,2$.
<!-- end lem-14 -->
<!-- notns-2: body_md -->
\label{notations Q estimate}
    Given a set of frequency $k_1,k_2,...,k_6,p_1,p_2,...,p_5 \in \mathbb{Z}$, we denote :
    \begin{itemize}
        \item $k_{(1)},...,k_{(6)}$ a rearrangement of the $k_j$ such that 
    \begin{equation*}
        |k_{(1)}| \geq |k_{(2)}| \geq ... \geq |k_{(6)}| 
    \end{equation*}
    \item $p_{(1)},...,p_{(6)}$ a rearrangement of the $p_j$ such that 
    \begin{equation*}
        |p_{(1)}| \geq |p_{(2)}| \geq ... \geq |p_{(5)}| 
    \end{equation*}
     \item $n_{(1)},n_{(2)},...,n_{(10)}$ a rearrangement of $k_2,...,k_6,p_1,...,p_5$ such that 
    \begin{equation*}
        |n_{(1)}| \geq |n_{(2)}| \geq ... \geq |n_{(10)}| 
    \end{equation*} 
    \end{itemize}
    Also, in the sequel we will use :
    \begin{itemize}
        \item the letter $M_j$ for the localization of the frequency $k_j$,
        \item the letter $P_j$ for the localization of the frequency $p_j$,
    \end{itemize}
    Finally, $N_{(1)} \geq N_{(2)} \geq ... \geq N_{(10)}$ will be a non-increasing rearrangement of $P_1,...,P_5,M_2,...,M_6$.
<!-- end notns-2 -->
<!-- rem-20: body_md -->
-- when $k_1-k_2+...-k_6=0$, we have $ |k_{(1)}| \sim |k_{(2)}|$.\\
  -- when $k_1=p_1-p_2+...+p_5$, we have $|p_{(1)}| \sim |p_{(2)}|$ or $|p_{(1)}| \sim |k_1|$.\\
  -- when $k_1-k_2+...-k_6=0$ and  $k_1=p_1-p_2+...+p_5$, we have $|n_{(1)}| \sim |n_{(2)}|$.
<!-- end rem-20 -->
<!-- proof-30: body_md -->
\underline{Step 1, Deterministic estimate :}
    Let $w \in H^{s-\frac{1}{2}-}(\mathbb{T})$. For convenience, for any dyadic number $N$ we denote $w_k^N := \1_{|k|\sim N}|w_k|$.  We start by taking the absolute value and summing over dyadic blocks
    \begin{equation*}
        \left| \mathcal Q(w) \right| \lesssim \sum_{M_1,...,M_6,P_1,...,P_5} \mathfrak{Q}(M_1,...,M_6,P_1,...,P_5)
    \end{equation*}
    where $M_1,...,M_6,P_1,...,P_5$ are dyadic-valued and 
    \begin{equation*}
        \mathfrak{Q}(M_1,...,M_6,P_1,...,P_5) := \sum_{\substack{k_1-k_2+...-k_6=0 \\ p_1-p_2+...+p_5 =k_1 \\\Omega(\vec{k}) \neq 0}} \big| \frac{\psi_{2s}(\vec{k})}{ \Omega(\vec{k})} \big| |w_{p_1}^{P_1}...w_{p_5}^{P_5}w_{k_2}^{M_2}...w_{k_6}^{M_6}| \cdot \1_{|k_1| \sim M_1}
    \end{equation*}  
        We decompose $\mathfrak{Q}$ as $\mathfrak{Q} = \mathfrak{Q}^{(D)} + \mathfrak{Q}^{(W)}$, according to the decomposition of $\mathcal Q$.\\
        
    In regard to \eqref{T_1 dyadic block} and \eqref{dyadic estimate T_1} from the proof of Proposition~\ref{prop continuity of Qs,N and deterministic estimate}, we have:
    \begin{equation*}
             \mathfrak{Q}(M_1,...,P_5) \lesssim
              M_{(1)}^{2s-2+\varepsilon} M_{(3)}^{2}  \left( P_{(2)} P_{(3)} P_{(4)} P_{(5)}\right)^{\frac{1}{2}}  \prod_{j=1}^5  
\left\lVert w^{P_j} \right\rVert 
_{\mathbb{L}^2} \prod_{j=2}^6  
\left\lVert w^{M_j} \right\rVert 
_{\mathbb{L}^2} 
    \end{equation*}
    Using Notations \ref{notations Q estimate}, it means that 
        \begin{equation}\label{first bound Q_M1...M6,P1...P5}
             \mathfrak{Q}(M_1,...,P_5) \lesssim
              M_{(1)}^{2s-2+\varepsilon} M_{(3)}^{2}  \left( P_{(2)} P_{(3)} P_{(4)} P_{(5)}\right)^{\frac{1}{2}}  \prod_{j=1}^{10}  
\left\lVert w^{N_j} \right\rVert 
_{\mathbb{L}^2}
    \end{equation}
     Moreover, for $1<\sigma'<\sigma<s-\frac{1}{2}$, we have : 
    \begin{equation}\label{w^N(j) L2}
        \prod_{j=1}^{10}  
\left\lVert w^{N_j} \right\rVert 
_{\mathbb{L}^2} \lesssim (N_{(1)}^{-\sigma}  
\left\lVert u \right\rVert_{H^{\sigma}}  
)(N_{(2)}^{-\sigma'}  
\left\lVert u \right\rVert 
_{H^{\sigma'}})(N_{(3)}N_{(4)}...N_{(10)})^{-1}  
\left\lVert u \right\rVert 
_{H^1}^8
    \end{equation}
    Then, since $N_{(1)} \sim N_{(2)}$, and writing $\sigma'$ as: 
    \begin{equation*}
        \sigma' = \alpha 1 + (1-\alpha) \sigma
    \end{equation*}
    for $\alpha \in (0,1)$, we deduce from \eqref{w^N(j) L2}, by interpolating $H^{\sigma'}$ between $H^1$ and $H^{\sigma}$, that: 
    \begin{equation*}
        \begin{split}
            \prod_{j=1}^{10}  
\left\lVert w^{N_j} \right\rVert 
_{\mathbb{L}^2} & \lesssim N_{(1)}^{-2\sigma +\alpha(\sigma-1)}(N_{(3)}N_{(4)}...N_{(10)})^{-1}  
\left\lVert u \right\rVert 
_{H^1}^{8+\alpha}  
\left\lVert u \right\rVert 
^{2-\alpha}_{H^{\sigma}} \\
            & \lesssim N_{(1)}^{-2\sigma +\alpha(s-\frac{3}{2})}(N_{(3)}N_{(4)}...N_{(10)})^{-1}  
\left\lVert u \right\rVert 
_{H^1}^{8+\alpha}  
\left\lVert u \right\rVert 
^{2-\alpha}_{H^{\sigma}}, \hspace{0.3cm} (\textnormal{because $\alpha(\sigma-1) < \alpha(s-3/2)$ })
        \end{split}
    \end{equation*}
    
        Plugging this into \eqref{first bound Q_M1...M6,P1...P5}, we obtain 
    \begin{equation*}
        \mathfrak{Q}(M_1,...,P_5) \lesssim N_{(1)}^{-2\sigma +\alpha(s-\frac{3}{2})} M_{(1)}^{2s-2+\varepsilon} M_{(3)}^{2}  \left( P_{(2)} P_{(3)} P_{(4)} P_{(5)}\right)^{\frac{1}{2}}(N_{(3)}N_{(4)}...N_{(10)})^{-1}  
\left\lVert u \right\rVert 
_{H^1}^{8+\alpha}  
\left\lVert u \right\rVert 
^{2-\alpha}_{H^{\sigma}}
    \end{equation*} 
    Using the facts $M_{(1)}\lesssim N_{(1)}$ and $N_{(1)} \sim N_{(2)}$, and also Remark \ref{rem cut-off H1}, we deduce that 
    \begin{equation}\label{Q pre-deterministic estimate}
        \begin{split}
       \1_{\{\mathcal C(u) \leq R\}} \mathfrak{Q}&(M_1,...,P_5) \\
       & \lesssim_{\varepsilon,R} N_{(1)}^{2(s-\sigma-1) + \varepsilon +\alpha(s-\frac{3}{2})} M_{(3)}^{2}  \left( P_{(2)} P_{(3)} P_{(4)} P_{(5)}\right)^{\frac{1}{2}}N^2_{(1)}(\overbrace{N_{(1)}N_{(2)}N_{(3)}N_{(4)}...N_{(10)}}^{=M_2...M_6 P_1...P_5})^{-1}  
\left\lVert u \right\rVert 
^{2-\alpha}_{H^{\sigma}} \\
        & \lesssim N_{(1)}^{2(s-\sigma) + \varepsilon +\alpha(s-\frac{3}{2})} M_{(3)}^{2} (M_2...M_6)^{-1} P_{(1)}^{-1}\left( P_{(2)} P_{(3)} P_{(4)} P_{(5)}\right)^{-\frac{1}{2}}  
\left\lVert u \right\rVert 
^{2-\alpha}_{H^{\sigma}} \\
        & \lesssim \begin{cases}
            N_{(1)}^{2(s-\sigma) - \frac{3}{2} + \varepsilon +\alpha(s-\frac{3}{2})}  
\left\lVert u \right\rVert 
^{2-\alpha}_{H^{\sigma}}, \hspace{1.9cm} \textnormal{if $(N_{(1)},N_{(2)}) \in \{ P_1,...,P_5\}^2$} \\
            N_{(1)}^{2(s-\sigma-1) + \varepsilon +\alpha(s-\frac{3}{2})} N_{(3)} N_{(4)}^{-\frac{1}{2}}  
\left\lVert u \right\rVert 
^{2-\alpha}_{H^{\sigma}}, \hspace{0.4cm} \textnormal{if $(N_{(1)},N_{(2)}) \notin \{ P_1,...,P_5\}^2$}
        \end{cases}
        \end{split}
    \end{equation} 

Here, we used estimates on $ M_{(3)}^{2} (M_2...M_6)^{-1} P_{(1)}^{-1}\left( P_{(2)} P_{(3)} P_{(4)} P_{(5)}\right)^{-\frac{1}{2}}$ in terms of the $N_j$, which are gathered in the following lemma. 
\begin{lem}\label{lem M3^2 Mj^-1 P1^-1 Pj^-1/2}
\begin{itemize}
    \item[--]If  $(N_{(1)},N_{(2)}) \in \{ P_1,...,P_5\}^2$, then 
    \begin{equation*}
        M_{(3)}^{2} (M_2...M_6)^{-1} P_{(1)}^{-1}\left( P_{(2)} P_{(3)} P_{(4)} P_{(5)}\right)^{-\frac{1}{2}} \lesssim N_{(1)}^{-\frac{3}{2}}
    \end{equation*}
    \item[--] If $(N_{(1)},N_{(2)}) \notin \{ P_1,...,P_5\}^2$, then 
    \begin{equation*}
        M_{(3)}^{2} (M_2...M_6)^{-1} P_{(1)}^{-1}\left( P_{(2)} P_{(3)} P_{(4)} P_{(5)}\right)^{-\frac{1}{2}} \lesssim N_{(1)}^{-2}N_{(3)}N_{(4)}^{-\frac{1}{2}}
    \end{equation*}
\end{itemize}
\end{lem}
For clarity, we postpone the proof of Lemma~\ref{lem M3^2 Mj^-1 P1^-1 Pj^-1/2} for the end of this section. \\
To conclude the first step of the proof, using \eqref{Gaussian moments} in \eqref{Q pre-deterministic estimate} yields:

    \begin{equation}\label{Q deterministic estimate}
        
\left\lVert \1_{\{\mathcal C(u) \leq R\}} \mathfrak{Q}(M_1,...,P_5) \right\rVert 
_{\mathbb{L}^p(d\mu_s)} \lesssim \begin{cases}
            N_{(1)}^{2(s-\sigma) - \frac{3}{2} + \varepsilon +\alpha(s-\frac{3}{2})} p^{\frac{2-\alpha}{2}}, \hspace{1.9cm} \textnormal{if  $(N_{(1)},N_{(2)}) \in \{ P_1,...,P_5\}^2$} \\
            N_{(1)}^{2(s-\sigma-1) + \varepsilon +\alpha(s-\frac{3}{2})} N_{(3)} N_{(4)}^{-\frac{1}{2}} p^{\frac{2-\alpha}{2}}, \hspace{0.4cm} \textnormal{if $(N_{(1)},N_{(2)}) \notin \{ P_1,...,P_5\}^2$}
        \end{cases}
    \end{equation}
where the constant depends on $s,R,\sigma$ and $\varepsilon$. This is the deterministic estimate we will work with later in the proof. We stress the fact that \eqref{Q deterministic estimate} is true for $\mathfrak{Q}$ and also for $\mathfrak{Q}^{(D)}$ and $\mathfrak{Q}^{(W)}$ (with the exact same proof).\\ 

\underline{Step 2, Estimates for $\mathcal Q^{(D)}$ and $\mathcal Q^{(W)}$ :} \\

\textbullet Let us begin with the estimate for $\mathcal Q^{(D)}$. Recall that in $\mathcal Q^{(D)}$ we sum over the set $\mathcal I_D$ defined in \eqref{I_D}. And, the constraints in $\mathcal I_D$ imply that the dyadic integers (from the dyadic decomposition) must satisfy one of the following conditions :
\begin{align*}
    (N_{(1)},N_{(2)}) &\in \{P_1,...,P_5\}^2 &  &\textbf{or} & N_{(3)} &\lesssim N_{(1)}^{1-\delta_0} & &\textbf{or} & N_{(4)} &\gtrsim N_{(3)}^{\delta_0}
\end{align*}

In the first situation, when $(N_{(1)},N_{(2)}) \in \{P_1,...,P_5\}^2$, \eqref{Q deterministic estimate} 
(with $\mathfrak{Q}^{(D)}$ instead of $\mathfrak{Q}$) yields:
\begin{equation*}
     
\left\lVert \1_{\{\mathcal C(u) \leq R\}} \mathfrak{Q}^{(D)}(M_1,...,P_5) \right\rVert 
_{\mathbb{L}^p(d\mu_s)} \lesssim  N_{(1)}^{2(s-\sigma) - \frac{3}{2} + \varepsilon +\alpha(s-\frac{3}{2})} p^{\frac{2-\alpha}{2}}
\end{equation*}

And, the exponent of $N_{(1)}$ satisfy :
\begin{equation*}
        \begin{cases}
            2(s-\sigma) - \frac{3}{2} +\varepsilon+\alpha(s-\frac{3}{2}) > -\frac{1}{2} \\
            2(s-\sigma) - \frac{3}{2}+\varepsilon+\alpha(s-\frac{3}{2}) \longrightarrow -\frac{1}{2} \hspace{0.2cm} \text{as} \begin{cases}
                \varepsilon \rightarrow 0 \\
                \alpha \rightarrow 0 \\
                \sigma \rightarrow s -\frac{1}{2}
            \end{cases}
        \end{cases}
\end{equation*}
Thus, for $\varepsilon$ and $\alpha$ close enough to $0$ and $\sigma$ close enough to $s-\frac{1}{2}$, we have 
\begin{equation*}
     
\left\lVert \1_{\{\mathcal C(u) \leq R\}} \mathfrak{Q}^{(D)}(M_1,...,P_5) \right\rVert 
_{\mathbb{L}^p(d\mu_s)} \lesssim  N_{(1)}^- p^{\frac{2-\alpha}{2}}
\end{equation*}

Now, in the second situation when $(N_{(1},N_{(2)}) \notin \{P_1,...,P_5\}^2$ \textbf{and :} $N_{(3)} \lesssim N_{(1)}^{1-\delta_0}$ \textbf{or}  $N_{(4)} \gtrsim N_{(3)}^{\delta_0}$ , \eqref{Q deterministic estimate} yields :
\begin{equation*}
     
\left\lVert \1_{\{\mathcal C(u) \leq R\}} \mathfrak{Q}^{(D)}(M_1,...,P_5) \right\rVert 
_{\mathbb{L}^p(d\mu_s)} \lesssim  N_{(1)}^{2(s-\sigma -1) + \varepsilon +\alpha(s-\frac{3}{2})} N_{(3)} N_{(4)}^{-\frac{1}{2}}p^{\frac{2-\alpha}{2}}
\end{equation*}

And since the exponent of $N_{(1)}$ satisfy :
 \begin{equation*}
        \begin{cases}
            2(s-\sigma-1)+\varepsilon+\alpha(s-\frac{3}{2}) > -1 \\
            2(s-\sigma-1)+\varepsilon+\alpha(s-\frac{3}{2}) \longrightarrow -1 \hspace{0.2cm} \text{as} \begin{cases}
                \varepsilon \rightarrow 0 \\
                \alpha \rightarrow 0 \\
                \sigma \rightarrow s -\frac{1}{2}
            \end{cases}
        \end{cases}
    \end{equation*}
we deduce that for a fixed $\delta_0 \in (0,1)$ and for $\varepsilon$ and $\alpha$ close enough to $0$ and $\sigma$ close enough to $s-\frac{1}{2}$, we have again
\begin{equation*}
     
\left\lVert \1_{\{\mathcal C(u) \leq R\}} \mathfrak{Q}^{(D)}(M_1,...,P_5) \right\rVert 
_{\mathbb{L}^p(d\mu_s)} \lesssim  N_{(1)}^- p^{\frac{2-\alpha}{2}}
\end{equation*}

Finally, summing over the dyadic integers $M_1,...,M_6,P_1,...,P_5$, this estimate for both situations leads to
\begin{equation*}
     
\left\lVert \1_{\{\mathcal C(u) \leq R\}} \mathcal Q^{(D)} \right\rVert 
_{\mathbb{L}^p(d\mu_s)} \lesssim p^{\frac{2-\alpha}{2}}
\end{equation*}
which is the desired estimate. \\

\textbullet Next, in order to finish the proof of Lemma~\ref{lem Q1,Q2 estimate}, we need the same estimate for the contribution $\mathcal Q^{(W)}$. For this term, while the estimate \eqref{Q deterministic estimate} is not conclusive, we are in a situation where we can make use of Wiener chaos. Recall that in $\mathcal Q^{(W)}$, we sum over the set $\mathcal I_W$ defined in \eqref{I_W}. Even though the following method is very similar to the one used for estimating $\mathcal R^{(W)}$ in Section~\ref{section Estimates for the weight of the weighted Gaussian measures} (see the proof of Lemma~\ref{lem R_s,N L^p estimate}), we re-perform the analysis in detail. \\

As usual, we start by decomposing $\mathcal Q^{(W)}$ as\footnote{For the analysis below, we need to keep the complex conjugation bars, so here we don't use $\mathfrak{Q}^{(W)}$} $\mathcal Q^{(W)} = \sum_{M_1,...,M_6,P1,...,P_5} \mathcal Q^{(W)}_{M_1,...,M_6,P1,...,P_5}$, where :
\begin{equation*}
    \mathcal Q^{(W)}_{M_1,...,M_6,P1,...,P_5} := \sum_{\mathcal I_W}\frac{\psi_{2s}(\vec{k})}{ \Omega(\vec{k})} w_{p_1} 
  \overline{w_{p_2}} 
  ...w_{p_5} 
  \overline{w_{k_2}} 
  ... 
  \overline{w_{k_6}} 
   \left(\prod_{j=1}^6 \1_{|k_j|\sim M_j} \right) \left(\prod_{j=1}^5 \1_{p_j \sim P_j}\right)
\end{equation*}
Henceforth, we denote $w_{k_j}^{M_j} := \1_{|k_j|\sim N_j} w_{k_j}$ and $w_{p_j}^{P_j} := \1_{|p_j|\sim P_j} w_{p_j}$ for better readability. \\

Without loss of generality, we only prove the estimate for the contribution in $\mathcal Q^{(W)}$ where the three highest frequencies are $k_2,k_3$ and $k_4$, because the other cases are identical. \\
    Again we denote $\mathcal B_{\ll N_{(3)}}$ the $\sigma$-algebra generated by Gaussians $\left( g_k \right)_{|k|\leq N_{(3)}/100}$. Since we only need to consider the contribution when $N_{(1)}$ is large, we can assume that $N_{(1)}$ is sufficiently large to ensure $N_{(4)}\leq N_{(3)}/100$. This follows from the constraints in $\mathcal I_W$ which imply $N_{(3)} \gtrsim N_{(1)}^{1-\delta_0}$ and $N_{(4)} \lesssim N_{(3)}^{\delta_0}$. Thus, for $N_{(1)}$ large enough, we have $N_{(3)}^{\delta_0} \ll N_{(3)}$, ensuring that $N_{(4)}\leq N_{(3)}/100$. \\
 As a consequence, we have that the random variables :
    \begin{equation*}
        \begin{split}
        & w_{k_2}^{M_2}, w_{k_3}^{M_3}, w_{k_4}^{M_4} \hspace{0.2cm} \textnormal{are independent of $\mathcal B_{\ll N_{(3)}}$}, \\
        & w_{k_5}^{M_5}, w_{k_6}^{M_6},w_{p_1}^{P_1},w_{p_2}^{P_2},w_{p_3}^{P_3},w_{p_4}^{P_4},w_{p_5}^{P_5} \hspace{0.2cm} \textnormal{are $\mathcal B_{\ll N_{(3)}}$ mesurable}.
        \end{split}
    \end{equation*}
    Now, identically to \eqref{R L^p less than L^p_cond Linfty}, we have
    \begin{equation}\label{Q L^p less than L^p_cond Linfty}
             
\left\lVert \1_{\{ \mathcal C(u) \leq R \}} \mathcal Q_{M_1,...,M_6,P_1,...,P_5}^{(W)} \right\rVert 
_{\mathbb{L}^p(d\mu_s)} \leq  \Big\| \big\| \mathcal Q_{M_1,...,M_6,P_1,...,P_5}^{(W)}\big\|_{\mathbb{L}^p(d\mu_s|\mathcal B_{\ll N_{(3)}})} \cdot \1_{ B_R^{H^1}}(P_{N_{(3)/100}}u)\Big\|_{\mathbb{L}^\infty(d\mu_s)}
    \end{equation}
    
    And, the conditional Wiener-chaos estimate from Lemma~\ref{lem Wiener chaos} (with $m=3$), followed by  Lemma~\ref{L2 estimate with orthogonality} combined with the absence of paring (see Paragraph \ref{absence of pairing}), allows us to obtain : 
    \begin{equation}\label{Q application Wiener chaos}
        \begin{split}
            & 
\left\lVert  \mathcal Q_{M_1,...,M_6,P_1,...,P_5}^{(W)} \right\rVert 
_{\mathbb{L}^p(d\mu_s|\mathcal B_{\ll N_{(3)}})}  \lesssim p^{\frac{3}{2}}  
\left\lVert  \mathcal Q_{M_1,...,M_6,P_1,...,P_5}^{(W)} \right\rVert 
_{\mathbb{L}^2(d\mu_s|\mathcal B_{\ll N_{(3)}})} \\
            & \lesssim p^{\frac{3}{2}} (N_{(1)} N_{(2)} N_{(3)})^{-s} \bigg( \sum_{k_2,k_3,k_4} \Big| \sum_{\substack{k_1,k_5,k_6 \\ p_1,p_2,p_3,p_4,p_5}} C(\vec{k},\vec{p}) \cdot \frac{\psi_{2s}(\vec{k})}{\Omega(\vec{k})}w_{p_1}^{P_1} 
  \overline{w_{p_2}^{P_2}} 
  w_{p_3}^{P_3} 
  \overline{w_{p_4}^{P_4}} 
  w_{p_5}^{P_5}w_{k_5}^{M_5} 
  \overline{w_{k_6}^{M_6}} 
    \Big|^2 \bigg)^{\frac{1}{2}}
        \end{split}
    \end{equation}
    where we gathered all the constraints into the term :
    \begin{equation*}
        C(\vec{k},\vec{p}) := \1_{k_1-k_2+...-k_6=0} \cdot \1_{p_1-p_2+...+p_5 =k_1} \cdot \1_{\Omega(\vec{k}) \neq 0} \cdot \prod_{j=1}^6 \1_{|k_j| \sim M_j} \prod_{j=1}^5 \1_{|p_j| \sim P_j}
    \end{equation*}
    Next, by Cauchy-Schwarz,
    \begin{equation*}
        \begin{split}
        &\sum_{k_2,k_3,k_4}  \bigg|\sum_{\substack{k_1,k_5,k_6 \\ p_1,p_2,p_3,p_4,p_5}} C(\vec{k},\vec{p}) \cdot\frac{\psi_{2s}(\vec{k})}{\Omega(\vec{k})}w_{p_1}^{P_1}...w_{p_5}^{P_5}w_{k_5}^{M_5} 
  \overline{w_{k_6}^{M_6}} 
   \bigg|^2 \\
        & \lesssim  \sum_{k_2,k_3,k_4} \bigg( \sum_{\substack{k_1,k_5,k_6 \\ p_1,p_2,p_2,p_4,p_5}} C(\vec{k},\vec{p}) \cdot \Big| \frac{\psi_{2s}(\vec{k})}{\Omega(\vec{k})} \Big|^2 |w_{p_1}^{P_1}...w_{p_5}^{P_5}w_{k_5}^{M_5}|^2 \bigg) \bigg( \sum_{\substack{k_1,k_5,k_6 \\ p_1,p_2,p_2,p_4,p_5}} C(\vec{k},\vec{p}) |w_{k_6}^{M_6}|^2 \bigg) 
        \end{split}
    \end{equation*}
    From Lemma~\ref{lemma psi estimate} we get $\left| \frac{\psi_{2s}(\vec{k})}{\Omega(\vec{k})} \right| \lesssim |k_{(1)}|^{2s-2}(1+\frac{|k_{(3)}|^2}{|\Omega(\vec{k})|}) \lesssim |k_{(1)}|^{2s-2} |k_{(3)}|^2 \lesssim N_{(1)}^{2s-2} N_{(3)}^2$. Then, on the one hand:
    \begin{equation*}
        \begin{split}
            \sum_{\substack{k_1,k_5,k_6 \\ p_1,p_2,p_2,p_4,p_5}} C(\vec{k},\vec{p}) \cdot & \Big| \frac{\psi_{2s}(\vec{k})}{\Omega(\vec{k})} \Big|^2 |w_{p_1}^{P_1}...w_{p_5}^{P_5}w_{k_5}^{M_5}|^2  \lesssim (N_{(1)}^{2s-2} N_{(3)}^2)^2  \sum_{\substack{k_1,k_5,k_6 \\ p_1,p_2,p_2,p_4,p_5}} C(\vec{k},\vec{p}) \cdot |w_{p_1}^{P_1}...w_{p_5}^{P_5}w_{k_5}^{M_5}|^2 \\
            & \lesssim (N_{(1)}^{2s-2} N_{(3)}^2)^2 \sum_{\substack{k_5 \\ p_1,p_2,p_2,p_4,p_5}} |w_{p_1}^{P_1}...w_{p_5}^{P_5}w_{k_5}^{M_5}|^2 \cdot \underbrace{\sum_{k_1,k_6} \1_{k_6=k_1-k_2...+k_5} \cdot \1_{p_1-p_2+...+p_5 =k_1}}_{\leq 1} \\
            & \lesssim (N_{(1)}^{2s-2} N_{(3)}^2  
\left\lVert w^{P_1} \right\rVert 
_{\mathbb{L}^2}... 
\left\lVert w^{P_5} \right\rVert 
_{\mathbb{L}^2} 
\left\lVert w^{M_5} \right\rVert 
_{\mathbb{L}^2})^2 \\
            & \lesssim \left(N_{(1)}^{2s-2} N_{(3)}^2 (P_1...P_5 M_5)^{-1} 
\left\lVert w^{P_1} \right\rVert 
_{H^1}... 
\left\lVert w^{P_5} \right\rVert 
_{H^1} 
\left\lVert w^{M_5} \right\rVert 
_{H^1}\right)^2
        \end{split}
    \end{equation*}
    and on the other hand,
    \begin{equation*}
            \sum_{\substack{k_1,k_2,k_3,k_4,k_5,k_6 \\ p_1,p_2,p_2,p_4,p_5}} C(\vec{k},\vec{p}) |w_{k_6}^{N_6}|^2 = \sum_{k_6} |w_{k_6}^{N_6}|^2 \cdot \sum_{\substack{k_1,k_2,k_3,k_4,k_5\\ p_1,p_2,p_2,p_4,p_5}} C(\vec{k},\vec{p})
            \lesssim N_{(2)}N_{(3)}P_1...P_5 M_5 \cdot (M_6^{-1} 
\left\lVert w^{M_6} \right\rVert 
_{H^1})^2
    \end{equation*}
    where we used the counting bound from Lemma~\ref{lem counting bound}. We deduce from the two inequalities above that
    \begin{equation*}
    \begin{split}
        \biggl( \sum_{k_2,k_3,k_4} \big| \sum_{\substack{k_1,k_5,k_6 \\ p_1,p_2,p_3,p_4,p_5}} &C(\vec{k},\vec{p}) \cdot \frac{\psi_{2s}(\vec{k})}{\Omega(\vec{k})}w_{p_1}^{P_1} 
  \overline{w_{p_2}^{P_2}} 
  w_{p_3}^{P_3} 
  \overline{w_{p_4}^{P_4}} 
  w_{p_5}^{P_5}w_{k_5}^{M_5} 
  \overline{w_{k_6}^{M_6}} 
    \big|^2 \biggr)^{\frac{1}{2}}  \\
        & \lesssim N_{(1)}^{2s-2} N_{(3)}^2 N_{(1)}^{\frac{1}{2}} N_{(3)}^{\frac{1}{2}} 
\left\lVert w^{P_1} \right\rVert 
_{H^1}... 
\left\lVert w^{P_5} \right\rVert 
_{H^1} 
\left\lVert w^{M_5} \right\rVert 
_{H^1}  
\left\lVert w^{M_6} \right\rVert 
_{H^1} \\
        & \lesssim N_{(1)}^{2s-\frac{3}{2}} N_{(3)}^{\frac{5}{2}}  
\left\lVert w^{P_1} \right\rVert 
_{H^1}... 
\left\lVert w^{P_5} \right\rVert 
_{H^1} 
\left\lVert w^{M_5} \right\rVert 
_{H^1}  
\left\lVert w^{M_6} \right\rVert 
_{H^1} 
    \end{split}
    \end{equation*}
    Coming back to \eqref{Q application Wiener chaos}, we deduce that 
    \begin{equation*}
          
\left\lVert  \mathcal Q_{M_1,...,M_6,P_1,...,P_5}^{(W)} \right\rVert 
_{\mathbb{L}^p(d\mu_s|\mathcal B_{\ll N_{(3)}})} \lesssim p^{\frac{3}{2}} N_{(1)}^{-\frac{3}{2}} N_{(3)}^{\frac{5}{2}-s}  
\left\lVert w^{P_1} \right\rVert 
_{H^1}... 
\left\lVert w^{P_5} \right\rVert 
_{H^1} 
\left\lVert w^{M_5} \right\rVert 
_{H^1}  
\left\lVert w^{M_6} \right\rVert 
_{H^1}  
    \end{equation*}
    And plugging this into \eqref{Q L^p less than L^p_cond Linfty}, we obtain :
    \begin{equation*}
         
\left\lVert \1_{\{ \mathcal C(u) \leq R \}} \mathcal Q_{M_1,...,M_6,P_1,...,P_5}^{(W)} \right\rVert 
_{\mathbb{L}^p(d\mu_s)} \lesssim_R p^{\frac{3}{2}}  N_{(1)}^{-\frac{3}{2}} N_{(3)}^{\frac{5}{2}-s}
    \end{equation*}
    Interpolating the above inequality with \eqref{Q deterministic estimate} (more precisely \eqref{Q deterministic estimate} with $\mathfrak{Q}^{(W)}$ instead of $\mathfrak{Q}$), we can conclude in the same way as what we did with $\mathcal R^{(W)}$ in the proof of Lemma~\ref{lem R_s,N L^p estimate} (in particular using again Lemma~\ref{lem theta exponent < 1 on p and negative exponent on N_{(1)}}).
<!-- end proof-30 -->
<!-- lem-15: body_md -->
\label{lem M3^2 Mj^-1 P1^-1 Pj^-1/2}
\begin{itemize}
    \item[--]If  $(N_{(1)},N_{(2)}) \in \{ P_1,...,P_5\}^2$, then 
    \begin{equation*}
        M_{(3)}^{2} (M_2...M_6)^{-1} P_{(1)}^{-1}\left( P_{(2)} P_{(3)} P_{(4)} P_{(5)}\right)^{-\frac{1}{2}} \lesssim N_{(1)}^{-\frac{3}{2}}
    \end{equation*}
    \item[--] If $(N_{(1)},N_{(2)}) \notin \{ P_1,...,P_5\}^2$, then 
    \begin{equation*}
        M_{(3)}^{2} (M_2...M_6)^{-1} P_{(1)}^{-1}\left( P_{(2)} P_{(3)} P_{(4)} P_{(5)}\right)^{-\frac{1}{2}} \lesssim N_{(1)}^{-2}N_{(3)}N_{(4)}^{-\frac{1}{2}}
    \end{equation*}
\end{itemize}
<!-- end lem-15 -->
<!-- head-1: body_md -->
\begin{proof}[Proof of Lemma~\ref{lem M3^2 Mj^-1 P1^-1 Pj^-1/2}]Recall that we use Notations \ref{notations Q estimate}. \\
\textbullet Assume first that $(N_{(1)},N_{(2)}) \in \{ P_1,...,P_5\}^2$. Then, $P_{(1)}^{-1} P_{(2)}^{-\frac{1}{2}} \lesssim N_{(1)}^{-\frac{3}{2}}$. Moreover, we have
\begin{equation*}
    M_{(3)}^{2} (M_2...M_6)^{-1} \leq M_{(3)}^{2} (M_{(2)}M_{(3)}...M_{(6)})^{-1} \leq (M_{(4)}M_{(5)}M_{(6)})^{-1} \lesssim 1
\end{equation*}
Combining these two inequalities, we obtain 
\begin{equation*}
     M_{(3)}^{2} (M_2...M_6)^{-1} P_{(1)}^{-1}\left( P_{(2)} P_{(3)} P_{(4)} P_{(5)}\right)^{-\frac{1}{2}} \lesssim  N_{(1)}^{-\frac{3}{2}}(P_{(3)}P_{(4)}P_{(5)})^{-\frac{1}{2}} \lesssim  N_{(1)}^{-\frac{3}{2}}
\end{equation*}
which is the desired estimate. \bigskip

\textbullet Now, assume that $(N_{(1)},N_{(2)}) \notin \{ P_1,...,P_5\}^2$. It means that :
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}
    (N_{(1)},N_{(2)}) \in \{M_2,...,M_6\}^2 \hspace{0.2cm} & \textbf{or} 
         \left( \hspace{0.2cm} N_{(1)} \in \{M_2,...,M_6\} \hspace{0.2cm} \textbf{and} \hspace{0.2cm} N_{(2)} \in \{P_1,...,P_5\} \hspace{0.2cm} \right) \hspace{0.2cm} \\
         & \textbf{or} \left( \hspace{0.2cm}
         N_{(2)} \in \{M_2,...,M_6\} \hspace{0.2cm} \textbf{and} \hspace{0.2cm} N_{(1)} \in \{P_1,...,P_5\} \hspace{0.2cm} \right)
\end{split}
\end{equation*}
-- Fristly, we suppose that $(N_{(1)},N_{(2)}) \in \{M_2,...,M_6\}^2$. Then, we note that $N_{(3)} \in \{M_2,...,M_6 \}$ \textbf{or} $ P_{(1)} = N_{(3)}$. And also,
\begin{equation*}
    N_{(4)} \in \{M_2,...,M_6\}  \hspace{0.4cm} \textbf{or}  \hspace{0.4cm} N_{(4)} \in \{P_1,...,P_5\}
\end{equation*}
Considering these facts (and still the fact that $N_{(1)} \sim N_{(2)}$), we deduce that
\begin{equation*}
     M_{(3)}^{2} (M_2...M_6)^{-1} P_{(1)}^{-1}\left( P_{(2)} P_{(3)} P_{(4)} P_{(5)}\right)^{-\frac{1}{2}} \lesssim M_{(3)}^2 N_{(1)}^{-2}N_{(3)}^{-1}N_{(4)}^{-\frac{1}{2}}
\end{equation*}
Using then the fact that $M_{(3)} \lesssim N_{(3)}$, we have 
\begin{equation*}
     M_{(3)}^{2} (M_2...M_6)^{-1} P_{(1)}^{-1}\left( P_{(2)} P_{(3)} P_{(4)} P_{(5)}\right)^{-\frac{1}{2}} \lesssim  N_{(1)}^{-2}N_{(3)} N_{(4)}^{-\frac{1}{2}}
\end{equation*}
which is the desired inequality. \\
--Secondly, we suppose that $N_{(1)} \in \{M_2,...,M_6\} \hspace{0.2cm} \textbf{and} \hspace{0.2cm} N_{(2)} \in \{P_1,...,P_5\}$. We consider two cases. \\
$a)$ The first one is when $M_1 \in \{ M_{(1)},M_{(2)},M_{(3)}\}$. In that case, $M_{(4)},M_{(5)},M_{(6)},P_{(2)},...,P_{(5)}$ are seven indices out of the ten indices $N_j$ (that would not have been the case if $M_{(1)} \in \{M_{(4)},M_{(5)},M_{(6)}\}$, because according to Notations \ref{notations Q estimate}, $M_1$ is not one of the $N_j$). As a consequence, 
\begin{equation*}
   \max \{M_{(4)},M_{(5)},M_{(6)},P_{(2)},...,P_{(5)}\} \geq N_{(4)} \hspace{0.3cm}  \textnormal{so,} \hspace{0.3cm}(M_{(4)}M_{(5)}M_{(6)})^{-1}(P_{(2)}...P_{(5)})^{-\frac{1}{2}} \lesssim N_{(4)}^{-\frac{1}{2}}
\end{equation*}
On the other hand, using the fact that $M_{(1)} \sim M_{(2)}$, we have 
\begin{equation*}
     M_{(3)}^{2} (M_2 M_3...M_6)^{-1} \lesssim  M_{(3)}^{2} (M_{(2)}M_{(3)}...M_{(6)})^{-1} \lesssim M_{(1)}^{-1} M_{(3)} (M_{(4)}M_{(5)}M_{(6)})^{-1}
\end{equation*}
Combining these two inequalities and recalling that $M_{(1)},P_{(1)} \sim N_{(1)}$, we obtain
\begin{equation*}
    M_{(3)}^{2} (M_2...M_6)^{-1} P_{(1)}^{-1}\left( P_{(2)} P_{(3)} P_{(4)} P_{(5)}\right)^{-\frac{1}{2}} \lesssim N_{(1)}^{-2} M_{(3)}N_{(4)}^{-\frac{1}{2}} \lesssim N_{(1)}^{-2} N_{(3)}N_{(4)}^{-\frac{1}{2}}
\end{equation*}
$b)$ The second case we consider is when $M_1 \in \{ M_{(4)},M_{(5)},M_{(6)}\}$. In that case, $\{ M_{(1)},M_{(2)},M_{(3)}\} \subset \{M_2,M_3,...,M_6 \}$. Thus,
\begin{equation*}
    (M_2...M_6)^{-1} \lesssim (M_{(1)}M_{(2)}M_{(3)}M_{(5)}M_{(6)})^{-1}
\end{equation*}
so,
\begin{equation*}
    M_{(3)}^2(M_2...M_6)^{-1} \lesssim N_{(1)}^{-2}M_{(3)}
\end{equation*}
and,
\begin{equation*}
     M_{(3)}^{2} (M_2...M_6)^{-1} P_{(1)}^{-1}\left( P_{(2)} P_{(3)} P_{(4)} P_{(5)}\right)^{-\frac{1}{2}} \lesssim N_{(1)}^{-3}M_{(3)} \lesssim N_{(1)}^{-3}N_{(3)}
\end{equation*}
which is an even better estimate than the one we desired. \\
--Finally, the case  $N_{(2)} \in \{M_2,...,M_6\} \hspace{0.2cm} \textbf{and} \hspace{0.2cm} N_{(1)} \in \{P_1,...,P_5\}$ is identical to the previous one. \\
Hence, the proof of Lemma~\ref{lem M3^2 Mj^-1 P1^-1 Pj^-1/2} is finished.

\end{proof}


\appendix

<!-- thm-4: body_md -->
\label{thm local wellposedness}
    Let $\sigma \geq 1$. Let $t_0 \in \mathbb{R}$. Both equation \eqref{NLS} and truncated equation \eqref{truncated equation} are locally well-posed in $H^{\sigma}(\mathbb{T})$, in the sense that for any $R_0>0$, there exists $T_0>0$ such that for every $ 
\left\lVert u \right\rVert 
_{H^{\sigma}} \leq R_0$ there exists a unique $u \in \mathcal C([ t_0-T_0,t_0+T_0],H^{\sigma}(\mathbb{T}))$ that satisfies the Duhamel formula :
    \begin{equation}
        u(t) = e^{i(t-t_0)\partial_x^2}u_0 -i \int_{t_0}^t e^{i(t-\tau)\partial_x^2}(|u(\tau)|^4u(\tau))d\tau
    \end{equation}
    for all $|t-t_0|\leq T_0$. And, for every $N \in \mathbb{N}$, there exists a unique $v_N \in \mathcal C([ t_0-T_0,t_0+T_0],H^{\sigma}(\mathbb{T})) $ that satisfies the Duhamel formula :
    \begin{equation}
        v_N(t) = e^{i(t-t_0)\partial_x^2}u_0 -i \int_{t_0}^t e^{i(t-\tau)\partial_x^2}\Pi_N(|\Pi_N v_N(\tau)|^4 \Pi_N v_N(\tau))d\tau
    \end{equation}
    for all $|t-t_0|\leq T_0$.
<!-- end thm-4 -->
<!-- rem-21: body_md -->
It is important to notice that the existence time $T_0 >0$ is the same for both NLS and truncated equation and does not depend on the integer $N \in \mathbb{N}$.
<!-- end rem-21 -->
<!-- proof-32: body_md -->
To show Theorem~\ref{thm local wellposedness}, we apply a fixed point argument. Fix $R_0>0$ and $|| u_0||_{H^{\sigma}} \leq R_0 $. For $T>0$, we denote 
    \begin{equation*}
        X_T := \mathcal C([t_0-T,t_0,+T],H^{\sigma}(\mathbb{T}))
    \end{equation*}
which is a Banach space when endowed with the sup norm 
\begin{equation*}
     
\left\lVert u \right\rVert 
_{X_T} := \underset{\tau \in [t_0-T,t_0,+T]}{\textnormal{sup}}  
\left\lVert u(\tau) \right\rVert 
_{H^{\sigma}} 
\end{equation*} 
For every $N\in \mathbb{N} \cup \{ \infty\}$, let us consider the well-defined map 
    \begin{equation*}
        \begin{split}
           \Gamma_N : \hspace{0.1cm} & X_T \longrightarrow X_T \\
            & u \longmapsto e^{i(t-t_0)\partial_x^2}u_0 - i \int_{t_0}^t e^{i(t -\tau)\partial_x^2}\Pi_N (|\Pi_N u(\tau)|^4 \Pi_N u(\tau)) d\tau
        \end{split}
    \end{equation*}
where by convention $\Pi_{\infty}= id$. We recall the crucial point that $||\Pi_N u ||_{H^{\sigma}} \leq  
\left\lVert u \right\rVert 
_{H^{\sigma}}$. Thanks to that point, every estimate below are uniform in $N$ so that every constant below does not depend on N.\\

Using now the facts that $H^{\sigma}(\mathbb{T})$ is an algebra (since $\sigma \geq 1 > \frac{1}{2}$) and $e^{i(t-t_0)\partial_x^2}$ is a linear isometry on $H^{\sigma}(\mathbb{T})$, we have for some constant $C_0 > 0$,
\begin{equation}\label{gamma u estimate lwp}
     
\left\lVert \Gamma_N u \right\rVert 
_{X_T} \leq  
\left\lVert u_0 \right\rVert 
_{H^{\sigma}} + C_0 T  
\left\lVert u \right\rVert 
_{X_T}^5 
\end{equation}

In addition, using the multilinearity of $(u_1,u_2,u_3,u_4,u_5) \longmapsto u_1  
  \overline{u_2} 
   u_3  
  \overline{u_4} 
  u_5 $ we have for some constant $C_1 > 0$,
\begin{equation} \label{gamma u - gamma v estimate lwp}
    \begin{split}
     
\left\lVert \Gamma_N u - \Gamma_N v \right\rVert 
_{X_T} & = \left\lVert \int_{t_0}^t e^{i(t -\tau)\partial_x^2} \Pi_N(|\Pi_Nu(\tau)|^4\Pi_Nu(\tau)- |\Pi_Nv(\tau)|^4 \Pi_Nv(\tau))d\tau \right\rVert_{X_T} \\
    & \leq C_1 T ( 
\left\lVert u \right\rVert 
^4_{X_T} +  
\left\lVert v \right\rVert 
^4_{X_T}) 
\left\lVert u-v \right\rVert 
_{X_T}
    \end{split}
\end{equation}
Let $R > 2R_0$ (for example $R= 1 + 2R_0$) and $T_0 := \frac{1}{3 \text{max}(C_0,C_1) R^4}$. Fix $0<T \leq T_0$ and denote by $ 
  \overline{B} 
  _R(T)$ the closed centered ball in $X_T$ of radius $R$. We get from \eqref{gamma u estimate lwp} and \eqref{gamma u - gamma v estimate lwp} and our choice of the parameters $R$ and $T_0$ that for any $u,v \in  
  \overline{B} 
  _R(T)$,
\begin{equation}
  ||\Gamma_N u||_{ 
  \overline{B} 
  _R(T)} \leq \frac{R}{2} + \frac{R}{2} \leq R 
\end{equation}
and,
\begin{equation}
|| \Gamma_N u - \Gamma_N v ||_{ 
  \overline{B} 
  _R(T)} \leq 2C_1 T R^4   
\left\lVert u-v \right\rVert 
_{ 
  \overline{B} 
  _R(T)} \leq \frac{2}{3}  
\left\lVert u-v \right\rVert 
_{ 
  \overline{B} 
  _R(T)}
\end{equation}
These two estimates imply that the map $\Gamma_N$ is a contraction from (the complete space) $ 
  \overline{B} 
  _R(T)$ to itself. Hence, applying the Banach's fixed point theorem to the map 
\begin{equation*}
    \Gamma_N :  
  \overline{B} 
  _R(T) \longrightarrow  
  \overline{B} 
  _R(T)
\end{equation*}
leads to the existence part of Theorem~\ref{thm local wellposedness}. However, through classical considerations, we can prove that the uniqueness holds in the entire space $\mathcal C([ t_0-T,t_0+T],H^{\sigma}(\mathbb{T}))$. So the proof is completed.
<!-- end proof-32 -->
<!-- cor-4: body_md -->
\label{cor maximal solution NLS} Let $\sigma \geq1$. For every $u_0 \in H^{\sigma}(\mathbb{T})$, there exists a unique maximal solution $u \in \mathcal C(I_{max}(u_0),H^{\sigma}(\mathbb{T}))$ of \eqref{NLS} where $I_{max}(u_0)$ is an open interval containing 0. Moreover, if $I_{max}(u_0)$ is strictly included in $\mathbb{R}$, then 
\begin{equation*}
     
\left\lVert u(t) \right\rVert 
_{H^{\sigma}} \longrightarrow +\infty
\end{equation*}
as $t \longrightarrow \partial I_{max}(u_0)$.
<!-- end cor-4 -->
<!-- cor-5: body_md -->
\label{cor maximal solution truncated equation}
   Let $\sigma \geq1$. For every $u_0 \in H^{\sigma}(\mathbb{T})$ and every $N \in \mathbb{N}$, there exists a unique maximal solution $u_N \in \mathcal C(I_{max,N}(u_0),H^{\sigma}(\mathbb{T}))$ of \eqref{truncated equation} where $I_{max,N}(u_0)$ is an open interval containing 0. Moreover, if $I_{max,N}(u_0)$ is strictly included in $\mathbb{R}$, then 
\begin{equation*}
    ||u_N(t)||_{H^{\sigma}} \longrightarrow +\infty
\end{equation*}
as $t \longrightarrow \partial I_{max,N}(u_0)$.
<!-- end cor-5 -->
<!-- prop-19: body_md -->
\label{prop exponential bound} Let $u_0 \in H^{\sigma}(\mathbb{T})$. There exists a constant $C_0 > 0$ only depending on $ 
\left\lVert u \right\rVert 
_{H^1(\mathbb{T})}$ and $\sigma\geq 1$, such that
\begin{equation}\label{exponential bound for NLS solution}
     
\left\lVert u(t) \right\rVert 
_{H^{\sigma}} \leq  
\left\lVert u \right\rVert 
_{H^{\sigma}} e^{C_0|t|}, \hspace{0.1cm} \hspace{0.1cm}\textnormal{for all} \hspace{0.1cm} t \in I_{max}(u_0)
\end{equation}
    and,
\begin{equation}\label{exponential bound for truncated solution}
   ||u_N(t)||_{H^{\sigma}} \leq  
\left\lVert u \right\rVert 
_{H^{\sigma}} e^{C_0|t|},  \hspace{0.1cm} \hspace{0.1cm} \textnormal{for all} \hspace{0.1cm} t \in I_{max,N}(u_0)
\end{equation}
where $u$ is the maximal solution of \eqref{NLS} and $u_N$ is the maximal solution of \eqref{truncated equation}. Moreover, we can explicitly choose $C_0 \leq C_{\sigma} (1+  
\left\lVert u \right\rVert 
_{H^1(\mathbb{T})})^{12}$ where $C_{\sigma} >0$ depends only on $\sigma$.
<!-- end prop-19 -->
<!-- proof-33: body_md -->
We use the convention $\Pi_{\infty} = id$, $u_{\infty} = u$ and $I_{max,\infty}(u_0) = I_{max}(u_0)$. Let $N \in \mathbb{N} \cup \{ \infty \}$ and $t \in I_{max,N}(u_0)$. Passing to the $H^{\sigma}$-norm in the Duhamel formula
    \begin{equation*}
        u_N(t) = e^{i(t)\partial_x^2}u_0 -i \int_{0}^t e^{i(t-\tau)\partial_x^2}\Pi_N(|\Pi_N u_N(\tau)|^4 \Pi_N u_N(\tau))d\tau
    \end{equation*}
    we get that, for some constant $C>0$ (only depending on $\sigma$),
    \begin{equation}\label{exponential bound, grönwall}
        \begin{split}
            ||u_N(t)||_{H^{\sigma}} & \leq  
\left\lVert u \right\rVert 
_{H^{\sigma}} + \mid \int_0^t  
\left\lVert |\Pi_N u_N(\tau)|^4 \Pi_N u_N(\tau) \right\rVert 
_{H^{\sigma}} d\tau\mid \\
            & \leq  
\left\lVert u \right\rVert 
_{H^{\sigma}} + C \mid \int_0^t  
\left\lVert u_N(\tau) \right\rVert 
_{H^{\sigma}} 
\left\lVert u_N(\tau) \right\rVert 
^4_{W(\mathbb{T})} d\tau \mid 
        \end{split}
    \end{equation}
The crucial point of the proof is that $ 
\left\lVert u_N(\tau) \right\rVert 
_{W(\mathbb{T})}$ is bounded by the $H^1(\mathbb{T})$-norm of the initial data. Indeed, using the mass and Hamiltonian conservation 
\begin{equation*}
    \begin{split}
         
\left\lVert u_N(\tau) \right\rVert 
_{W(\mathbb{T})} & \leq  
\left\lVert u_N(\tau) \right\rVert 
_{H^1(\mathbb{T})} \\
        & \leq ( 
\left\lVert u_N(\tau) \right\rVert 
^2_{\mathbb{L}^2} +  
\left\lVert \partial_xu_N(\tau) \right\rVert 
^2_{\mathbb{L}^2})^{\frac{1}{2}} \\
        & \lesssim \left(  
\left\lVert u_N(\tau) \right\rVert 
^2_{\mathbb{L}^2} + \left(\frac{1}{2} 
\left\lVert \partial_xu_N(\tau) \right\rVert 
^2_{\mathbb{L}^2} + \frac{1}{6} 
\left\lVert u_N(\tau) \right\rVert 
^6_{\mathbb{L}^6}\right) \right)^{\frac{1}{2}} \\
        & \lesssim ( 
\left\lVert u \right\rVert 
^2_{\mathbb{L}^2} + \frac{1}{2} 
\left\lVert \partial_xu_0 \right\rVert 
^2_{\mathbb{L}^2} + \frac{1}{6} 
\left\lVert u \right\rVert 
^6_{\mathbb{L}^6})^{\frac{1}{2}} \\
        & \leq C'_0
     \end{split}   
\end{equation*}
where we can choose $C'_0 \sim (1 +  
\left\lVert u \right\rVert 
_{H^1(\mathbb{T})})^3$, because $H^1(\mathbb{T})$ embeds continuously in $\mathbb{L}^6(\mathbb{T})$. Now, plugging this bound into \eqref{exponential bound, grönwall}, we get 
\begin{equation*}
    ||u_N(t)||_{H^{\sigma}} \leq  
\left\lVert u \right\rVert 
_{H^{\sigma}} + C_0 \mid \int_0^t   
\left\lVert u_N(\tau) \right\rVert 
_{H^{\sigma}} d\tau \mid
\end{equation*}
where we can choose $C_0 \sim (1 +  
\left\lVert u \right\rVert 
_{H^1(\mathbb{T})})^{12}$. Then, applying Gronwall's inequality, we obtain 
\begin{equation*}
    ||u_N(t)||_{H^{\sigma}} \leq  
\left\lVert u \right\rVert 
_{H^{\sigma}} e^{C_0|t|}
\end{equation*}
which is the desired bound.
<!-- end proof-33 -->
<!-- thm-5: body_md -->
For every $u_0 \in H^{\sigma}(\mathbb{T})$, each maximal  solution of \eqref{NLS} and \eqref{truncated equation} is global. In other words,
    \begin{equation*}
        I_{max}(u_0), I_{max,N}(u_0) = +\infty
    \end{equation*}
    for all $N \in \mathbb{N}$.
<!-- end thm-5 -->
<!-- proof-34: body_md -->
The estimates from Proposition~\ref{prop exponential bound} imply that the $H^{\sigma}$-norm of both solutions does not blow up in finite time. Therefore, Corollaries \ref{cor maximal solution NLS} and \ref{cor maximal solution truncated equation} lead to the result.
<!-- end proof-34 -->
<!-- prop-20: body_md -->
\label{appendix prop first approximation prop}
    Let $\sigma \geq 1$. Let $R>0$ and $T>0$. There exists a constant $\Lambda(R,T) > 0$ only depending on $T,R$ and $\sigma$, such that for any $u_0 \in  
    B_{R}^{H^{\sigma}} 
    $,
    \begin{equation*}
        \sup_{|t| \leq T}   
\left\lVert \Phi(t)u_0 \right\rVert_{H^{\sigma}}  
 + \sup_{|t| \leq T}   
\left\lVert \Phi_N(t)u_0 \right\rVert_{H^{\sigma}}  
 \leq \Lambda(R,T), \hspace{0.1cm} \hspace{0.1cm} \forall N \in \mathbb{N}
    \end{equation*}
<!-- end prop-20 -->
<!-- proof-35: body_md -->
This is a consequence of Proposition~\ref{prop exponential bound}. For example we can take 
    \begin{equation*}
        \Lambda(R,T) = R e^{C_{\sigma}(1+R)^{12}T}
    \end{equation*}
    for a certain constant $C_{\sigma}>0$ only depending on $\sigma$.
<!-- end proof-35 -->
<!-- prop-21: body_md -->
\label{prop continuity of the flow}Let $t \in \mathbb{R}$.
For every $N\in \mathbb{N} \cup \{ \infty \}$, the map
    \begin{equation*}
        \begin{split}
            \Phi_N(t) : \hspace{0.1cm} & H^{\sigma}(\mathbb{T}) \longrightarrow H^{\sigma}(\mathbb{T}) \\
                        & u \longmapsto \Phi_N(t)u
        \end{split}
    \end{equation*}
is continuous.
<!-- end prop-21 -->
<!-- proof-36: body_md -->
For better readability, we only provide the proof for $\Phi(t)$.
    Let $u,v \in H^{\sigma}(\mathbb{T})$. Without loss of generality, we can assume that $  
\left\lVert u \right\rVert_{H^{\sigma}}  
 \leq R $ and $  
\left\lVert v \right\rVert_{H^{\sigma}}  
 \leq R$ for some $R>0$. We invoke $\Lambda(R,t)>0$ from the Proposition~\ref{appendix prop first approximation prop}. Firstly, using the Duhamel formula and passing to the $H^{\sigma}(\mathbb{T})$-norm we get that for all $s \leq t$
    \begin{equation*}
          
\left\lVert \Phi(s)v - \Phi(s)u \right\rVert_{H^{\sigma}}  
 \leq   
\left\lVert v-u \right\rVert_{H^{\sigma}}  
 + C \Lambda(R,t)^4 \mid \int_0^s   
\left\lVert \Phi(\tau)v - \Phi(\tau)u \right\rVert_{H^{\sigma}}  
d\tau \mid
    \end{equation*}
    Secondly, the Gronwall's inequality yields 
    \begin{equation*}
          
\left\lVert \Phi(t)v - \Phi(t)u \right\rVert_{H^{\sigma}}  
 \leq   
\left\lVert v-u \right\rVert_{H^{\sigma}}  
 e^{C \Lambda(R,t)^4 |t|}
    \end{equation*}
    In particular,
    \begin{equation*}
          
\left\lVert \Phi(t)v - \Phi(t)u \right\rVert_{H^{\sigma}}  
  
\underset{v \rightarrow u}{\longrightarrow} 
 0
    \end{equation*}
<!-- end proof-36 -->
<!-- prop-22: body_md -->
\label{prop bicontinuity of the flow}
    For every $N\in \mathbb{N} \cup \{ \infty \}$, the map
    \begin{equation*}
        \begin{split}
            \Phi_N : \hspace{0.1cm} \mathbb{R} &\times H^{\sigma}(\mathbb{T}) \longrightarrow H^{\sigma}(\mathbb{T}) \\
             & (t,u) \longmapsto \Phi_N(t)u
        \end{split}
    \end{equation*}
    is continuous.
<!-- end prop-22 -->
<!-- proof-37: body_md -->
For better readability, we only provide the proof for $\Phi$.
We fix $t \in \mathbb{R}$ and $u \in H^{\sigma}(\mathbb{T})$ and we show that 
\begin{equation*}
      
\left\lVert \Phi(t+h)(u+\delta u) - \Phi(t)u \right\rVert_{H^{\sigma}}  
 \longrightarrow 0, \hspace{0.5cm} \text{as $h \rightarrow 0 $ and $\delta u \rightarrow 0$}
\end{equation*}
We denote $F(\tau,v) := |\Phi(\tau)v|^4\Phi(\tau)v$. Let us compute the difference $\Phi(t+h)(u+\delta u) - \Phi(t)u$ using the Duhamel formula. 
\begin{equation*}
    \begin{split}
        &\Phi(t+h)(u+\delta u) - \Phi(t)u  =  \Bigl(\Phi(t+h)(u+\delta u) - \Phi(t+h)u\Bigr) + \Bigl(\Phi(t+h)u -\Phi(t)u\Bigr)\\
    & = e^{i(t+h)\partial_x^2} \delta u - i \int_0^{t+h} e^{i(t+h-\tau)\partial_x^2}(F(\tau,u+\delta u)-F(\tau,u)) d\tau \\
   & + e^{it\partial_x^2}(e^{ih\partial_x^2}-1)u -i \int_0^{t+h} e^{i(t+h-\tau)\partial_x^2} F(\tau,u) d\tau + i \int_0^t e^{i(t-\tau)\partial_x^2} F(\tau,u) d\tau \\
   & = e^{i(t+h)\partial_x^2} \delta u  + e^{it\partial_x^2}(e^{ih\partial_x^2} -1)u - i \int_0^{t+h} e^{i(t+h-\tau)\partial_x^2}(F(\tau,u+\delta u)-F(\tau,u)) d\tau \\
   & -i \int_t^{t+h} e^{i(t+h-\tau)\partial_x^2} F(\tau,u) d\tau  -i \int_0^{t} e^{i(t-\tau)\partial_x^2}(e^{ih\partial_x^2}-1) F(\tau,u) d\tau
    \end{split}
\end{equation*}

Furthermore, without loss of generality we can assume that $t+h \leq t+1 =: T$ and $  
\left\lVert u+\delta u \right\rVert_{H^{\sigma}}  
 \leq   
\left\lVert u \right\rVert_{H^{\sigma}}  
+1 =: R$. Now, we invoke $\Lambda(R,T)>0$ from Proposition~\ref{appendix prop first approximation prop}. Passing to the $H^{\sigma}(\mathbb{T})$-norm in the above formula we have 
\begin{equation*}
    \begin{split}
           
\left\lVert \Phi(t+h)(u+\delta u) - \Phi(t)u \right\rVert_{H^{\sigma}}  
 & \leq   
\left\lVert \delta u \right\rVert_{H^{\sigma}}  
 +   
\left\lVert (e^{ih\partial_x^2}-1)u \right\rVert_{H^{\sigma}}  
 \\
        & + C \Lambda(R,T)^4 \mid \int_0^T   
\left\lVert \Phi(\tau)(u+\delta u)- \Phi(\tau)u \right\rVert_{H^{\sigma}}  
 d\tau \mid \\
        & + |h| \Lambda(R,T)^5 + \mid \int_0^t   
\left\lVert (e^{ih\partial_x^2}-1)F(\tau,u) \right\rVert_{H^{\sigma}}  
 d\tau \mid 
    \end{split}
\end{equation*}
Using the continuity of $v \longmapsto \Phi(\tau)v$ (Proposition~\ref{prop continuity of the flow}) and the dominated convergence theorem, we deduce that the right hand side tends to $0$ as $h \rightarrow 0 $ and $\delta u \rightarrow 0$. So the proof of Proposition~\ref{prop bicontinuity of the flow} is complete.
<!-- end proof-37 -->
<!-- prop-23: body_md -->
\label{appendix second approximation prop}
    Let $\sigma \geq 1$. Let $K$ be a compact subset of $H^{\sigma}(\mathbb{T})$ and $T>0$. Then, uniformly in $|t| \leq T$ and $u_0 \in K$,
    \begin{equation*}
         \lim_{N \rightarrow +\infty}   
\left\lVert \Phi(t)u_0-\Phi_N(t)u_0 \right\rVert_{H^{\sigma}}  
 = 0,
    \end{equation*}
In other words,
\begin{equation*}
    \sup_{|t|\leq T} \hspace{0.1cm} \sup_{u_0 \in K} \hspace{0.1cm}   
\left\lVert \Phi(t)u_0-\Phi_N(t)u_0 \right\rVert_{H^{\sigma}}  
  
\underset{N \rightarrow +\infty}{\longrightarrow} 
 0  
\end{equation*}
<!-- end prop-23 -->
<!-- proof-38: body_md -->
First, from the compactness of $K$, we invoke $R>0$ such that $K \subset  
    B_{R}^{H^{\sigma}} 
    $, where $ 
    B_{R}^{H^{\sigma}} 
    $ is the closed centered ball of radius $R$ in $H^{\sigma}(\mathbb{T})$. We then invoke $\Lambda(R,T)>0$ from Proposition~\ref{appendix prop first approximation prop}. Now, we set $R_1 := 1 + 2\Lambda(R,T)$ and invoke $\delta = \delta(R_1) > 0$ the local existence time associated to $R_1$ from the local theory (Theorem~\ref{thm local wellposedness}). These parameters ensure that for every $N \in \mathbb{N} \cup \{ \infty\}$ and $u_0 \in  
    B_{R}^{H^{\sigma}} 
    $, the Duhamel map,
\begin{equation*}
        \begin{split}
           \Gamma_N :  \hspace{0.1cm} & 
  \overline{B} 
  _{R_1}(\delta)  \longrightarrow  
  \overline{B} 
  _{R_1}(\delta) \\
            & u \longmapsto e^{it\partial_x^2}u_0 - i \int_{0}^t e^{i(t -\tau)\partial_x^2}\Pi_N (|\Pi_N u(\tau)|^4 \Pi_N u(\tau)) d\tau
        \end{split}
    \end{equation*}
is a contraction, with a universal contraction coefficient $0<\gamma<1$ (for example $\gamma = \frac{2}{3}$ as in the proof of Theorem~\ref{thm local wellposedness}), where $ 
  \overline{B} 
  _{R_1}(\delta)$ is the closed centered ball in $\mathcal C([-\delta,\delta],H^{\sigma}(\mathbb{T}))$ of radius $R_1$. \\

\underline{Step 1: Local-time convergence}  \\

Firstly, we prove the local property
\begin{equation}\label{local approximation estimate}
    \sup_{|t|\leq \delta} \hspace{0.1cm} \sup_{u_0 \in K} \hspace{0.1cm}   
\left\lVert \Phi(t)u_0-\Phi_N(t)u_0 \right\rVert_{H^{\sigma}}  
  
\underset{N \rightarrow +\infty}{\longrightarrow} 
 0
\end{equation}
Let $u_0 \in  
    B_{R}^{H^{\sigma}} 
    $. We denote $u(t) = \Phi(t)u_0 $ and $u_N(t) = \Phi_N(t)u_0$. Since $u$ and $u_N$ are respectively the fixed point of $\Gamma_{\infty}$ and $\Gamma_N$, we have
\begin{equation*}
    \begin{split}
         
\left\lVert u -u_N \right\rVert 
_{ 
  \overline{B} 
  _{R_1}(\delta)} & =  
\left\lVert \Gamma_{\infty}u - \Gamma_N u_N \right\rVert 
_{ 
  \overline{B} 
  _{R_1} (\delta)} \\
        & \leq  
\left\lVert \Gamma_{\infty}u - \Gamma_N u \right\rVert 
_{ 
  \overline{B} 
  _{R_1}(\delta)} +  
\left\lVert \Gamma_N u - \Gamma_N u_N \right\rVert 
_{ 
  \overline{B} 
  _{R_1}(\delta)} \\
        & \leq  
\left\lVert \Gamma_{\infty}u - \Gamma_N u \right\rVert 
_{ 
  \overline{B} 
  _{R_1}(\delta)} + \gamma  
\left\lVert u -u_N \right\rVert 
_{ 
  \overline{B} 
  _{R_1}(\delta)}
    \end{split}
\end{equation*}
Therefore,
\begin{equation*}
     
\left\lVert u -u_N \right\rVert 
_{ 
  \overline{B} 
  _{R_1}(\delta)} \leq \frac{1}{1-\gamma}  
\left\lVert \Gamma_{\infty}u - \Gamma_N u \right\rVert 
_{ 
  \overline{B} 
  _{R_1}(\delta)}
\end{equation*}
Hence, to prove \eqref{local approximation estimate}, it suffices to show that
\begin{equation*}
    \sup_{u_0 \in K}  
\left\lVert \Gamma_{\infty}u - \Gamma_N u \right\rVert 
_{ 
  \overline{B} 
  _{R_1}(\delta)}  
\underset{N \rightarrow +\infty}{\longrightarrow} 
 0
\end{equation*}
Next, for every $|t|\leq \delta$ we have,
\begin{equation*}
    \begin{split}
         & \Gamma_{\infty}u(t) - \Gamma_N u(t) = -i \int_0^t e^{i(t-\tau)\partial_x^2}(|u(\tau)|^4u(\tau) - \Pi_N(|\Pi_Nu(\tau)|^4\Pi_Nu(\tau)))d\tau \\
         & = -i \int_0^t e^{i(t-\tau)\partial_x^2}\Pi_N^{\perp}(|u(\tau)|^4u(\tau))d\tau -i \int_0^t e^{i(t-\tau)\partial_x^2}\Pi_N(|u(\tau)|^4u(\tau) - 
         |\Pi_Nu(\tau)|^4\Pi_Nu(\tau))d\tau
    \end{split}
\end{equation*}
So passing to the sup norm we get,
\begin{equation*}
    \begin{split}
         
\left\lVert \Gamma_{\infty}u - \Gamma_N u \right\rVert 
_{ 
  \overline{B} 
  _{R_1}(\delta)} & \leq  \delta  \hspace{0.1cm} \sup_{|\tau|\leq \delta}   
\left\lVert \Pi_N^{\perp}(|u(\tau)|^4u(\tau)) \right\rVert_{H^{\sigma}}  
 \\
        & + C \delta \hspace{0.1cm} \sup_{|\tau| \leq \delta}   
\left\lVert u(\tau)- \Pi_N u(\tau) \right\rVert_{H^{\sigma}}  
(  
\left\lVert u(\tau) \right\rVert_{H^{\sigma}}  
^4+   
\left\lVert \Pi_N u(\tau) \right\rVert_{H^{\sigma}}  
^4) \\
        & \leq C \delta(\sup_{|\tau|\leq \delta}   
\left\lVert \Pi_N^{\perp}(|u(\tau)|^4u(\tau)) \right\rVert_{H^{\sigma}}  
 + \sup_{|\tau|\leq \delta}  
\left\lVert \Pi_N^{\perp}u(\tau) \right\rVert_{H^{\sigma}}  
 \Lambda(R,T)^4 )
    \end{split}
\end{equation*}
Taking the supremum over $u_0 \in K$ we then obtain,
\begin{equation}\label{estimate sup over t and K}
    \begin{split}
         \sup_{u_0 \in K} &  
\left\lVert \Gamma_{\infty}u - \Gamma_N u \right\rVert 
_{ 
  \overline{B} 
  _{R_1}(\delta)} \\ 
        & \leq C\delta (\sup_{u_0 \in K} \sup_{|\tau|\leq \delta}   
\left\lVert \Pi_N^{\perp}(|u(\tau)|^4u(\tau)) \right\rVert_{H^{\sigma}}  
 + \Lambda(R,T)^4 \sup_{u_0 \in K}  \sup_{|\tau|\leq \delta}   
\left\lVert \Pi_N^{\perp}u(\tau) \right\rVert_{H^{\sigma}}  
 )
  \end{split}
\end{equation}
Besides, based on a classical result in functional analysis (see Lemma~\ref{lem cvgce on compact set of bdd lin map}), $\Pi_N^{\perp}$ satisfies the key property of converging uniformly to $0$ on compact sets as $N \rightarrow + \infty$. At the same time, the two following sets 
\begin{align*}
    K_1 :&= \{\Phi(\tau)u_0 : \hspace{0.1cm} u_0 \in K, \hspace{0.1cm} |\tau|\leq \delta \},  &  K_2:&= \{|\Phi(\tau)u_0|^4\Phi(\tau)u_0 : \hspace{0.1cm} u_0 \in K, \hspace{0.1cm} |\tau|\leq \delta \}
\end{align*}
are compacts in $H^{\sigma}(\mathbb{T})$. Indeed, it results from the facts that the map 
\begin{equation*}
    \begin{split}
         & \mathbb{R} \times H^{\sigma}(\mathbb{T}) \longrightarrow H^{\sigma}(\mathbb{T}) \\
                    & (t,u_0) \longmapsto \Phi(t)u_0
    \end{split} 
\end{equation*}
and the map
\begin{equation*}
    \begin{split}
        & H^{\sigma}(\mathbb{T})^5 \longrightarrow H^{\sigma}(\mathbb{T}) \\
         (u_1,u_2&,u_3,u_4,u_5) \longmapsto u_1  
  \overline{u_2} 
   u_3  
  \overline{u_4} 
   u_5
    \end{split}
\end{equation*}
are continuous and the fact that the image of a compact set under a continuous map is compact. Now, rewriting \eqref{estimate sup over t and K} we get
\begin{equation*}
    \begin{split}
         \sup_{u_0 \in K}  
\left\lVert \Gamma_{\infty}u -\Gamma_N u \right\rVert 
_{ 
  \overline{B} 
  _{R_1}(\delta)} & \leq C\delta (\sup_{w_2 \in K_2} \Pi_N^{\perp} w_2 + \Lambda(R,T)^4 \sup_{w_1 \in K_1} \Pi_N^{\perp} w_1) \\
         &  
\underset{N \rightarrow \infty}{\longrightarrow} 
 0
    \end{split}
\end{equation*}
And this implies the desired local property \eqref{local approximation estimate}. \\

\underline{Step 2: Long-time convergence} \\

Secondly, we complete the proof of Proposition~\ref{appendix second approximation prop} by iterating this local argument. Let $m := \lfloor \frac{T}{\delta}\rfloor + 1$, and for any integer $|k| \leq m$, let $I_k := [k\delta-\delta,k\delta+\delta]$. We show that for any $|k| \leq$ m,
\begin{equation}\label{local approximation propagated}
    \sup_{t \in I_k} \hspace{0.1cm} \sup_{u_0 \in K} \hspace{0.1cm}   
\left\lVert \Phi(t)u_0-\Phi_N(t)u_0 \right\rVert_{H^{\sigma}}  
  
\underset{N \rightarrow +\infty}{\longrightarrow} 
 0  
\end{equation}
If we do so, the proof of Proposition~\ref{appendix second approximation prop} will be completed. At this stage, we know that \eqref{local approximation propagated} is true when $k=0$. Now, we assume that \eqref{local approximation propagated} is true for some integer $|k|\leq m-1$ and we show that \eqref{local approximation propagated} is still true for every integer $|k'| = |k|+1$. Also, without loss of generality, we assume that $k \geq 0$ and $k'=k+1$. The crucial point here is that since we chose $R_1 = 1 + 2\Lambda(R,T)$, we have that for every $N \in \mathbb{N} \cup \{ \infty\}$ and $u_0 \in  
    B_{R}^{H^{\sigma}} 
    $, the Duhamel map
\begin{equation*}
        \begin{split}
           \Gamma_N :  \hspace{0.1cm} & 
  \overline{B} 
  _{R_1}^{(k)}(\delta)  \longrightarrow  
  \overline{B} 
  ^{k}_{R_1}(\delta) \\
            & u \longmapsto e^{i(t-t_{k})\partial_x^2}u_N(t_k) - i \int_{t_{k}}^t e^{i(t -\tau)\partial_x^2}\Pi_N (|\Pi_N u(\tau)|^4 \Pi_N u(\tau)) d\tau
        \end{split}
    \end{equation*}
is a contraction with a universal contraction coefficient $0<\gamma<1$, where $t_{k}:= k \delta$, $u_{\infty}(t_k):=u(t_{k})$, and $ 
  \overline{B} 
  _{R_1}^{(k)}(\delta)$ is the closed centered ball in $\mathcal C([t_k-\delta,t_k+\delta],H^{\sigma}(\mathbb{T}))$ of radius $R_1$. \\

Now, doing the same calculations as in the first step of the proof we obtain,
\begin{equation*}
     
\left\lVert u -u_N \right\rVert 
_{ 
  \overline{B} 
  ^{(k)}_{R_1}(\delta)} \leq \frac{1}{1-\gamma}  
\left\lVert \Gamma_{\infty}u - \Gamma_N u \right\rVert 
_{ 
  \overline{B} 
  ^{(k)}_{R_1}(\delta)}
\end{equation*}
and, 
\begin{equation*}
    \begin{split}
         \sup_{u_0 \in K} &  
\left\lVert \Gamma_{\infty}u - \Gamma_N u \right\rVert 
_{ 
  \overline{B} 
  ^{(k)}_{R_1}(\delta)} \leq \sup_{u_0 \in K} \sup_{t \in I_k}   
\left\lVert e^{i(t-t_k)\partial_x^2}(u(t_k)-u_N(t_k)) \right\rVert_{H^{\sigma}}  
 \\
        & + C\delta (\sup_{u_0 \in K} \sup_{\tau \in I_k}   
\left\lVert \Pi_N^{\perp}(|u(\tau)|^4u(\tau)) \right\rVert_{H^{\sigma}}  
 + \Lambda(R,T)^4 \sup_{u_0 \in K}  \sup_{\tau \in I_k}   
\left\lVert \Pi_N^{\perp}u(\tau) \right\rVert_{H^{\sigma}}  
 )
  \end{split}
\end{equation*}
On the right hand side, the first term : 
\begin{equation*}
    \sup_{u_0 \in K} \sup_{t \in I_k}   
\left\lVert e^{i(t-t_k)\partial_x^2}(u(t_k)-u_N(t_k)) \right\rVert_{H^{\sigma}}  
 = \sup_{u_0 \in K}   
\left\lVert u(t_k)-u_N(t_k) \right\rVert_{H^{\sigma}}  

\end{equation*}
tends to $0$ as $N \longrightarrow +\infty$ by our assumption. And, we handle the remaining term in the same way as in the first part of the proof. Finally \eqref{local approximation propagated} is true for all $|k|\leq m$, so the proof of Proposition~\ref{appendix second approximation prop} is completed.
<!-- end proof-38 -->
<!-- cor-6: body_md -->
\label{appendix set approximation}
    Let $\sigma \geq 1$, $T>0$ and let $K$ be a compact subset of $H^{\sigma}(\mathbb{T})$. Then, 
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item for any $\varepsilon > 0$, there exists $N_0 \in \mathbb{N}$ such that for all $N\geq N_0$
    \begin{equation*}
        \Phi_N(t)(K) \subset \Phi(t)(K) +  
    B_{\varepsilon}^{H^{\sigma}} 
    
    \end{equation*}
    for all $|t| \leq T$.
    \item for any $\varepsilon > 0$, there exists $N_1 \in \mathbb{N}$ such that for all $N\geq N_1$
    \begin{equation*}
        \Phi(t)(K) \subset \Phi_N(t)(K +  
    B_{\varepsilon}^{H^{\sigma}} 
    )
    \end{equation*}
    for all $|t| \leq T$.
    \end{enumerate}
<!-- end cor-6 -->
<!-- proof-39: body_md -->
Let $\varepsilon >0$.
    \begin{itemize}
        \item For the first point, we take $u_0 \in K$ and we write 
        \begin{equation}\label{phiN = phi + (phiN - phi)}
            \Phi_N(t)u_0 = \Phi(t)u_0 + \left( \Phi_N(t)u_0 - \Phi(t)u_0 \right)
        \end{equation}
        From Proposition \ref{appendix second approximation prop}, there exists $N_0 \in \mathbb{N}$ such that for all $N \geq N_0$ 
        \begin{equation*}
           \sup_{|t| \leq T} \sup_{v_0 \in K}   
\left\lVert \Phi_N(t)v_0 - \Phi(t)v_0 \right\rVert_{H^{\sigma}}  
 \leq \varepsilon
        \end{equation*}
        Thus, for all $N \geq N_0$, $\Phi_N(t)u_0 - \Phi(t)u_0 \in  
    B_{\varepsilon}^{H^{\sigma}} 
    $ for all $|t|\leq T$ and all $u_0 \in K$. Coming back to \eqref{phiN = phi + (phiN - phi)}, it implies that for all $N \geq N_0$
        \begin{equation*}
            \Phi_N(t)u_0 \in \Phi(t)(K) +  
    B_{\varepsilon}^{H^{\sigma}} 
    
        \end{equation*}
        for all $u_0 \in K$ and all $|t|\leq T$.
        \item The second point is a consequence of the first one. Let $|t|\leq T$. From the continuity of the map $\Phi(t)$ (see Proposition \ref{prop continuity of the flow}) we have that $\Phi(t)(K)$ is a compact subset of $H^{\sigma}(\mathbb{T})$. So from the first point there exists $N_1 \in \mathbb{N}$ such that for all $N\geq N_1$ 
        \begin{equation*}
            \Phi_N(-\tau)\left(\Phi(t)(K) \right) \subset \Phi(-\tau)\Phi(t)(K) +  
    B_{\varepsilon}^{H^{\sigma}} 
     
        \end{equation*}
        for all $|\tau| \leq T$. In particular, for $\tau = t$ we have :
        \begin{equation*}
            \Phi_N(-t)\left(\Phi(t)(K) \right) \subset \Phi(-t)\Phi(t)(K) +  
    B_{\varepsilon}^{H^{\sigma}} 
     = K +  
    B_{\varepsilon}^{H^{\sigma}} 
    
        \end{equation*}
        Applying $\Phi_N(t)$ to this we obtain 
        \begin{equation*}
            \Phi(t)(K) \subset \Phi_N(t) \left(  K +  
    B_{\varepsilon}^{H^{\sigma}} 
     \right)
        \end{equation*}
    \end{itemize}
    This concludes the proof of Corollary \ref{appendix set approximation}.
<!-- end proof-39 -->
<!-- prop-24: body_md -->
\label{structure of the truncated flow}
\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=0cm] We have the following properties ;
      \item The truncated flow $\Phi_N(t)$ commute with the frequency projector $\Pi_N$, that is
    \begin{equation*}
     \Phi_N(t) \circ \Pi_N = \Pi_N \circ \Phi_N(t)
     \end{equation*}
    As a consequence, the truncated flow $\Phi_N(t)$ maps the finite-dimensional space $E_N$ to itself. Moreover, the induced map 
    \begin{equation*}
        \begin{split}
        \widetilde{\Phi}_N(t) : \hspace{0.1cm} & E_N \longrightarrow E_N \\
                          & u_0 \longmapsto \Phi_N(t)(u_0)
        \end{split}
    \end{equation*}
    is the flow of the ODE
    \begin{equation}\label{FNLS}
    \begin{cases}
        i\partial_t u + \partial_x^2 u = \Pi_N \left(|u|^4u \right) \\
        u|_{t=0} = u_0 \in E_N
    \end{cases}
    \tag{FNLS}
\end{equation}
which can be seen as the finite-dimensional Hamiltonian equation on $E_N$ : 
\begin{equation*}
    \begin{cases}
        i\partial_t u = \frac{\partial H_N}{\partial  
  \overline{u} 
  }(u) \\
        u|_{t=0} = u_0 \in E_N
    \end{cases}
\end{equation*}
with Hamiltonian $H_N(u) := \frac{1}{2}  
\left\lVert \partial_x^2u \right\rVert 
^2_{\mathbb{L}^2(\mathbb{T})} + \frac{1}{6}  
\left\lVert u \right\rVert 
_{\mathbb{L}^6(\mathbb{T})}^6$, for $u \in E_N$.


\item The truncated flow $\Phi_N(t)$ commute with $\Pi_N^{\perp}$, that is
    \begin{equation*}
     \Phi_N(t) \circ \Pi_N^{\perp} = \Pi_N^{\perp} \circ \Phi_N(t)
     \end{equation*}
    As a consequence, the truncated flow $\Phi_N(t)$ maps the space $E_N^{\perp}$ to itself. Moreover, the induced map 
    \begin{equation*}
        \begin{split}
        \Phi^{\perp}_N(t) : \hspace{0.1cm} & E_N^{\perp} \longrightarrow E_N^{\perp} \\
                          & u_0 \longmapsto \Phi_N(t)(u_0)
        \end{split}
    \end{equation*}
    is the solution of the linear Schrödinger equation 
\begin{equation*}
    \begin{cases}
        i\partial_t u + \partial_x^2 u = 0 \\
        u|_{t=0} = u_0 \in E_N^{\perp}
    \end{cases}
\end{equation*}
Hence, $\Phi^{\perp}_N(t)$ coincide with the linear operator $e^{it\partial_x^2}$ on $E_N^{\perp}$.

\item  The truncated flow $\Phi_N(t)$ can be factorized as $(\widetilde{\Phi}_N(t),e^{it\partial_x^2})$ on $E_N \times E_N^{\perp}$. In other words, for every $u_0 \in H^{\sigma}(\mathbb{T})$,
 \begin{equation*}
     \Phi_N(t)(u_0) = \widetilde{\Phi}_N(t) \Pi_N u_0  +  e^{it\partial_x^2} \Pi_N^{\perp}u_0
 \end{equation*}
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end prop-24 -->
<!-- proof-40: body_md -->
Let $u_0 \in L^2(\mathbb{T})$.
    \begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=0cm]
        \item \textbullet \hspace{0.1cm} $\Phi_N(t)$ is the flow of \eqref{truncated equation}. And, when we apply $\Pi_N$ to equation \eqref{truncated equation}, we see that $\Pi_N \Phi_N(t) u_0$ is the solution of the equation 
        \begin{equation*}
            \begin{cases}
                 i\partial_t u + \partial_x^2 u  = \Pi_N \left(|\Pi_Nu|^4\Pi_Nu \right) =\Pi_N \left(|u|^4u \right) \\
                 u|_{t=0} = \Pi_N u_0 
            \end{cases}
        \end{equation*}
        On the other hand, from the definition of the flow of \eqref{truncated equation}, the solution of the equation above is none other than $\Phi_N(t)\Pi_N u_0$ itself. This means that 
        \begin{equation*}
            \Pi_N \Phi_N(t) u_0=\Phi_N(t)\Pi_N u_0
        \end{equation*}
\textbullet \hspace{0.1cm} Next, we show that \eqref{FNLS} can be seen as a finite-dimensional Hamiltonian equation on $E_N$. Every element $u \in E_N$ can be decompose as 
\begin{equation*}
    u = v + i w
\end{equation*}
where 
\begin{equation*}
    \begin{split}
        v &= \sum_{|k|\leq N} \textnormal{Re}(u_k)e^{ikx} =: \sum_{|k|\leq N} v_ke^{ikx} \in E_N \\
        w &= \sum_{|k|\leq N}\textnormal{Im}(u_k) e^{ikx} =: \sum_{|k|\leq N} w_ke^{ikx} \in E_N
    \end{split}
\end{equation*}
Furthermore, we invoke the operators 
\begin{equation*}
    \begin{split}
    &  \frac{\partial}{\partial  
  \overline{u} 
  _k} := \frac{\partial}{\partial v_k} + i \frac{\partial}{\partial w_k} \\
    & \frac{\partial}{\partial  
  \overline{u} 
  } := \frac{\partial}{\partial v} + i \frac{\partial}{\partial w} =:  \sum_{|k|\leq N}  e^{ikx}  \frac{\partial}{\partial v_k} + i \sum_{|k|\leq N}  e^{ikx}  \frac{\partial}{\partial w_k}
    \end{split}
\end{equation*}
and also the function 
\begin{equation*}
    \begin{split}
         H_N : \hspace{0.1cm} & E_N \longrightarrow \mathbb{R} \\
            & u \longmapsto \frac{1}{2}  
\left\lVert \partial_x^2u \right\rVert 
^2_{\mathbb{L}^2(\mathbb{T})} + \frac{1}{6}  
\left\lVert u \right\rVert 
_{\mathbb{L}^6(\mathbb{T})}^6
    \end{split}
\end{equation*} 
By performing elementary computations, we see that we can rewrite \eqref{FNLS} as 
\begin{equation*}
        \begin{cases}
        i\partial_t u= \frac{\partial H_N}{\partial  
  \overline{u} 
  }(u) \\
        u|_{t=0} = u_0 
    \end{cases}
    \tag{FNLS}
\end{equation*}
This means that \eqref{FNLS} is an Hamiltonian equation on $E_N$ with associated Hamiltonian $H_N$.

\bigskip

        \item Once again, applying $\Pi_N^{\perp}$ to equation \eqref{truncated equation}, we see that $\Pi_N^{\perp} \Phi_N(t)u_0$ is the solution of the equation 
        \begin{equation*}
            \begin{cases}
                i\partial_t u + \partial_x^2 u = 0 \\
        u|_{t=0} = \Pi_N^{\perp} u_0 
            \end{cases}
        \end{equation*}
        This means that 
        \begin{equation}\label{free Schro on hf}
            \Pi_N^{\perp} \Phi_N(t)u_0 = e^{it\partial_x^2}\Pi_N^{\perp}u_0
        \end{equation}
        Furthermore, $\Pi_N \Phi_N(t) \Pi_N^{\perp}u_0$ is the solution of the equation 
        \begin{equation*}
            \begin{cases}
                 i\partial_t u + \partial_x^2 u  = \Pi_N \left(|\Pi_Nu|^4\Pi_Nu \right) \\
                 u|_{t=0} = 0
            \end{cases}
        \end{equation*}
        Thus, $\Pi_N \Phi_N(t) \Pi_N^{\perp}u_0$ is none other than $0$, and we obtain from \eqref{free Schro on hf} that
        \begin{equation*}
            \Phi_N(t) \Pi_N^{\perp}u_0 = \Pi_N^{\perp} \Phi_N(t) \Pi_N^{\perp}u_0 = e^{it\partial_x^2}\Pi_N^{\perp}u_0 = \Pi_N^{\perp} \Phi_N(t)u_0
        \end{equation*}
        \item As a consequence of the two previous points, we can write 
        \begin{equation*}
            \begin{split}
                \Phi_N(t)u_0 &= \Pi_N \Phi_N(t)u_0 + \Pi_N^{\perp}\Phi_N(t)u_0 \\
                & = \Phi_N(t)\Pi_N u_0 + \Phi_N(t)\Pi_N^{\perp}u_0 \\
                & = \underbrace{\widetilde{\Phi}_N(t) \Pi_N u_0}_{\in E_N} + \underbrace{e^{it\partial_x^2} \Pi_N^{\perp}u_0}_{\in E_N^{\perp}}
            \end{split}
        \end{equation*}
    \end{enumerate}
